agent_reasoning:
The bug-introducing commit (netrc parser rewrite) added logic to fill in a blank password when a login was found without one, but didn't handle the case where parsing succeeds via a 'default' stanza that provides neither login nor password. That case fell through to the generic "success" path, returning NETRC_SUCCESS despite carrying no real credential information. This retcode is used by lib/url.c's override_login() to mark the connection as netrc-authenticated, which relaxes redirect protections in the HTTP layer, allowing credential leakage across hosts.

The fix restructures the post-loop retcode handling in lib/netrc.c to add an else-if branch: when there is no password and no login (the 'default with no credentials' case), retcode is set to NETRC_FILE_MISSING instead of remaining as success. This preserves the existing blank-password-fill behavior for the "login found but no password" case, while correctly reporting failure when nothing was actually found.

I applied this as a direct edit to lib/netrc.c's `out:` block, converting the single `if(!retcode && !password && our_login)` check into a nested `if(!retcode) { if(...) ... else if(!login && !password) retcode = NETRC_FILE_MISSING; }` structure, matching the fix commit exactly. No other files needed changes since the vulnerability's exploitation path (lib/url.c, lib/http.c) already correctly relies on the retcode value returned by parsenetrc(); only the retcode computation itself was wrong.
commit_message:
netrc: address several netrc parser flaws

- make sure that a match that returns a username also returns a
  password, that should be blank if no password is found

- fix handling of multiple logins for same host where the password/login
  order might be reversed.

- reject credentials provided in the .netrc if they contain ASCII control
  codes - if the used protocol does not support such (like HTTP and WS do)

Reported-by: Harry Sintonen

Add test 478, 479 and 480 to verify. Updated unit 1304.

Closes #15586

findings.message: parsenetrc() (in lib/netrc.c) treats a matching '.netrc' 'default' stanza as a successful lookup (retcode = NETRC_SUCCESS) even when that stanza specifies neither a 'login' nor a 'password' token. At the function's 'out:' label, the block `if(!retcode && !password && our_login) { password = strdup(""); ... }` only guards against a missing *password* by substituting an empty string; it never checks whether *login* was also never found. As a result, when the 'default' entry supplies no credentials at all, parsenetrc() still returns NETRC_SUCCESS while leaving the caller's existing *loginp/*passwordp values untouched (since !specific_login they are simply reassigned to whatever `login`/`password` already held, effectively the caller-supplied values from a previous host lookup). In lib/url.c's override_login(), a NETRC_SUCCESS return sets conn->bits.netrc = TRUE, which lib/http.c's Curl_http_output_auth() and Curl_auth_allowed_to_host() treat as an explicit signal that it is 'safe' to resend Authorization credentials even after following a redirect (Location:) to a different host, bypassing the normal same-host check. Consequently, when a user has a netrc 'default' entry with no login/password and follows an HTTP redirect (e.g. through a reused/keep-alive proxy connection, or any path where the pre-existing user/password value is retained), the credentials obtained for the first host are wrongly re-sent (leaked) to the second, unrelated host.
findings.suggestion: Treat a matched 'default' (or 'machine') stanza that yields neither a login nor a password as 'not found' rather than a successful match, so the caller does not mistakenly mark the connection as netrc-authenticated and bypass the same-host credential-reuse protection. Explicitly check for the no-login-and-no-password case and return NETRC_FILE_MISSING in that situation instead of NETRC_SUCCESS.
findings.title: .netrc 'default' entry without login/password is treated as a successful credential match

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability is a thread-safety (data race) bug: `ldap_set_option(NULL, ...)` in the OpenLDAP code path sets TLS options (LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_CACERTFILE, LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_REQUIRE_CERT) on the global OpenLDAP context rather than on a per-connection handle. In a multi-threaded application using libcurl, this means TLS configuration from one transfer (e.g., disabling certificate verification, or setting a specific CA file) could silently propagate to concurrent LDAPS transfers in other threads. The root cause was that `ldap_init()` was called *after* the TLS option calls, so no valid per-connection handle existed yet and NULL was used as a workaround. The on-disk code fixes this by calling `ldap_init()` (or `ldap_sslinit()` on WIN32) before any `ldap_set_option()` calls, then passing the returned handle to all subsequent option-setting calls, ensuring all options are scoped to the specific connection being established.

pr_description:
This change restructures the LDAP connection setup so that `ldap_init()` (or `ldap_sslinit()` on Windows) is called before any `ldap_set_option()` calls. Previously, options such as `LDAP_OPT_NETWORK_TIMEOUT`, `LDAP_OPT_PROTOCOL_VERSION`, `LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_CACERTFILE`, and `LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_REQUIRE_CERT` were set with a `NULL` connection handle, which in the OpenLDAP API designates the global default context.

The new approach:
- Calls `ldap_sslinit()` (WIN32 SSL) or `ldap_init()` (all other paths, except Novell SSL which uses `ldapssl_init()` and initializes its own handle) upfront, before any option-setting code.
- Passes the per-connection handle (`server`) to all subsequent `ldap_set_option()` calls, ensuring options are scoped to that connection only.
- Removes the now-redundant `ldap_init()` call that was previously placed after the TLS option setup in the OpenLDAP path.
- Removes the `ldap_start_tls_s()` call that was unreachable/unnecessary in this flow.
- Adjusts the non-SSL else branch to only perform `ldap_init()` for the Novell SDK path, which requires separate initialization sequencing.

This eliminates a class of connection setup errors and improves clarity around when each SDK's connection handle is first made available.

findings.message: In lib/ldap.c, the function ldap_do() calls ldap_set_option() with NULL as the first argument for several TLS-critical options (LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_REQUIRE_CERT, LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_CACERTFILE, LDAP_OPT_NETWORK_TIMEOUT, LDAP_OPT_PROTOCOL_VERSION). Passing NULL to ldap_set_option() sets the option on the global/default LDAP context rather than a per-connection handle. In a multi-threaded environment this is a data race: when one thread configures LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_REQUIRE_CERT to LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_NEVER (to disable certificate verification for a specific transfer), that setting is written to the process-wide global context and will be observed by all other concurrently executing ldap_do() threads. A transfer that legitimately required strict certificate verification (LDAP_OPT_X_TLS_DEMAND) could therefore silently inherit the weakened setting, leading to unauthenticated TLS connections.
findings.suggestion: Call ldap_init() (or ldap_sslinit() on Windows) before invoking ldap_set_option(), then pass the returned server handle instead of NULL to all ldap_set_option() calls. This scopes the options to the per-connection handle rather than the global LDAP context.
findings.title: Global LDAP option mutation via NULL handle in multi-threaded LDAPS

agent_reasoning: The intro commit inverted the guard so the wolfSSL branch only ran wolfSSL_check_domain_name()/returned CURLE_PEER_FAILED_VERIFICATION when peer->sni was non-NULL, with no else-branch failure. Since peer->sni is left unset for IP-address targets, QUIC connections to IP literals over wolfSSL skipped host/cert verification entirely (fail-open), allowing an on-path attacker to present any certificate undetected (CVE-2025-4947). The fix computes snihost = peer->sni ? peer->sni : peer->hostname and always invokes wolfSSL_check_domain_name on it when verifyhost is set, so verification runs unconditionally (fail-closed) regardless of whether SNI was used.

findings.message: In Curl_vquic_tls_verify_peer(), the wolfSSL branch only performs the peer certificate / hostname check when peer->sni is non-NULL: `if(peer->sni && wolfSSL_check_domain_name(ctx->ssl, peer->sni) == SSL_FAILURE) return CURLE_PEER_FAILED_VERIFICATION;`. Prior to this commit the condition was `if(!peer->sni || wolfSSL_check_domain_name(...) == SSL_FAILURE) return CURLE_PEER_FAILED_VERIFICATION;`, i.e. a missing SNI value caused verification to fail closed. This commit flipped the logic so that when peer->sni is NULL (which happens when the connection target is specified as a literal IP address rather than a hostname, since libcurl does not set an SNI value for IP literals), the entire check is skipped and the function falls through to `return result;` with result left at CURLE_OK. This means the wolfSSL QUIC/HTTP3 backend silently accepts any server certificate for IP-address URLs, with no hostname/cert validation performed at all, enabling MITM/impersonation attacks against QUIC connections to IP-address hosts.
findings.suggestion: Do not gate the certificate/hostname check on peer->sni being set. Use peer->hostname as a fallback identity to check against when peer->sni is NULL, and always perform the wolfSSL_X509_check_host/wolfSSL_check_domain_name call so that IP-address targets are still subjected to certificate verification.
findings.title: QUIC+wolfSSL certificate verification skipped when peer->sni is NULL (e.g. IP-address hosts)

This made the certificate check conditional on SNI presence rather than always running, so hosts without an SNI value (IP-literal targets) got no verification at all, while the overall result variable defaulted to CURLE_OK.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix c6ae07c6a541 on top of intro 1aea05a6c269 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): curl's cookie path sanitization function sanitize_cookie_path() in lib/cookie.c, after being refactored in commit 1aea05a6c2 to use Curl_memdup0() for allocating the sanitized path buffer, incorrectly strips a lone leading slash '/' as if it were a trailing slash to remove, because its trailing-slash check `if(len && cookie_path[len-1]=='/')` did not exclude the len==1 case. This produces a zero-length sanitized path, which Curl_memdup0() then allocates as a minimal 1-byte (NUL-only) buffer. Code elsewhere in cookie.c's replace_existing() (added years earlier, in 2018, to prevent non-secure sites from overriding secure cookies) assumes any stored cookie path has at least one character after its first byte and unconditionally calls strchr(clist->spath + 1, '/'), reading one byte past the newly undersized 1-byte allocation. Root cause: A 2025 refactor of sanitize_cookie_path() (converting it to use strparse/Curl_memdup0 helpers) preserved pre-existing trailing-slash-stripping logic verbatim but changed the underlying allocation strategy from strdup-then-mutate (which always kept a buffer sized to the original, pre-mutation string) to Curl_memdup0(cookie_path, len) which allocates exactly len+1 bytes. This exposed a latent off-by-one logic flaw: stripping the lone '/' of a path=="/" cookie, which previously was harmless because the oversized strdup buffer absorbed the resulting empty string, now yields a buffer sized exactly to the (now zero) length, breaking the implicit invariant relied upon elsewhere (replace_existing's strchr(spath+1,...)) that a cookie path string has at least one byte available after index 0.

findings.message: sanitize_cookie_path() computes the sanitized cookie path length `len` and then does `if(len && cookie_path[len - 1] == '/') len--;` before calling `Curl_memdup0(cookie_path, len)`, which allocates exactly `len + 1` bytes. When the incoming cookie path is exactly "/" (len == 1), this trailing-slash check fires even though the single '/' is the leading (and only) character, decrementing len to 0. Curl_memdup0() then allocates a 1-byte buffer containing just a NUL terminator ('\0') for co->spath/clist->spath. Later, in replace_existing() (same file), when comparing a new non-secure cookie against an existing secure cookie, the code executes `sep = strchr(clist->spath + 1, '/');` unconditionally assuming spath has at least one character beyond index 0. Since spath is now a 1-byte allocation holding only the NUL terminator at index 0, `clist->spath + 1` points one byte past the end of that heap allocation, and strchr() reads from that out-of-bounds address. This is reachable via: (1) set a `secure` cookie for https://target with path "/", (2) have curl contact http://target with the same cookie, (3) have the insecure site set the same-named cookie with `path="/"`, which triggers replace_existing()'s secure-cookie overlay check and the OOB strchr() read on the previously stored secure cookie's 1-byte spath.
findings.suggestion: Only strip the trailing slash when the path has more than one character, i.e. require `len > 1` instead of just `len` before decrementing, so that a path consisting solely of "/" is preserved as a one-character string (which still allocates a 2-byte buffer: '/' + NUL). Additionally, guard the later strchr(spath + 1, ...) call in replace_existing() with a check that spath[0] is non-NUL before dereferencing spath + 1, and assert the invariant that sanitized paths are never empty.

agent_reasoning: The fix commit changes ws_enc_add_cntrl() to only record the pending control frame instead of immediately encoding/flushing it regardless of how much unsent data is already queued in ws->sendbuf. It moves the actual "add pending control frame to sendbuf" logic into ws_flush(), gated by a check that there is enough free space in the sendbuf (Curl_bufq_len < chunk_size), so PONGs are only appended when the buffer isn't already backed up. It also updates ws_cw_write() to call ws_flush() after processing decoded data (with CURLE_AGAIN treated as OK) so pending control frames get a chance to be flushed opportunistically. I applied these same edits directly: stripped the immediate add+flush from ws_enc_add_cntrl (added (void)data since data param is now unused there), added a space-based gate + ws_enc_add_pending call at the top of ws_flush, and restructured ws_cw_write to fall through to a final ws_flush call via a `result = CURLE_OK` initializer and `goto out` from the CURLE_AGAIN path. This matches the fix commit's non-test changes to lib/ws.c exactly, adapted to the on-disk code (which uses `unsigned char *` instead of `uint8_t *` naming, but is otherwise structurally identical).
commit_message:
websocket: handling of PONG frames

The auto PONG frames were inserted into the connection at the time
a PING had been decoded, irregardless if an upstream frame was just
in the middle of being assembled.

Add PONG frames only to the buffer if there is no frame currently
assemebled and, if it is, set the control frame aside. This control
frame is then added on the first opportunity of a "clean" send buffer.

There is only a single control frame set aside at a time. This means
a double PING will, when the PONG cannot be sent right away, only
send the last PONG.

I imagine this is fine. We want to prevent the endless buffering of
PONG frames on a connection where the server sends but does no receives.

Reported-by: Calvin Ruocco
Fixes #16706
Closes #18479
fix_commit_message:
ws: make pong sending lazy

Do not send PONG frames unless there is sufficient space left in the
websocket send buffer. A server might be lazy in reading our data and
intermediary PONG frames can be skipped by a client (RFC 6455, ch.
5.5.3).

Add test case measuring no real RSS increase on a server blasting with
PING frames.

Closes #21911

a PING had been decoded, irregardless if an upstream frame was just
in the middle of being assembled.

Add PONG frames only to the buffer if there is no frame currently
assemebled and, if it is, set the control frame aside. This control
frame is then added on the first opportunity of a "clean" send buffer.

There is only a single control frame set aside at a time. This means
a double PING will, when the PONG cannot be sent right away, only
send the last PONG.

I imagine this is fine. We want to prevent the endless buffering of
PONG frames on a connection where the server sends but does no receives.

Reported-by: Calvin Ruocco
Fixes #16706
Closes #18479

findings.message: ws_enc_add_cntrl() unconditionally encodes the latest pending control (PONG) frame into ws->sendbuf and attempts an immediate ws_flush() whenever the encoder is not in the middle of streaming another frame's payload (ws->enc.payload_remain == 0). This check only guards against corrupting an in-flight frame encoding; it does NOT verify that previously encoded/queued bytes already sitting in ws->sendbuf have actually been transmitted to the peer. Because ws->sendbuf is created with BUFQ_OPT_SOFT_LIMIT (lib/ws.c, Curl_bufq_init2 call for ws->sendbuf), writes to it never fail due to capacity - the bufq simply allocates additional chunks as needed. If the remote peer is slow to read (or a malicious WebSocket server never reads at all) while continuously sending PING frames, curl's automatic-PONG feature will repeatedly call ws_enc_add_pending()+ws_flush() for every PING received. Each call appends a freshly encoded PONG frame (header+payload) onto whatever unsent backlog already exists in sendbuf, and since enc.payload_remain becomes 0 as soon as a frame's bytes are copied into the bufq (regardless of whether the socket actually accepted any of it), there is no bound on how large ws->sendbuf can grow. A remote server can therefore flood curl with rapid PING frames while never draining the TCP connection, causing curl's process memory to grow without limit until exhaustion (CVE-2026-11586).
findings.suggestion: Do not eagerly add/flush a pending control frame on every incoming PING. Only encode and enqueue the pending PONG when there is remaining free space in the send buffer (e.g. Curl_bufq_len(&ws->sendbuf) < ws->sendbuf.chunk_size), and otherwise leave it as the single 'pending' frame to be added lazily the next time the send buffer is actually flushed with room to spare (as done in the later fix, which moves the ws_enc_add_pending() call into ws_flush() gated by a buffer occupancy check). This bounds sendbuf growth to roughly one chunk and allows RFC 6455 ch. 5.5.3 to be honored by skipping stale/intermediate PONGs when the peer is not reading.
findings.title: Unbounded growth of WebSocket sendbuf via eager auto-PONG encoding

Combined with a soft-limit bufq for ws->sendbuf that never rejects writes for being 'too full', this allows unbounded accumulation of unsent PONG frame bytes when the remote peer stops reading from the connection while continuing to send PING frames.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f1a39f221d57 on top of intro 34fa034d9a39 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): libcurl's connection-reuse logic for HTTP Negotiate (SPNEGO/Kerberos) authentication contained a copy-paste error introduced when the `url_match_auth_nego` function was added. The function incorrectly tested NTLM flags (`want_ntlm_http`, `want_proxy_ntlm_http`) instead of Negotiate flags (`want_nego_http`, `want_proxy_nego_http`) when deciding whether to enforce strict, state-based connection reuse. Because Negotiate authenticates connections (not individual requests), this flaw allowed libcurl to reuse a connection already authenticated under one user's credentials for a subsequent request that specified different credentials, effectively sending the second request as the first user. Root cause: When commit 34fa034 added `url_match_auth_nego` as a Negotiate-specific analogue of the existing `url_match_auth_ntlm`, the critical guard `if(m->want_ntlm_http || m->want_proxy_ntlm_http)` was copied from the NTLM function without changing the flag names to their Negotiate counterparts. Since these NTLM flags are never set during a Negotiate-only request, the block that records connection candidates and enforces fully-negotiated-connection selection (`m->found`, `m->force_reuse`, early return FALSE) was effectively unreachable, and the function always returned TRUE for Negotiate connections that passed the credential string comparison.

findings.message: In `url_match_auth_nego()`, the condition `if(m->want_ntlm_http || m->want_proxy_ntlm_http)` was copied verbatim from `url_match_auth_ntlm()` but never updated for Negotiate. Because `want_ntlm_http` and `want_proxy_ntlm_http` are always FALSE when the request uses Negotiate auth, the entire block that: (1) records the connection candidate via `m->found = conn`, (2) checks whether the GSS/Kerberos negotiation is already complete, and (3) sets `m->force_reuse` or returns FALSE to keep searching for a better connection — is dead code for Negotiate. As a result the function falls through to `return TRUE` unconditionally for any Negotiate connection that passes the credential string comparison, bypassing the state-machine check that is essential because Negotiate authenticates *connections*, not individual requests. A subsequent HTTP request with different user credentials that targets the same server can therefore wrongfully reuse a connection that is already fully authenticated under a different user's Kerberos/SPNEGO context.
findings.suggestion: Replace `m->want_ntlm_http || m->want_proxy_ntlm_http` with `m->want_nego_http || m->want_proxy_nego_http` so the guard condition matches the authentication method being checked by the surrounding function.

agent_reasoning: The bug is a use-after-free: `req->path` was set to point into the middle of `smbc->share`, which is connection-owned memory. When the connection is destroyed first (e.g. due to an error or reuse scenario), `smbc->share` is freed but `req->path` still references that memory. Any subsequent access to `req->path` (e.g. when building SMB tree-connect or open messages) constitutes a use-after-free. The fix avoids this entirely by making `smb_parse_url_path()` store a `strdup()`-ed copy of the path in `req->path`, giving the easy handle its own independent copy with the correct lifetime. The corresponding `smb_done()` cleanup now also frees `req->path` to avoid a memory leak.

pr_description:
The SMB request struct (`smb_request`) stores a `path` field that was previously set as a pointer directly into the middle of `smbc->share` (the connection's heap-allocated share string). This created a lifetime mismatch: the easy handle owns `smb_request`, but the memory it pointed to was owned by the connection's `smb_conn`. If the connection is torn down before the easy handle is cleaned up, `req->path` would reference freed memory.

This change makes `smb_parse_url_path()` store an independent copy of the path in `req->path` via `strdup()`, so the easy handle's request struct is fully self-contained and does not depend on connection-level memory remaining valid.

Additionally:
- `smb_done()` now frees `req->path` before releasing the `smb_request` struct, preventing a memory leak.
- `smb_parse_url_path()` calls `Curl_safefree(smbc->share)` before reassigning it, so repeated calls (e.g. on connection reuse) do not leak the previous share string.
- The path-normalisation loop now uses a separate variable `s` to avoid advancing `slash` past the start of the path string.
pr_title: smb: fix req->path lifetime by copying it at parse time

findings.message: In smb_parse_url_path(), req->path is set to point directly into the middle of smbc->share (a string allocated for and owned by the connection struct). When the SMB connection is freed while the easy handle's smb_request still lives, smbc->share is freed by smb_conn_dtor(), leaving req->path as a dangling pointer. On any subsequent access to req->path (e.g., when building SMB tree-connect or file-open messages), the program reads from freed heap memory. The destructor smb_easy_dtor() even contained a comment acknowledging this exact problem but without fixing it. The fundamental mistake is that req->path borrows a pointer into connection-lifetime memory but is stored in a request (easy-handle-lifetime) struct without making a private copy.

related_locations.description: Destructor comment acknowledges the UAF but does not fix it; req->path is never freed separately, so no Curl_safefree() is called on it.
req->path is read when building SMB messages; this is where the dangling pointer dereference occurs on connection reuse.

findings.suggestion: Make req->path an owned copy rather than a borrowed pointer. Use curlx_strdup(slash) to allocate an independent copy and free it in smb_easy_dtor() with Curl_safefree(req->path). Also call Curl_safefree(smbc->share) before re-assigning it in smb_parse_url_path() to avoid a memory leak on connection reuse.

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability was that url_match_auth_ntlm (or the equivalent inline block in older code) allowed a Negotiate-authenticated connection to be reused as a candidate for NTLM upgrade, because the only guard was `http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE`. pr_description:
When libcurl looks for an existing connection to reuse for an HTTP+NTLM request, it allows a neutral (unauthenticated) connection to be "upgraded" — i.e., adopted by the NTLM handshake. The eligibility check was: the connection's NTLM state must be `NTLMSTATE_NONE`.

However, a connection that completed Negotiate (SPNEGO/Kerberos) authentication also has `http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE`, because NTLM and Negotiate are tracked separately. Without an additional guard, such a Negotiate-authenticated connection could be incorrectly reused by a request carrying different credentials, effectively sending that request over the first user's established channel.

This change extends the eligibility check so that, when `USE_SPNEGO` is compiled in, a connection is only eligible for NTLM upgrade if **both** `http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE` and `http_negotiate_state == GSS_AUTHNONE`. On builds without SPNEGO support the behaviour is unchanged.

The updated comment makes the intent explicit: the connection can be upgraded only when it has no authentication of any kind ongoing.

findings.message: In url_match_auth_ntlm(), when an NTLM-wanting request encounters a connection with mismatched credentials, the code checks only that conn->http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE before marking the connection as a reuse candidate. It does not also verify that conn->http_negotiate_state == GSS_AUTHNONE. A connection previously authenticated via HTTP Negotiate (SPNEGO/Kerberos) will have http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE (since it never entered the NTLM state machine), so it passes this check and is wrongly selected for reuse by a different user's request. The second request then proceeds over a connection that is still authenticated as user1 while the caller believes it is mixing credentials for user2.
findings.suggestion: When USE_SPNEGO is compiled in, guard the 'found = conn' assignment with an additional check that conn->http_negotiate_state == GSS_AUTHNONE. This ensures a connection that completed Negotiate authentication is not recycled for a different user's NTLM request.

ground_truth.root_cause: The connection-reuse predicate url_match_auth_ntlm() was designed to allow a neutral (unauthenticated) connection to be 'upgraded' to NTLM. Its guard — http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE — successfully excludes in-progress or completed NTLM connections, but it does not exclude in-progress or completed Negotiate (SPNEGO) connections because those never set the NTLM state flag. The necessary second condition (http_negotiate_state == GSS_AUTHNONE) was absent from the time the feature was introduced in 2019 until the fix in 2026.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 51905671e07f on top of intro d646d5a13099 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): When curl is built with Apple SecTrust support (USE_APPLE_SECTRUST) and `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` is set to require OCSP stapling, a TLS server that omits the OCSP response is not rejected. The `ossl_apple_verify()` function converts the -1 sentinel returned by `SSL_get_tlsext_status_ocsp_resp()` to 0 and invokes `Curl_vtls_apple_verify()` with empty OCSP data. Apple's SecTrust validates the certificate chain without OCSP, returns success, and curl accepts the connection — silently bypassing the OCSP stapling requirement. Root cause: Commit d646d5a1309 ("openssl: fix the ocsp len arg to Curl_vtls_apple_verify") was intended to stop -1 from being passed as a length to Apple's SecTrust API, but it only zeroed `ocsp_len` without adding any subsequent enforcement that OCSP data must be present when `verifystatus` is required. The pre-existing `ossl_apple_verify()` function had no such guard either, so the normalization silently created a bypass path.

commit_message:
openssl: fix the ocsp len arg to Curl_vtls_apple_verify

If it has no data, pass in a zero.

Fixes #19303
Reported-by: Harry Sintonen
Closes #19305

findings.message: In `ossl_apple_verify()`, when `verifystatus` is enabled (OCSP stapling required) and the TLS server sends no OCSP response, `SSL_get_tlsext_status_ocsp_resp()` returns -1. The code silently converts this -1 to 0 and calls `Curl_vtls_apple_verify()` with zero-length OCSP data. Apple's SecTrust does not fail when OCSP data is absent, so verification succeeds and `*pverified` is set to TRUE. There is no subsequent check that OCSP was required but missing. The connection is therefore accepted without any OCSP validation, completely bypassing the user's `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` request.
findings.suggestion: After detecting `ocsp_len < 0` (no OCSP response), record that OCSP data was missing. After `Curl_vtls_apple_verify()` succeeds, check whether OCSP was missing and required (`conn_config->verifystatus && !octx->reused_session`). If so, set `*pverified = TRUE`, emit `failf(data, "No OCSP response received")`, and return `CURLE_SSL_INVALIDCERTSTATUS`.
findings.title: Missing OCSP stapling enforcement when server omits OCSP response

fix_commit.author: Stefan Eissing

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Missing OCSP stapling enforcement when server omits OCSP response
Related location for: Missing OCSP stapling enforcement when server omits OCSP response

ground_truth.root_cause: Commit d646d5a1309 ("openssl: fix the ocsp len arg to Curl_vtls_apple_verify") was intended to stop -1 from being passed as a length to Apple's SecTrust API, but it only zeroed `ocsp_len` without adding any subsequent enforcement that OCSP data must be present when `verifystatus` is required. The pre-existing `ossl_apple_verify()` function had no such guard either, so the normalization silently created a bypass path.

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit added libgsasl-based SCRAM-SHA-1/256 SASL support, including Curl_auth_gsasl_is_supported() which frees gsasl->ctx via gsasl_done() on client_start failure but does not null the pointer. Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup() unconditionally calls gsasl_done(gsasl->ctx) again later, causing a double free. I applied the fix commit's equivalent edits: set gsasl->ctx = NULL after the gsasl_done() call in the failure path, added a compile-time version guard requiring libgsasl 1.6.0+ (the version where gsasl_finish() was made NULL-safe), and documented the new minimum dependency version in docs/INTERNALS.md. These are the same conceptual changes as fix_sha, adapted to the file structure at intro_sha (which differs somewhat from the fix's base, e.g. INTERNALS.md formatting and unconditional `return true;` vs `return TRUE;`, and no curl_trc.h include yet).

fix_commit_message:
gsasl: fix potential double free

Also:
- require libgsasl 1.6.0+ (2010-12-14) for a `gsasl_finish()` that
  handles a NULL argument.
  Ref: https://gitlab.com/gsasl/gsasl/-/commit/b550032df8488a9ceaa3cfd4c634947d8f219717

Reported-by: Joshua Rogers (Aisle Research)

Closes #21609

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

findings.message: Curl_auth_gsasl_is_supported() calls gsasl_init(&gsasl->ctx) to allocate a GSASL context, then calls gsasl_client_start(). If gsasl_client_start() fails, the function calls gsasl_done(gsasl->ctx) to release the context and returns FALSE, but it never resets gsasl->ctx to NULL. The struct gsasldata that embeds gsasl->ctx persists as part of the connection/easy handle state, and Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup() (invoked from Curl_auth_cleanup() during normal teardown) unconditionally calls gsasl_done(gsasl->ctx) again before finally NULLing it. Because the first gsasl_done() call already freed the underlying GSASL context but left the stale, non-NULL pointer in gsasl->ctx, the second call in Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup() operates on an already-freed pointer, resulting in a double free of the same memory.
findings.suggestion: After releasing the GSASL context with gsasl_done() on the error path in Curl_auth_gsasl_is_supported(), immediately set gsasl->ctx = NULL so that later cleanup code (Curl_auth_gsasl_cleanup()) cannot free the same pointer again. This is exactly the change later applied in commit 3da249e1f0716c06644ed3522a37a8bf81808012.

agent_reasoning: The bug introduced by d5e83eb745 put both the old-credential cleanup and the new-credential assignment inside guards that check whether the parsed username (`u`) and password (`p`) are non-NULL. When an application passes NULL to CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD (the conventional way to clear credentials), setstropt_userpwd returns success but leaves `u` and `p` as NULL. Both guards are therefore skipped, so the stale `data->set.str[STRING_PROXYUSERNAME]` and `data->set.str[STRING_PROXYPASSWORD]` pointers are never freed or overwritten. On any subsequent proxy-authenticated transfer the old credentials are still present and will be used, which is a credential-persistence vulnerability. The fix moves the `Curl_safefree` calls for both credential strings outside the `u`/`p` guards, inside only a `if(!result)` check, so they are always cleared on a successful (including NULL) call. URL-decode and re-assign then only happens when the respective parsed token is non-NULL, preserving correct behaviour for non-NULL inputs.

pr_description:
When CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD is set to NULL, the proxy username and password stored in the handle should be cleared so that subsequent transfers do not reuse stale credentials.

Previously, the `Curl_safefree` calls and the URL-decode assignments for the proxy username and password were placed inside `if(!result && u)` / `if(!result && p)` guards. This meant that passing NULL caused the old credential strings to be silently retained.

This change restructures the CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD handler so that:
1. Both proxy credential strings are unconditionally freed (via `Curl_safefree`) whenever no prior error has occurred.
2. URL-decoding and re-assignment of the username only happens if `u` is non-NULL.
3. URL-decoding and re-assignment of the password only happens if `p` is non-NULL (and there is no prior error).

This ensures that calling `curl_easy_setopt(handle, CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD, NULL)` correctly clears any previously configured proxy credentials, and also avoids a memory leak caused by overwriting the old string pointers without freeing them first.
pr_title: setopt: clear proxy auth credentials properly when NULL is passed

findings.message: Curl_pretransfer() refreshes the internal bufref that stores the HTTP Referer: header value from data->set.str[STRING_SET_REFERER] on every transfer. Before this commit, lib/setopt.c called Curl_bufref_set(&data->state.referer, s->str[STRING_SET_REFERER], 0, NULL) unconditionally whenever CURLOPT_REFERER was set, so passing NULL correctly cleared the internal buffer as well as the string option. This commit moved the bufref update into Curl_pretransfer() but guarded it with `if(data->set.str[STRING_SET_REFERER])` and removed the unconditional call in setopt.c, without adding a corresponding else-branch to clear data->state.referer when the option string is NULL. As a result, once an application has set a Referer via CURLOPT_REFERER and later calls curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_REFERER, NULL) to explicitly disable it, data->set.str[STRING_SET_REFERER] becomes NULL but the previously populated data->state.referer bufref is never cleared, so the stale Referer: header value continues to be sent on subsequent requests (as long as automatic referer following via Location: is not also involved), potentially leaking sensitive URL/referrer information to servers the application did not intend to disclose it to.
findings.suggestion: Add an else branch that frees/clears data->state.referer when data->set.str[STRING_SET_REFERER] is NULL, mirroring what the removed unconditional Curl_bufref_set(NULL) call previously achieved in setopt.c. This was later fixed exactly this way in commit 862e8a74a8 by adding `else Curl_bufref_free(&data->state.referer);` after the STRING_SET_REFERER check.

pr_title: transfer: clear the old autoreferer

agent_reasoning: Without this change, mqtt_doing() captures `mq->sendleftovers` into a local `ptr`, calls mqtt_send(data, ptr, ...), and unconditionally frees `ptr` afterward. mqtt_send() only rewrites `mq->sendleftovers`/`mq->nsend` on the full-send or partial-send-with-successful-memdup paths; if Curl_memdup() returns NULL (OOM) it returns CURLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY while `mq->sendleftovers` still references the original (soon to be double-freed) allocation. mqtt_doing() then frees `ptr` (the same address), so `mq->sendleftovers` becomes a dangling pointer rather than NULL. Because mqtt_done() (added to free any leftover at completion) also calls Curl_safefree(mq->sendleftovers), the dangling pointer gets freed a second time — a double-free reachable via a transfer that experiences a short write followed by an allocation failure, matching the oss-fuzz report. The fix detaches `mq->sendleftovers`/`mq->nsend` (setting them to NULL/0) before the retry call, so mqtt_send() can only ever leave `mq->sendleftovers` as NULL or a newly, distinctly allocated buffer — never the same pointer that mqtt_doing() is about to free — eliminating the double-free while preserving normal send/retry behavior.

Oss-fuzz found an issue when the "sendleftovers" pointer could leak memory.
Fix this by always freeing it (if still assigned) in the done function.

Bug: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=43515
Closes #8274

location.description: Second free of sendleftovers in the newly added done callback.

findings.message: The retry frees a captured sendleftovers pointer after mqtt_send returns an allocation error, but the MQTT owner still retains it. The newly added mqtt_done callback frees that same pointer again.

related_locations.description: Retry captures and frees the old remainder without clearing its owner.

findings.title: Double free of MQTT send remainder after retry allocation failure

fix_commit.message: mqtt: convert sendleftovers to dynbuf

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Double free of MQTT send remainder after retry allocation failure
Related location for: Double free of MQTT send remainder after retry allocation failure

ground_truth.root_cause: mqtt_doing captures mq->sendleftovers and frees the captured pointer after mqtt_send, while mq->sendleftovers can still own that same allocation if the retry exits on an allocation error. The newly added mqtt_done then frees it again. A supported repair may keep the 2022 char-pointer representation: detach the old remainder from the MQTT owner and clear its count before retrying; free only the captured old allocation afterward; have mqtt_done free any remainder still owned at completion. Preserve successful MQTT send behavior and avoid APIs that do not link in a normal 2022 build.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 5fbd78eb2dc4 on top of intro f78700814d70 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): A lower-trust HTTP/2 peer can keep a legitimate multiplexed libcurl download stalled after the embedding pauses and resumes a slow consumer. The functional introduction newly wired that application state to the HTTP/2 stream receive window. Root cause: The new write_paused bridge makes cf_h2_update_local_win shrink the receive window to zero. On unpause, the updater calls nghttp2_submit_window_update without first setting nghttp2's internal local window size; a stream that reaches zero can remain blocked. The later fix calls the missing setter.
commit_message:
client writer: handle pause before deocding

Adds a "cw-pause" client writer in the PROTOCOL phase that buffers
output when the client paused the transfer. This prevents content
decoding from blowing the buffer in the "cw-out" writer.

Added test_02_35 that downloads 2 100MB gzip bombs in parallel and
pauses after 1MB of decoded 0's.

This is a solution to issue #16280, with some limitations:
- cw-out still needs buffering of its own, since it can be paused
  "in the middle" of a write that started with some KB of gzipped
  zeros and exploded into several MB of calls to cw-out.
- cw-pause will then start buffering on its own *after* the write
  that caused the pause. cw-pause has no buffer limits, but the
  data it buffers is still content-encoded.
  Protocols like http/1.1 stop receiving, h2/h3 have window sizes,
  so the cw-pause buffer should not grow out of control, at least
  for these protocols.
- the current limit on cw-out's buffer is ~75MB (for whatever
  historical reason). A potential content-encoding that blows 16KB
  (the common h2 chunk size) into > 75MB would still blow the buffer,
  making the transfer fail. A gzip of 0's makes 16KB into ~16MB, so
  that still works.

A better solution would be to allow CURLE_AGAIN handling in the client
writer chain and make all content encoders handle that. This would stop
explosion of encoding on a pause right away. But this is a large change
of the deocoder operations.

Reported-by: lf- on github
Fixes #16280
Closes #16296

fix_commit_message:
http2: fix stream window size after unpausing

When pausing a HTTP/2 transfer, the stream's local window size
is reduced to 0 to prevent the server from sending further data
which curl cannot write out to the application.

When unpausing again, the stream's window size was not correctly
increased again. The attempt to trigger a window update was
ignored by nghttp2, the server never received it and the transfer
stalled.

Add a debug feature to allow use of small window sizes which
reproduces this bug in test_02_21.

Fixes #16955
Closes #16960

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

pr_description:
Adds a "cw-pause" client writer in the PROTOCOL phase that buffers
output when the client paused the transfer. This prevents content
decoding from blowing the buffer in the "cw-out" writer.

Added test_02_35 that downloads 2 100MB gzip bombs in parallel and
pauses after 1MB of decoded 0's.

This is a solution to issue #16280, with some limitations:
- cw-out still needs buffering of its own, since it can be paused
  "in the middle" of a write that started with some KB of gzipped
  zeros and exploded into several MB of calls to cw-out.
- cw-pause will then start buffering on its own *after* the write
  that caused the pause. cw-pause has no buffer limits, but the
  data it buffers is still content-encoded.
  Protocols like http/1.1 stop receiving, h2/h3 have window sizes,
  so the cw-pause buffer should not grow out of control, at least
  for these protocols.
- the current limit on cw-out's buffer is ~75MB (for whatever
  historical reason). A potential content-encoding that blows 16KB
  (the common h2 chunk size) into > 75MB would still blow the buffer,
  making the transfer fail. A gzip of 0's makes 16KB into ~16MB, so
  that still works.

A better solution would be to allow CURLE_AGAIN handling in the client
writer chain and make all content encoders handle that. This would stop
explosion of encoding on a pause right away. But this is a large change
of the deocoder operations.

Reported-by: lf- on github
Fixes #16280
Closes #16296
pr_title: client writer: handle pause before deocding

findings.message: pubkey_pem_to_der() strips newlines/CRs from the base64 body found between the '-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----' and '-----END PUBLIC KEY-----' markers by appending each non-newline character into a dynbuf (pbuf) via Curl_dyn_addn(). If the PEM content between the markers consists solely of '\n'/'\r' characters (or is empty), Curl_dyn_addn() is never called, so pbuf's internal buffer (bufr) is never allocated and remains NULL. The code then unconditionally calls 'Curl_base64_decode(Curl_dyn_ptr(&pbuf), der, der_len)'. Curl_dyn_ptr() simply returns s->bufr, i.e. NULL in this case, which is then passed as the source string into the base64 decoder, which dereferences it (e.g. to compute strlen/read characters), causing a NULL pointer dereference. This is reachable via CURLOPT_PINNEDPUBLICKEY when an attacker-controlled or malformed PEM-format public key file/pinned key value is supplied that contains an empty or whitespace-only body between the BEGIN/END markers.
findings.suggestion: Before calling Curl_base64_decode(), check whether any data was actually written into pbuf (e.g. via Curl_dyn_len(&pbuf) == 0) and return CURLE_BAD_CONTENT_ENCODING in that case instead of passing a possibly-NULL pointer into the decoder.

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: NULL pointer dereference in pubkey_pem_to_der() on empty PEM body

ground_truth.root_cause: When pubkey_pem_to_der() was converted from a fixed malloc'd buffer (which was always allocated to at least 1 byte, guaranteeing a valid, if empty, C string) to a lazily-allocated dynbuf (struct dynbuf), the code failed to account for the case where zero bytes are ever appended to the dynbuf. In that case Curl_dyn_ptr()/curlx_dyn_ptr() legitimately returns NULL (mirroring the dynbuf's internal unallocated state), but the caller did not check for this before handing the pointer to the base64 decoder.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix cbf261e2de9f on top of intro 460ead61b6fe via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (Other): lib/vtls/rustls.c performs ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) configuration handling. When an ECHConfig list is supplied via the command line as base64, the decoded raw bytes are allocated inside curl's own base64-decode routine, which allocates memory through curl's (potentially overridden / memory-tracked) allocator wrappers. However, rustls.c releases that buffer using a bare `free()` call rather than curl's matching deallocation macro, because the file never includes curl_memory.h/memdebug.h. Additionally, a local cipher-suites buffer in the same file is allocated/freed with raw malloc()/free() rather than curl's allocator wrappers, bypassing curl's memory usage tracking. The fix adds the two missing includes at the end of the include block so that curl_memory.h's macro redefinitions of malloc/calloc/realloc/free/strdup apply throughout the file, making all allocations and frees in rustls.c go through the same (possibly overridden) allocator, resolving the invalid free reported by Valgrind (and curl's own memdebug system) in non-unity builds. Root cause: lib/vtls/rustls.c calls Curl_base64_decode() (which allocates through curl's internal, overridable malloc) to obtain the ECHConfig buffer but frees it with the plain libc free() because the translation unit never included curl_memory.h/memdebug.h, which are what redirect malloc/free calls in a given .c file to curl's tracked/overridable allocator functions. This mismatch between the allocator used to obtain memory and the deallocator used to release it is only safe by coincidence in default (no override, no memdebug) builds; it becomes an invalid free once curl's memory function overrides or memory debugging are engaged.

findings.message: In init_config_builder_ech(), when an ECHConfig is supplied via the command line, the base64-decoded buffer `ech_config` is allocated by Curl_base64_decode() (curlx_base64_decode in later refactors), which performs its allocation through curl's internal, potentially-overridden malloc (curl_malloc / memory-tracking wrappers activated via curl_memory.h / memdebug.h when included by the allocating translation unit). In the cleanup path of init_config_builder_ech(), the buffer is released with a plain, unqualified `free(ech_config)` call. Because lib/vtls/rustls.c does not include "../curl_memory.h" / "../memdebug.h", this free() resolves to the plain libc free() instead of curl's matching deallocation function (Curl_cfree / memdebug free). When curl is built with memory-function overrides (curl_global_init_mem / CURLOPT allocator overrides) or with the debug memory tracker (CURLDEBUG/memdebug), the allocation and the free happen through mismatched allocator APIs. This causes an invalid free (reported by Valgrind and curl's own memory-tracking layer), and can lead to memory corruption or crashes/undefined behavior in builds that use custom allocators, since the pointer being freed was not actually obtained from the allocator that services the raw free() call.
findings.suggestion: Include "../curl_memory.h" and "../memdebug.h" (as the last includes) in lib/vtls/rustls.c so that malloc/calloc/realloc/free used throughout the file (including this free(ech_config) and the local cipher_suites malloc/free pair) resolve to curl's memory-tracked / overridable allocator wrappers, matching the allocator used by Curl_base64_decode(). This ensures the allocation and free are performed through the same allocator API, eliminating the invalid free detected by Valgrind and enabling correct behavior when memory-function overrides are supplied by the application.

Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): The curl command-line tool's read callback (tool_read_cb in src/tool_cb_rea.c) was modified to support non-blocking STDIN reads on Windows when the user specifies `-T .` (upload from stdin). agent_reasoning: The cookie refactor changed Curl_cookie_getlist() to return a list of pointers into the live cookie jar instead of copied Cookie structs, but Curl_http_cookies() still released the share lock immediately after the getlist call, before iterating the list to build the Cookie header. agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix ad147ec53de8 on top of intro d3d90ad9c005 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): tftp_state_timeout() in lib/tftp.c is responsible for detecting when the overall TFTP transfer time budget (as computed by Curl_timeleft()) has been exhausted. When it detects expiry (timeout_ms < 0), it marks internal state as timed out (TFTP_ERR_TIMEOUT / TFTP_STATE_FIN) but incorrectly returns the constant 0 rather than propagating the negative timeout value. The caller, tftp_multi_statemach(), relies exclusively on the returned value being negative to decide to abort the transfer with CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT. Because 0 is returned, the abort branch is skipped, effectively masking the detected timeout from the state machine driver and defeating the overall timeout enforcement for TFTP operations. Root cause: A refactor of the TFTP timeout logic (commit d3d90ad9c0) replaced the old wall-clock deadline comparison with a Curl_timeleft()-based negative-value convention, but in the branch that handles an already-expired timer it kept returning the literal 0 (a holdover from the old code's 'return 0' pattern for absolute timeout) instead of returning the negative timeout_ms. The same commit also tightened the caller's guard from '<= 0' to '< 0', which had previously masked this exact bug (0 used to also trigger the abort). The combination silently disables timeout propagation for the expired-timer branch.

findings.message: In tftp_state_timeout(), when Curl_timeleft() reports the overall operation time budget has been exhausted (timeout_ms < 0), the function sets state->error = TFTP_ERR_TIMEOUT and state->state = TFTP_STATE_FIN, but then returns the literal value 0 instead of propagating the negative timeout_ms. The sole caller, tftp_multi_statemach(), checks 'if(timeout_ms < 0)' to decide whether to abort the transfer with CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT. Because the return value is forced to 0 (which is not < 0), that abort path is never taken via this check, even though the state was already flagged as FIN/TFTP_ERR_TIMEOUT. This masks the properly detected timeout condition from the caller, defeating the overall-timeout enforcement for TFTP transfers and can allow the state machine to keep the transfer running (spinning in the event loop, potentially indefinitely / until other guards trigger) instead of promptly aborting with a timeout error as intended. This was introduced together with a change of the caller's guard from '<= 0' to '< 0' in the same commit, which made the masking effective (previously any non-positive return, including 0, would trigger the abort).
findings.suggestion: Return the negative timeout_ms value (instead of hard-coded 0) so that the caller's 'if(timeout_ms < 0)' check correctly detects the expired timer and aborts the transfer with CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT as intended.
findings.title: TFTP overall timeout expiry masked by tftp_state_timeout() returning 0 instead of negative value

Vulnerability (DataRace): Curl_ssl_scache_take() in lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c releases the SSL session cache mutex (Curl_ssl_scache_unlock) before it finishes reading shared state protected by that lock: specifically, the trace/log statement calls Curl_llist_count(&peer->sessions) to report the remaining number of cached sessions for the peer, but this call happens after the unlock. Any other thread sharing the same Curl_easy handle's session cache (multi-threaded libcurl usage sharing a share object / connection cache) can concurrently modify peer->sessions (or even free the peer) between the unlock and the count read, causing a race condition on the linked list. Root cause: When Curl_ssl_scache_take() was reworked to add QUIC 0RTT support and richer trace logging, the call to Curl_ssl_scache_unlock(data) was placed immediately after the critical section that removes/takes a session from the peer's session list, but before the subsequent trace-logging code that itself reads the same shared peer->sessions list (via Curl_llist_count) to report the remaining session count. This left a window where lock-protected data is read/used without holding the lock.

findings.message: In Curl_ssl_scache_take(), the SSL session cache lock is released via Curl_ssl_scache_unlock(data) before the trace logging code runs. The trace statement (CURL_TRC_CF / later CURL_TRC_SSLS) calls Curl_llist_count(&peer->sessions) to report how many sessions remain for that peer. Because this happens after the lock has already been released, another thread can concurrently mutate peer->sessions (adding/removing/destroying nodes, or even freeing/expiring the peer entry) between the unlock and the Curl_llist_count() call, resulting in a data race on the shared peer->sessions llist. This can produce an inconsistent/incorrect count in the trace output, and in the worst case (if the peer structure itself is freed by a concurrent scache_put/expire path) it could lead to a use-after-free style read on peer->sessions/peer. The unlock was moved up in front of the trace logic when this function was reworked to add QUIC 0RTT support, splitting what used to be a single 'take then trace' sequence under lock.
findings.suggestion: Move Curl_ssl_scache_unlock(data) to after the trace logging (i.e., after the entire if(s)/else block that reads peer->sessions), so the lock still protects all reads of the shared peer/session-list state used for the diagnostic count.

findings.message: In reuse_conn(), when an existing connection is reused, the `host` and `conn_to_host` struct hostname fields are moved (shallow-copied) from `old_conn` to `conn`. For `host`, both `rawalloc` and `encalloc` are correctly zeroed out on the source (`old_conn->host.rawalloc = NULL; old_conn->host.encalloc = NULL;`) after the copy, preventing the pointers from being freed twice. However, for `conn_to_host` only `rawalloc` is zeroed (`old_conn->conn_to_host.rawalloc = NULL;`) while `encalloc` is left untouched. Since `conn->conn_to_host = old_conn->conn_to_host;` is a shallow struct copy, both `conn->conn_to_host.encalloc` and `old_conn->conn_to_host.encalloc` now point at the same heap allocation. When `old_conn` is subsequently torn down (via conn_free(), which calls Curl_free_idnconverted_hostname() and frees `encalloc`), and later `conn->conn_to_host` is freed/reset (also via Curl_free_idnconverted_hostname(), e.g. on the next reuse or connection close), the same `encalloc` buffer is freed a second time, resulting in a double free / use-after-free that can be leveraged for memory corruption.
findings.suggestion: After copying old_conn->conn_to_host into conn->conn_to_host, fully clear the source struct (both rawalloc and encalloc, or the whole struct) so the moved-from connection no longer holds a live pointer to the transferred allocation. Best practice, as later adopted upstream, is to factor this move into a helper function that frees the destination's existing allocations, copies the struct, and then memsets the source struct to zero (or NULLs every pointer member) to fully sever ownership.

As a result, pop3->transfer could be computed from a stale/previous value of data->req.no_body, causing curl to misjudge whether a POP3 response body should be delivered to the caller, potentially corrupting output or transfer state, especially when a Curl_easy handle is reused across different POP3 commands. Root cause: A caller (pop3_perform) read a shared state field (data->req.no_body) to make a decision, while the callee it subsequently invokes (pop3_perform_command) is the one responsible for computing/updating that same field for the current operation. +  { "APOP", 4, FALSE, FALSE },

+  { "CAPA", 4, TRUE, TRUE },

+/* Return iff a command is defined as "multi-line" (RFC 1939),
+ * has a response terminated by a last line with a '.'.

+static bool pop3_is_multiline(const char *cmdline)
+{
+  size_t i;
+  for(i = 0; i < ARRAYSIZE(pop3cmds); ++i) {
+    if(strncasecompare(pop3cmds[i].name, cmdline, pop3cmds[i].nlen)) {

+  return TRUE;

findings.message: Commit 4cd10ee28b introduced logic in pop3_perform_command() that recomputes data->req.no_body based on whether the outgoing POP3 command is multi-line (data->req.no_body = !pop3_is_multiline(command);). However, pop3_perform() (the caller) reads data->req.no_body BEFORE calling pop3_perform_command(), using its value (set previously, e.g. from a prior request or left over from handle state) to decide whether pop3->transfer should be set to PPTRANSFER_INFO (no body transfer expected). Because pop3_perform_command() only updates data->req.no_body afterwards, pop3->transfer can end up reflecting the OLD no_body value instead of the value that was just computed for the current command. This means the transfer state machine can incorrectly believe a body transfer is or is not expected, causing curl to mishandle the POP3 response (e.g. treat data as headers-only when a body should be read, or vice versa), leading to incorrect state handling / data corruption for POP3 transfers, particularly across handle reuse where req.no_body carries over from an earlier request.
findings.suggestion: Reorder pop3_perform() so it calls pop3_perform_command() first (which computes the correct, up-to-date data->req.no_body for the current command), and only afterwards check data->req.no_body to decide whether pop3->transfer should be set to PPTRANSFER_INFO. This is exactly what the upstream fix (commit 67c4256f7e) does: it moves the pop3_perform_command() call before the data->req.no_body check in pop3_perform().

Vulnerability (DoubleFree): curl's RTMP protocol handler (lib/curl_rtmp.c) allocates an RTMP* handle and registers it into the connection's meta-data hash with a destructor (rtmp_conn_dtor) that will free it when the connection is torn down. findings.message: rtmp_setup_connection() allocates an RTMP handle with RTMP_Alloc() and immediately registers it in the connection's meta hash via Curl_conn_meta_set(conn, CURL_META_RTMP_CONN, r, rtmp_conn_dtor). From this point on, ownership of `r` is effectively transferred to the connection meta store, which will invoke rtmp_conn_dtor() (calling RTMP_Close(r) and RTMP_Free(r)) automatically whenever the connection's meta data is torn down (e.g. when the connectdata is destroyed after a failed connection setup). However, if the subsequent RTMP_SetupURL(r, data->state.url) call fails (e.g. because of a malformed rtmp:// URL), the code still executes the old cleanup path RTMP_Free(r) directly before returning CURLE_URL_MALFORMAT. Because `r` remains registered in the connection meta hash (it was never removed via Curl_conn_meta_remove), when the connection is later destroyed the meta destructor rtmp_conn_dtor() runs again and calls RTMP_Free(r) (and RTMP_Close(r)) a second time on the same pointer, resulting in a double-free / use-after-free that can be triggered simply by supplying a malformed RTMP URL.
findings.suggestion: Do not call RTMP_Free(r) manually in the URL-parse-error path once `r` has been registered with Curl_conn_meta_set() and an rtmp_conn_dtor is attached. Either remove the meta entry (Curl_conn_meta_remove) before freeing manually, or simply let the connection meta destructor perform the cleanup and just return the error code without freeing.

commit_message:
curl_get_line: enhance the API

To make sure callers can properly differentiate between errors and know
cleanly when EOF happens. Updated all users and unit test 3200.

findings.message: Curl_get_line() reads a config/cache/cookie/hsts/netrc file line by line using fgets() in a 'while(1)' loop. The rewritten loop sets `*eof = feof(input);` right after the fgets() call and only breaks out of the loop (returning) when `*eof` becomes true (real EOF) or a full line terminated by '\n' has been accumulated. It never calls ferror(input) to detect a genuine I/O read error. If fgets() fails due to an I/O error (e.g. the underlying FILE* is backed by a device, pipe, or network filesystem that returns an error rather than EOF), fgets() returns NULL while feof(input) remains false. In that case `*eof` stays false, `rlen` becomes 0 (since b is NULL), so none of the three possible loop-exit conditions (dynbuf append failure, trailing newline detected, or EOF reached) are met, and the loop immediately retries fgets() on the same broken stream forever. This is a regression versus the prior implementation, which contained an explicit 'else { ... else break; }' branch that terminated the loop (returning an error) when fgets() returned NULL and no buffered data was pending. The new code dropped that fallback without adding an equivalent ferror() check, turning a transient/permanent read error on any file parsed via Curl_get_line (cookie jar, alt-svc cache, HSTS cache, netrc, config files) into an unbounded CPU-spinning infinite loop — a denial-of-service hang.
findings.suggestion: After fgets() returns NULL, explicitly check ferror(input) in addition to feof(input), and return a read-error CURLcode (e.g. CURLE_READ_ERROR) immediately so the loop cannot spin forever on a persistent I/O error.
findings.title: Curl_get_line loops forever on fgets() read error instead of returning

Vulnerability (LogicError): curl's urlapi host normalization code (ipv4_normalize in lib/urlapi.c) can be tricked into accepting and normalizing a hostname whose final component is a malformed hex literal consisting only of the '0x' prefix with no digits (e.g. '127.1.0x', '127.0x', '127.0x.1', '127.1.1.0x') as if it were a valid, fully specified IPv4 address, due to an overly broad 'swallow a trailing dot' leniency check introduced to support legitimate trailing-dot IPv4 addresses (e.g. '127.1.'). Root cause: Commit 831a1514843bfa4d4d006627 (urlapi: consume trailing dots after IPv4 numerical addresses) replaced the previous unconditional 'if(rc) return HOST_NAME;' check after the number-parsing dispatch with a conditional that allows a failed parse to be tolerated when n is nonzero, rc == STRE_NO_NUM, and the cursor is at the end of the string -- intending to permit a trailing dot after the last IPv4 octet to be silently dropped. findings.message: ipv4_normalize() was changed to tolerate a failing numeric-parse (rc != 0) as a 'trailing dot was swallowed' case whenever the prior component index n is nonzero, the failure code is STRE_NO_NUM, and the cursor c now points at the string terminator. This check is applied uniformly after the '0'/'0x'/'0' (octal)/decimal number-parsing dispatch, but it does not distinguish between a genuine trailing-dot situation (e.g. '127.1.') and a component that began with the hex prefix '0x' but contained no hex digits after it (e.g. the final component in '127.1.0x'). In the latter case, curlx_str_hex() advances c past the consumed '0x' prefix, fails to find any digit, sets rc to STRE_NO_NUM, and leaves *c as '\0' (end of string) -- which makes the generic 'n && rc == STRE_NO_NUM && !*c' leniency check at line 534 treat the malformed '.0x' terminal component as if it were simply a legitimate trailing dot, decrementing n and accepting the host as a valid, fully-specified IPv4 address. This lets strings such as 'https://127.1.0x' normalize/parse as IPv4 host '127.0.0.1' even though '0x' is not a valid numeric component, which can confuse consumers that rely on urlapi's IPv4 host classification/normalization for security decisions (e.g. SSRF filtering, host allow/deny lists).
findings.suggestion: After the hex-specific parse (curlx_str_hex), immediately check its own rc and return HOST_NAME on failure before falling through to the generic/shared 'trailing dot' leniency check, since that generic check was designed only for the trailing-dot case and is not valid for a '0x' prefix with no following hex digits.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 041a6c36142f on top of intro b8bf2f4e1758 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): In common_init(), when parsing channel layouts from the deprecated 'ch_layouts' option string, av_realloc_array() is called to grow buf->channel_layouts. The return value is stored in the local variable 'tmp', but is never assigned back to buf->channel_layouts. Since av_realloc_array() may free the original buffer and return a pointer to a newly allocated buffer (or return a new allocation when the original pointer is NULL), buf->channel_layouts remains stale (NULL on the first iteration, or a dangling pointer on subsequent iterations). The immediately following memset() on line 208 dereferences buf->channel_layouts, causing a null pointer dereference crash (SEGV). Additionally, the memset only zeroes sizeof(*buf->channel_layouts) bytes (one element) instead of sizeof(*buf->channel_layouts) * 2 bytes (the new element plus the terminator), leaving the terminator element uninitialized. This is triggered by filter graphs containing abuffersink with channel layout options, e.g. 'abuffersink=::a'. Root cause: After calling av_realloc_array() to grow the channel_layouts array, the new pointer stored in 'tmp' was never assigned back to buf->channel_layouts. This is a classic realloc pattern bug where the caller forgets to update the original pointer. On the first iteration, buf->channel_layouts is NULL, so the memset writes to address 0x0. On subsequent iterations, if realloc moved the buffer, buf->channel_layouts becomes a dangling pointer (use-after-free). A secondary issue is that the memset only clears one element instead of two (the new entry plus the zero terminator).

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 0526535cd584 on top of intro 4ee05182b7cc via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): In audio_element_obu(), the num_parameters value is read from untrusted input via ffio_read_leb() without an upper bound check when audio_element_type is 0 (Channel representations). The IAMF specification allows at most 2 parameters for Channel representations (DEMIXING and RECON_GAIN), but the code only validates that num_parameters must be 0 for Scene representations (audio_element_type != 0). A crafted IAMF file can supply num_parameters > 2, causing the subsequent loop to call param_parse() with duplicate parameter types. When the same parameter type (e.g., DEMIXING) is parsed multiple times, the pointer in element->demixing_info or element->recon_gain_info is overwritten by a new allocation from av_iamf_param_definition_alloc(), leaking the previously allocated memory. This leads to uncontrolled memory consumption (memory leak) which can be exploited for denial of service. This is CVE-2025-1816. Root cause: Missing input validation: the code does not enforce the IAMF specification's constraint that Channel audio elements can have at most 2 parameters. The existing validation only checks that Scene representations have 0 parameters, but does not limit the count for Channel representations.

findings.message: In audio_element_obu(), the num_parameters value is read from untrusted input via ffio_read_leb() without an upper bound check when audio_element_type is 0 (Channel representations). The IAMF specification allows at most 2 parameters for Channel representations (DEMIXING and RECON_GAIN), but the code only validates that num_parameters must be 0 for Scene representations (audio_element_type != 0). A crafted IAMF file can supply num_parameters > 2, causing the subsequent loop to call param_parse() with duplicate parameter types. When the same parameter type (e.g., DEMIXING) is parsed multiple times, the pointer in element->demixing_info or element->recon_gain_info is overwritten by a new allocation from av_iamf_param_definition_alloc(), leaking the previously allocated memory. This leads to uncontrolled memory consumption (memory leak) which can be exploited for denial of service. This is CVE-2025-1816.
findings.suggestion: Add a constraint check that rejects num_parameters > 2 when audio_element_type is 0 (Channel representations), since the IAMF spec only defines two valid parameter types (DEMIXING and RECON_GAIN) for channel-based audio elements.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 35ea45835484 on top of intro f8d429e0c569 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (BufferOverflow): In filter_frame(), the index j is computed as s->fft_len - s->remaining_fill (later changed to s->fft_len/2 + s->remaining_fill_max - s->remaining_fill by a subsequent commit). After processing a CQT frame, s->remaining_fill is set to step, where step = sample_rate / (fps * count). When timeclamp and/or fps are low, fft_len can be small relative to step (e.g., timeclamp=0.01 at 44100Hz gives fft_len=512, while fps=15 count=5 gives step=588). This makes j negative (512 - 588 = -76). The subsequent loops iterate starting at m=0, writing to s->fft_data[j+m] with negative indices, causing heap buffer overflow (writes before the allocated buffer). This corrupts heap metadata, leading to SIGSEGV crashes, double-free errors, malloc assertion failures, and corrupted double-linked list errors depending on what memory is overwritten. The rewrite commit introduced this by changing fps from a bounded integer (10-100) to AV_OPT_TYPE_VIDEO_RATE with no practical lower bound, and removing the rate%(fps*count)==0 divisibility check, allowing step to exceed fft_len. Root cause: The rewrite of showcqt in commit f8d429e0c56 relaxed the fps parameter from a bounded integer (10-100) to an unbounded VIDEO_RATE type and removed the divisibility check (rate % (fps*count) == 0). This allowed configurations where the step size (sample_rate / (fps * count)) exceeds fft_len (2^ceil(log2(sample_rate * timeclamp))). After the first CQT plot, remaining_fill is set to step, and on the next loop iteration j = fft_len - remaining_fill becomes negative. The loop starting at m=0 then writes to fft_data at negative offsets, corrupting the heap. A subsequent commit (c4a3526b57d) further lowered the timeclamp minimum from 0.1 to 0.002, making the bug much easier to trigger with moderate fps values.
commit_message:
[Merged] avfilter/avf_showcqt: rewrite showcqt and add features

add yuv444p, yuv422p, and yuv420p output format (lower cpu usage
on ffplay playback because it does not do format conversion)
custom size with size/s option (fullhd option is deprecated)
custom layout with bar_h, axis_h, and sono_h option
support rational frame rate (within fps/r/rate option)
relaxed frame rate restriction (support fractional sample step)
support all input sample rates
separate sonogram and bargraph volume (with volume/sono_v and
volume2/bar_v)
timeclamp option alias (timeclamp/tc)
fcount option
gamma option alias (gamma/sono_g and gamma2/bar_g)
support custom frequency range (basefreq and endfreq)
support drawing axis using external image file (axisfile option)
alias for disabling drawing to axis (text/axis)
possibility to optimize it using arch specific asm code

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

+static void cqt_calc(FFTComplex *dst, const FFTComplex *src, const Coeffs *coeffs,
+                     int len, int fft_len)
+{
+    int k, x, i, j;
+    for (k = 0; k < len; k++) {
+        FFTComplex l, r, a = {0,0}, b = {0,0};
+
+        for (x = 0; x < coeffs[k].len; x++) {
+            FFTSample u = coeffs[k].val[x];
+            i = coeffs[k].start + x;
+            j = fft_len - i;
+            a.re += u * src[i].re;
+            a.im += u * src[i].im;
+            b.re += u * src[j].re;
+            b.im += u * src[j].im;
+        }
+
+        /* separate left and right, (and multiply by 2.0) */
+        l.re = a.re + b.re;
+        l.im = a.im - b.im;
+        r.re = b.im + a.im;
+        r.im = b.re - a.re;
+        dst[k].re = l.re * l.re + l.im * l.im;
+        dst[k].im = r.re * r.re + r.im * r.im;
+    }
+}

+static int init_cqt(ShowCQTContext *s)
+{
+    const char *var_names[] = { "timeclamp", "tc", "frequency", "freq", "f", NULL };
+    AVExpr *expr = NULL;
+    int rate = s->ctx->inputs[0]->sample_rate;
+    int nb_cqt_coeffs = 0, nb_cqt_coeffs_r = 0;
+    int k, x, ret;
+
+    if ((ret = av_expr_parse(&expr, s->tlength, var_names, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, s->ctx)) < 0)
+        goto error;
+
+    ret = AVERROR(ENOMEM);
+    if (!(s->coeffs = av_calloc(s->cqt_len * 2, sizeof(*s->coeffs))))
+        goto error;
+
+    for (k = 0; k < s->cqt_len; k++) {
+        double vars[] = { s->timeclamp, s->timeclamp, s->freq[k], s->freq[k], s->freq[k] };
+        double flen, center, tlength;
+        int start, end, m = (s->cqt_coeffs_type == COEFFS_TYPE_INTERLEAVE) ? (2 * k) : k;
+
+        if (s->freq[k] > 0.5 * rate)
+            continue;
+        tlength = clip_with_log(s->ctx, "tlength", av_expr_eval(expr, vars, NULL),
+                                TLENGTH_MIN, s->timeclamp, s->timeclamp, k);
+
+        flen = 8.0 * s->fft_len / (tlength * rate);
+        center = s->freq[k] * s->fft_len / rate;
+        start = fmax(0, ceil(center - 0.5 * flen));
+        end = fmin(s->fft_len, floor(center + 0.5 * flen));
+
+        s->coeffs[m].start = start & ~(s->cqt_align - 1);
+        s->coeffs[m].len = (end | (s->cqt_align - 1)) + 1 - s->coeffs[m].start;
+        nb_cqt_coeffs += s->coeffs[m].len;
+        if (!(s->coeffs[m].val = av_calloc(s->coeffs[m].len, sizeof(*s->coeffs[m].val))))
+            goto error;
+
+        if (s->cqt_coeffs_type == COEFFS_TYPE_INTERLEAVE) {
+            s->coeffs[m+1].start = (s->fft_len - end) & ~(s->cqt_align - 1);
+            s->coeffs[m+1].len = ((s->fft_len - start) | (s->cqt_align - 1)) + 1 - s->coeffs[m+1].start;
+            nb_cqt_coeffs_r += s->coeffs[m+1].len;
+            if (!(s->coeffs[m+1].val = av_calloc(s->coeffs[m+1].len, sizeof(*s->coeffs[m+1].val))))
+                goto error;
+        }
+
+        for (x = start; x <= end; x++) {
+            int sign = (x & 1) ? (-1) : 1;
+            double y = 2.0 * M_PI * (x - center) * (1.0 / flen);
+            /* nuttall window */
+            double w = 0.355768 + 0.487396 * cos(y) + 0.144232 * cos(2*y) + 0.012604 * cos(3*y);
+            w *= sign * (1.0 / s->fft_len);
+            s->coeffs[m].val[x - s->coeffs[m].start] = w;
+            if (s->cqt_coeffs_type == COEFFS_TYPE_INTERLEAVE)
+                s->coeffs[m+1].val[(s->fft_len - x) - s->coeffs[m+1].start] = w;
+        }
+    }
+
+    av_expr_free(expr);
+    if (s->cqt_coeffs_type == COEFFS_TYPE_DEFAULT)
+        av_log(s->ctx, AV_LOG_INFO, "nb_cqt_coeffs = %d.\n", nb_cqt_coeffs);
+    else
+        av_log(s->ctx, AV_LOG_INFO, "nb_cqt_coeffs = {%d,%d}.\n", nb_cqt_coeffs, nb_cqt_coeffs_r);
+    return 0;
+
+error:
+    av_expr_free(expr);
+    if (s->coeffs)
+        for (k = 0; k < s->cqt_len * 2; k++)
+            av_freep(&s->coeffs[k].val);
+    av_freep(&s->coeffs);
+    return ret;
+}

+static AVFrame *alloc_frame_empty(enum AVPixelFormat format, int w, int h)
+{
+    AVFrame *out;
+    out = av_frame_alloc();
+    if (!out)
+        return NULL;
+    out->format = format;
+    out->width = w;
+    out->height = h;
+    if (av_frame_get_buffer(out, 32) < 0) {
+        av_frame_free(&out);
+        return NULL;
+    }
+    if (format == AV_PIX_FMT_RGB24 || format == AV_PIX_FMT_RGBA) {
+        memset(out->data[0], 0, out->linesize[0] * h);
+    } else {
+        int hh = (format == AV_PIX_FMT_YUV420P || format == AV_PIX_FMT_YUVA420P) ? h / 2 : h;
+        memset(out->data[0], 16, out->linesize[0] * h);
+        memset(out->data[1], 128, out->linesize[1] * hh);
+        memset(out->data[2], 128, out->linesize[2] * hh);
+        if (out->data[3])
+            memset(out->data[3], 0, out->linesize[3] * h);
+    }
+    return out;
+}

+static enum AVPixelFormat convert_axis_pixel_format(enum AVPixelFormat format)
+{
+    switch (format) {

+        case AV_PIX_FMT_YUV444P: format = AV_PIX_FMT_YUVA444P; break;
+        case AV_PIX_FMT_YUV422P: format = AV_PIX_FMT_YUVA422P; break;
+        case AV_PIX_FMT_YUV420P: format = AV_PIX_FMT_YUVA420P; break;
+    }
+    return format;

intro_commit_message:
avfilter/avf_showcqt: rewrite showcqt and add features

add yuv444p, yuv422p, and yuv420p output format (lower cpu usage
on ffplay playback because it does not do format conversion)
custom size with size/s option (fullhd option is deprecated)
custom layout with bar_h, axis_h, and sono_h option
support rational frame rate (within fps/r/rate option)
relaxed frame rate restriction (support fractional sample step)
support all input sample rates
separate sonogram and bargraph volume (with volume/sono_v and
volume2/bar_v)
timeclamp option alias (timeclamp/tc)
fcount option
gamma option alias (gamma/sono_g and gamma2/bar_g)
support custom frequency range (basefreq and endfreq)
support drawing axis using external image file (axisfile option)
alias for disabling drawing to axis (text/axis)
possibility to optimize it using arch specific asm code

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
