+#define MIDL(type, ss)                                         \
+static unsigned midl_##ss(const type *const prev,              \
+                          const type *const next,              \
+                          int end, int x, int k)               \
+{                                                              \
+    return (prev[av_clip(x + k, 0, end)] +                     \
+            next[av_clip(x - k, 0, end)] + 1) >> 1;            \
+}
+
+MIDL(uint8_t, 8)
+MIDL(uint16_t, 16)
+
+#define MID4(type, ss)                                         \
+static unsigned mid4_##ss(const type *const prev,              \
+                          const type *const next,              \
+                          const type *const prev2,             \
+                          const type *const next2,             \
+                          int end, int x, int k, int depth)    \
+{                                                              \
+    return av_clip_uintp2_c((                                  \
+            9 * (prev[av_clip(x + k, 0, end)] +                \
+                 next[av_clip(x - k, 0, end)]) -               \
+            1 * (prev2[av_clip(x + k*3, 0, end)] +             \
+                 next2[av_clip(x - k*3, 0, end)]) + 8) >> 4,   \
+                 depth);                                       \
+}
+
+MID4(uint8_t, 8)
+MID4(uint16_t, 16)
+
+#define DIFF(type, ss)                                         \
+static unsigned diff_##ss(const type *const prev,              \
+                          const type *const next,              \
+                          int end, int x, int k, int j)        \
+{                                                              \
+    return FFABS(prev[av_clip(x + k + j, 0, end)] -            \
+                 next[av_clip(x - k + j, 0, end)]);            \
+}
+
+DIFF(uint8_t, 8)
+DIFF(uint16_t, 16)
+
+#define COST(type, ss)                                         \
+static unsigned cost_##ss(const type *const prev,              \
+                          const type *const next,              \
+                          int end, int x, int k)               \
+{                                                              \
+    const int m = midl_##ss(prev, next, end, x, k);            \
+    const int p = prev[x];                                     \
+    const int n = next[x];                                     \
+                                                               \
+    return FFABS(p - m) + FFABS(n - m);                        \
+}
+
+COST(uint8_t, 8)
+COST(uint16_t, 16)
+
+#define INTERPOLATE(type, atype, max, ss)                                      \
+static void interpolate_##ss(uint8_t *ddst,                                    \
+                             const uint8_t *const pprev_line,                  \
+                             const uint8_t *const nnext_line,                  \
+                             const uint8_t *const pprev2_line,                 \
+                             const uint8_t *const nnext2_line,                 \
+                             int x, int width, int rslope,                     \
+                             int redge, unsigned h, int depth,                 \
+                             int *K)                                           \
+{                                                                              \
+    type *dst = (type *)ddst;                                                  \
+    const type *const prev_line = (const type *const)pprev_line;               \
+    const type *const prev2_line = (const type *const)pprev2_line;             \
+    const type *const next_line = (const type *const)nnext_line;               \
+    const type *const next2_line = (const type *const)nnext2_line;             \
+    const int end = width - 1;                                                 \
+    const atype f = redge + 2;                                                 \
+    atype sd[S], sD[S], di = 0;                                                \
+    atype dmin = max;                                                          \
+    int k = *K;                                                                \
+                                                                               \
+    for (int i = -rslope; i <= rslope && abs(k) > rslope; i++) {               \
+        atype sum = 0;                                                         \
+                                                                               \
+        for (int j = -redge; j <= redge; j++) {                                \
+            sum += diff_##ss(prev_line,  next_line,  end, x, i, j);            \
+            sum += diff_##ss(prev2_line, prev_line,  end, x, i, j);            \
+            sum += diff_##ss(next_line,  next2_line, end, x, i, j);            \
+        }                                                                      \
+                                                                               \
+        sD[i + rslope]  =     sum;                                             \
+        sD[i + rslope] += f * cost_##ss(prev_line,  next_line,  end, x, i);    \
+        sD[i + rslope] += h * abs(i);                                          \
+                                                                               \
+        dmin = FFMIN(sD[i + rslope], dmin);                                    \
+    }                                                                          \
+                                                                               \
+    for (int i = -rslope; i <= rslope; i++) {                                  \
+        atype sum = 0;                                                         \
+                                                                               \
+        for (int j = -redge; j <= redge; j++) {                                \
+            sum += diff_##ss(prev_line,  next_line,  end, x, k + i, j);        \
+            sum += diff_##ss(prev2_line, prev_line,  end, x, k + i, j);        \
+            sum += diff_##ss(next_line,  next2_line, end, x, k + i, j);        \
+        }                                                                      \
+                                                                               \
+        sd[i + rslope]  =     sum;                                             \
+        sd[i + rslope] += f * cost_##ss(prev_line, next_line, end, x, k + i);  \
+        sd[i + rslope] += h * abs(k + i);                                      \
+                                                                               \
+        dmin = FFMIN(sd[i + rslope], dmin);                                    \
+    }                                                                          \
+                                                                               \
+    for (int i = -rslope; i <= rslope && abs(k) > rslope; i++) {               \
+        if (dmin == sD[i + rslope]) {                                          \
+            di = 1;                                                            \
+            k = i;                                                             \
+            break;                                                             \
+        }                                                                      \
+    }                                                                          \
+                                                                               \
+    for (int i = -rslope; i <= rslope && !di; i++) {                           \
+        if (dmin == sd[i + rslope]) {                                          \
+            k += i;                                                            \
+            break;                                                             \
+        }                                                                      \
+    }                                                                          \
+                                                                               \
+    dst[x] = mid4_##ss(prev_line, next_line, prev2_line, next2_line,           \
+                       end, x, k, depth);                                      \
+                                                                               \
+    *K = k;                                                                    \
+}

+INTERPOLATE(uint8_t,  unsigned, UINT_MAX, 8)
+INTERPOLATE(uint16_t, uint64_t, UINT64_MAX, 16)

+static int deinterlace_slice(AVFilterContext *ctx, void *arg,
+                             int jobnr, int nb_jobs)
+{
+    ESTDIFContext *s = ctx->priv;
+    ThreadData *td = arg;
+    AVFrame *out = td->out;
+    AVFrame *in = td->in;
+    const int rslope = s->rslope;
+    const int redge = s->redge;
+    const int half = s->half;
+    const int depth = s->depth;
+    const int interlaced = in->interlaced_frame;
+    const int tff = (s->field == (s->parity == -1 ? interlaced ? in->top_field_first : 1 :
+                                  s->parity ^ 1));
+
+    for (int plane = 0; plane < s->nb_planes; plane++) {
+        const uint8_t *src_data = in->data[plane];
+        uint8_t *dst_data = out->data[plane];
+        const int linesize = s->linesize[plane];
+        const int width = s->planewidth[plane];
+        const int height = s->planeheight[plane];
+        const int src_linesize = in->linesize[plane];
+        const int dst_linesize = out->linesize[plane];
+        const int start = (height * jobnr) / nb_jobs;
+        const int end = (height * (jobnr+1)) / nb_jobs;
+        const uint8_t *prev_line, *prev2_line, *next_line, *next2_line, *in_line;
+        uint8_t *out_line;
+        int y_out;
+
+        y_out = start + (tff ^ (start & 1));
+
+        in_line  = src_data + (y_out * src_linesize);
+        out_line = dst_data + (y_out * dst_linesize);
+
+        while (y_out < end) {
+            memcpy(out_line, in_line, linesize);
+            y_out += 2;
+            in_line  += src_linesize * 2;
+            out_line += dst_linesize * 2;
+        }
+
+        y_out = start + ((!tff) ^ (start & 1));
+        out_line = dst_data + (y_out * dst_linesize);
+
+        for (int y = y_out; y < end; y += 2) {
+            int y_prev2_in = y - 3;
+            int y_next2_in = y + 3;
+            int y_prev_in = y - 1;
+            int y_next_in = y + 1;
+            int k;
+
+            while (y_prev2_in < 0)
+                y_prev2_in += 2;
+
+            while (y_next2_in >= height)
+                y_next2_in -= 2;
+
+            while (y_prev_in < 0)
+                y_prev_in += 2;
+
+            while (y_next_in >= height)
+                y_next_in -= 2;
+
+            prev2_line = src_data + (y_prev2_in * src_linesize);
+            next2_line = src_data + (y_next2_in * src_linesize);
+
+            prev_line = src_data + (y_prev_in * src_linesize);
+            next_line = src_data + (y_next_in * src_linesize);
+
+            k = 0;
+
+            for (int x = 0; x < width; x++) {
+                s->interpolate(out_line,
+                               prev_line, next_line,
+                               prev2_line, next2_line,
+                               x, width, rslope, redge, half, depth, &k);
+            }
+
+            out_line += 2 * dst_linesize;
+        }
+    }
+
+    return 0;
+}
+
+static int filter(AVFilterContext *ctx, int is_second, AVFrame *in)
+{
+    ESTDIFContext *s = ctx->priv;
+    AVFilterLink *outlink = ctx->outputs[0];
+    AVFrame *out;
+    ThreadData td;
+
+    out = ff_get_video_buffer(outlink, outlink->w, outlink->h);
+    if (!out)
+        return AVERROR(ENOMEM);
+    av_frame_copy_props(out, in);
+    out->interlaced_frame = 0;
+    out->pts = s->pts;
+
+    td.out = out; td.in = in;
+    ctx->internal->execute(ctx, deinterlace_slice, &td, NULL,
+                           FFMIN(s->planeheight[1] / 2, s->nb_threads));
+
+    if (s->mode)
+        s->field = !s->field;
+
+    return ff_filter_frame(outlink, out);
+}
+
+static int config_input(AVFilterLink *inlink)
+{
+    AVFilterContext *ctx = inlink->dst;
+    ESTDIFContext *s = ctx->priv;
+    const AVPixFmtDescriptor *desc = av_pix_fmt_desc_get(inlink->format);
+    int ret;
+
+    if ((ret = av_image_fill_linesizes(s->linesize, inlink->format, inlink->w)) < 0)
+        return ret;
+
+    s->planeheight[1] = s->planeheight[2] = AV_CEIL_RSHIFT(inlink->h, desc->log2_chroma_h);
+    s->planeheight[0] = s->planeheight[3] = inlink->h;
+    s->planewidth[1] = s->planewidth[2] = AV_CEIL_RSHIFT(inlink->w, desc->log2_chroma_w);
+    s->planewidth[0] = s->planewidth[3] = inlink->w;
+
+    if (inlink->h < 3) {
+        av_log(ctx, AV_LOG_ERROR, "Video of less than 3 lines is not supported\n");
+        return AVERROR(EINVAL);
+    }
+
+    s->nb_planes = av_pix_fmt_count_planes(inlink->format);
+    s->nb_threads = ff_filter_get_nb_threads(ctx);
+    s->depth = desc->comp[0].depth;
+    s->interpolate = s->depth <= 8 ? interpolate_8 : interpolate_16;
+    s->half = 1 << (s->depth - 1);
+
+    return 0;
+}
+ static int filter_frame(AVFilterLink *inlink, AVFrame *in)
+{
+    AVFilterContext *ctx = inlink->dst;
+    ESTDIFContext *s = ctx->priv;
+    int ret;
+
+    if (!s->prev) {
+        s->prev = in;
+        return 0;
+    }
+
+    if ((s->deint && !in->interlaced_frame) || ctx->is_disabled) {
+        s->prev->pts *= 2;
+        ret = ff_filter_frame(ctx->outputs[0], s->prev);
+        s->prev = in;
+        return ret;
+    }
+
+    s->pts = s->prev->pts * 2;
+    ret = filter(ctx, 0, s->prev);
+    if (ret < 0 || s->mode == 0) {
+        av_frame_free(&s->prev);
+        s->prev = in;
+        return ret;
+    }
+
+    s->pts = s->prev->pts + in->pts;
+    ret = filter(ctx, 1, s->prev);
+    av_frame_free(&s->prev);
+    s->prev = in;
+    return ret;
+}
+
+static int request_frame(AVFilterLink *link)
+{
+    AVFilterContext *ctx = link->src;
+    ESTDIFContext *s = ctx->priv;
+    int ret;
+
+    if (s->eof)
+        return AVERROR_EOF;
+
+    ret = ff_request_frame(ctx->inputs[0]);
+
+    if (ret == AVERROR_EOF && s->prev) {
+        AVFrame *next = av_frame_clone(s->prev);
+
+        if (!next)
+            return AVERROR(ENOMEM);
+
+        next->pts = s->prev->pts + av_rescale_q(1, av_inv_q(ctx->outputs[0]->frame_rate),
+                                                ctx->outputs[0]->time_base);
+        s->eof = 1;
+        ret = filter_frame(ctx->inputs[0], next);
+    } else if (ret < 0) {
+        return ret;
+    }
+
+    return ret;
+}

+static av_cold void uninit(AVFilterContext *ctx)
+{
+    ESTDIFContext *s = ctx->priv;
+
+    av_frame_free(&s->prev);
+}

+    {
+        .name          = "default",
+        .type          = AVMEDIA_TYPE_VIDEO,

+        .config_props  = config_input,
+    },
+    { NULL }

+        .name          = "default",
+        .type          = AVMEDIA_TYPE_VIDEO,
+        .config_props  = config_output,

findings.message: In deinterlace_slice(), the per-thread row range [start, end) is computed as `(height * jobnr) / nb_jobs` and `(height * (jobnr+1)) / nb_jobs`, using plain `int` arithmetic for the multiplication `height * (jobnr+1)`. Because `height`, `jobnr`, and `nb_jobs` are all `int`, the multiplication is performed in 32-bit signed arithmetic before the division. For sufficiently tall frames combined with a large number of filter threads (large jobnr/nb_jobs), the intermediate product `height * (jobnr+1)` can exceed INT_MAX, causing signed integer overflow, which is undefined behavior in C. The resulting `start`/`end` values can become incorrect (e.g., negative or wrapped), leading to out-of-bounds row indices being used to compute `in_line`/`out_line` pointers (`src_data + (y_out * src_linesize)`), which can cause out-of-bounds reads/writes.
findings.suggestion: Promote the multiplication to a 64-bit type before dividing, and cast the result back to int, so that the intermediate product cannot overflow a 32-bit signed integer even for tall frames and many threads.
findings.suggestion_code:
const int start = (int)((int64_t)height * jobnr / nb_jobs);
const int end = (int)((int64_t)height * (jobnr + 1) / nb_jobs);

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 65fc0db581c4 on top of intro 425c3234206c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): libavformat/hlsenc.c's parse_playlist() function, when handling the `append_list` HLS flag for subtitle segments, calls `snprintf(vtt_file, len, vtt_basename, vtt_index)` where `vtt_basename` (derived from the configurable VTT/subtitle filename template) is used directly as the *format string* rather than as literal data. Because this filename-derived string is attacker/user influenced and can contain unexpected `%` conversion specifiers, this is an uncontrolled/user-controlled format string vulnerability that can cause crashes, out-of-bounds reads/information disclosure, or worse. Root cause: The code assumes that the VTT basename always contains a well-formed, single `%d`-style placeholder intended for the segment index and unconditionally forwards that string as the fmt argument of snprintf(), rather than treating the basename as opaque data and only substituting the index through a controlled, format-string-free mechanism.

findings.suggestion: Never pass user-derived data directly as the format string argument of a printf-family function. Instead, build the substitution safely, e.g. by using a helper that finds a literal placeholder pattern (like a numeric field or a known token) inside the basename and replaces it with the numeric index using a fixed, hard-coded format string, or by validating that vtt_basename contains exactly one safe %d/%0Nd-style specifier before use. The eventual fix introduced a dedicated `replace_int_data_in_filename()` helper that performs the substitution without treating the untrusted basename as a format string.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix b45a6d3f76f1 on top of intro 5fc9c79f53d7 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (IntegerOverflow): The ADPCM Silicon Graphics N64 decoder in libavcodec/adpcm.c computes a predictor 'delta' value by summing products of decoded sample codes and 16-bit filter coefficients that are read from (attacker-controlled) codec extradata. The multiplication of these signed int values can overflow the range of 'int', which is undefined behavior in C and was detected by UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer during fuzz testing (OSS-Fuzz). An earlier commit (0c7e0ed35b) had already changed the accumulator 'delta' to unsigned and cast the sum before division, addressing overflow in the addition, but the multiplication 'sf_codes[...] * coefs[...]' itself remained purely signed, so the intermediate product could still overflow before assignment/addition. Commit b45a6d3f76 fixes this remaining case by casting one operand of the multiplication to unsigned. findings.message: In the ADPCM_N64 decoder's sample reconstruction loop, the predictor 'delta' accumulates a running sum from multiplying decoded sample codes (sf_codes[]) with signed filter coefficients (coefs[]) taken directly from untrusted extradata. The multiplication 'sf_codes[(i-1) - k] * coefs[(o*8) + k]' is performed entirely in 'int' (signed) arithmetic. Because coefs[] values are attacker-controlled 16-bit values sign-extended into int, and sf_codes values can also be large (n * scale, where scale can be up to 1<<15), the product of two signed ints can exceed INT_MAX/underflow INT_MIN before being added into 'delta'. Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C and was flagged by fuzzing (UBSan). A previous partial fix (0c7e0ed35b) changed 'delta' itself to 'unsigned' and cast the final sum before dividing, which fixed overflow in the addition/division, but left the multiplication of two signed ints unprotected, so the overflow could still occur in the multiply step itself.
findings.suggestion: Cast one of the multiplicands to unsigned before multiplying so the multiply and accumulate happen entirely in unsigned arithmetic (which has well-defined wraparound semantics in C), matching the fix applied upstream: multiply by '(unsigned)coefs[(o*8) + k]' instead of the plain signed 'coefs[(o*8) + k]'. Also ensure the accumulator 'delta' itself is declared 'unsigned' (as later fixed in 0c7e0ed35b) and that the final sum is explicitly cast to 'int' before the division by 2048.
findings.title: Signed integer overflow in ADPCM_N64 delta accumulation multiplication

commit_message: avcodec/exr: add DWA decompression support

findings.message: In dwa_uncompress(), dc_w and dc_h (the number of 8x8 DC-coefficient blocks per row/column) are computed as td->xsize >> 3 and td->ysize >> 3. This integer division truncates (floors) instead of rounding up. When td->xsize or td->ysize is not a multiple of 8 (odd/non-block-aligned tile or scanline dimensions), the computed dc_w/dc_h is smaller than the actual number of 8x8 blocks that the main decode loop iterates over (for (y = 0; y < td->ysize; y += 8) / for (x = 0; x < td->xsize; x += 8)). The per-block DC index is later computed as `idx = (x >> 3) + (y >> 3) * dc_w + dc_w * dc_h * j;` and used to index into td->dc_data (cast to uint16_t*), which was allocated/populated based on dc_count derived from the bitstream, not from this truncated dc_w*dc_h product. Because dc_w*dc_h is smaller than the number of blocks actually visited, `idx` can run past the number of valid decoded DC values into unrelated/unallocated memory, or otherwise access memory that does not correspond to a real DC coefficient. This results in an out-of-bounds read (as identified by Google Big Sleep, BIGSLEEP-445392027-crash.exr) when decoding a maliciously crafted or malformed EXR file compressed with DWA and non-block-aligned tile/scanline dimensions.
findings.suggestion: Round dc_w and dc_h up to account for partial trailing 8x8 blocks, matching the block-iteration stride used later in the function, e.g. `(td->xsize + 7) >> 3` and `(td->ysize + 7) >> 3`. Additionally, since it is unclear whether the format even supports non-multiple-of-8 dimensions for DWA-compressed data, emit a sample request (avpriv_request_sample) when xsize/ysize are not multiples of 8 so real-world behavior can be verified.
findings.title: Truncated dc_w/dc_h computation causes out-of-bounds read of DC coefficient array in EXR DWA decompression

The decode loop that walks over blocks uses ceiling-like iteration (steps of 8 covering the full xsize/ysize including a partial last block), creating an inconsistency between the computed grid size (dc_w * dc_h) and the actual number of blocks processed.

Vulnerability (BufferOverflow): The ProRes RAW decoder (libavcodec/prores_raw.c), added in commit 589b3ed943, computed the 16-byte-aligned coded_width/coded_height for the decoded frame before calling ff_set_dimensions() to update avctx->width/height when the stream's resolution changes. ff_set_dimensions() internally also sets avctx->coded_width/coded_height (to the unaligned width/height), so calling it after the manual alignment assignment caused the aligned values to be discarded/overwritten with unaligned ones. Downstream code that allocates or writes to the frame buffer relies on coded_width/coded_height being 16-aligned, so when the actual width/height is not a multiple of 16 the buffer ends up undersized relative to what is written, causing a heap buffer overflow. This was found via OSS-Fuzz (case 438771336) and fixed in c9e93df4eed93fe0044c52d953688c4180de1d48 by simply reordering the two code blocks so the alignment assignment happens after ff_set_dimensions(). Root cause: Incorrect ordering of two dimension-setting operations: the aligned coded_width/coded_height assignment happened before a call to ff_set_dimensions(), which itself also assigns (unaligned) values to those same fields, silently overwriting the alignment performed just before it.

findings.message: In decode_frame() of the newly added ProRes RAW decoder, avctx->coded_width and avctx->coded_height are set to the 16-byte aligned values of the parsed frame width/height BEFORE the call to ff_set_dimensions(avctx, w, h). ff_set_dimensions() internally resets avctx->coded_width and avctx->coded_height back to the unaligned width/height (w, h) whenever the resolution changes from the previous frame. findings.suggestion: Move the assignment of avctx->coded_width/coded_height (using FFALIGN) to AFTER the call to ff_set_dimensions(), so the aligned coded dimensions are not overwritten by ff_set_dimensions()'s own (unaligned) coded_width/coded_height assignment.

Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): parse_itut_t35_metadata() in libavcodec/libdav1d.c parses ITU-T T.35 metadata OBUs emitted by the dav1d AV1 decoder. If an attacker supplies a crafted AV1 bitstream containing an ITU-T T.35 metadata OBU with country_code = 0xB5 and a payload shorter than 2 bytes (e.g. 1 byte), the unchecked read walks past the end of the allocated payload buffer, triggering a heap-buffer-overflow read of up to 2 bytes as confirmed by AddressSanitizer. Root cause: During a refactor that converted the country_code/provider_code dispatch logic in parse_itut_t35_metadata() into nested switch statements, the previously bounds-checked bytestream2_get_be16() call used to read provider_code was replaced by the unchecked bytestream2_get_be16u() variant for the US country_code case, without adding an explicit length check (bytestream2_get_bytes_left(&gb) < 2) beforehand. The analogous branch for the UK country code does include such a guard, but it was inconsistently omitted for the US branch, leaving a gap where attacker-controlled short payloads are read out of bounds.

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit added Decoder.subtitle_header as a shallow pointer copy of AVCodecContext->subtitle_header, creating a use-after-free once the AVCodecContext is closed/freed while the Decoder (and any consumer of dec.subtitle_header) may outlive it. findings.message: In dec_open(), the newly introduced Decoder.subtitle_header field is assigned directly from ist->dec_ctx->subtitle_header (a pointer owned/managed by the decoder's AVCodecContext, i.e. by libavcodec). No copy of the underlying buffer is made; Decoder.subtitle_header is simply an alias to memory owned by the AVCodecContext. When the AVCodecContext is later closed/freed (avcodec_free_context, e.g. during decoder teardown or dec_free), the buffer that subtitle_header points to can be released or reallocated by libavcodec, while consumers of Decoder.subtitle_header (e.g. the subtitle encoder path which reads dec->subtitle_header/subtitle_header_size to initialize its own codec context) may still read from it afterward, resulting in a use-after-free / dangling pointer read. The field was also declared as `const uint8_t *`, further indicating the intent was only to reference, not own, the memory, with no corresponding free path.
findings.suggestion: Deep-copy the subtitle_header buffer into memory owned by the Decoder struct instead of storing a raw pointer into the AVCodecContext. Allocate a buffer of subtitle_header_size (+1 for NUL termination, since ASS code assumes a null-terminated buffer), memcpy the contents, and free it explicitly when the Decoder is destroyed (dec_free). Change the field type from `const uint8_t *` to a mutable, decoder-owned `uint8_t *` so ownership is clear.
findings.title: Decoder.subtitle_header stores a borrowed pointer into the AVCodecContext, leading to use-after-free

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 770bc1c23a18 on top of intro baad75cafa6b via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (BufferOverflow): libavcodec/aac/aacdec_usac_mps212.c implements MPEG Surround (Mpsp212) lossless-data decoding for USAC AAC streams. The function ff_aac_ec_data_dec() calls get_freq_strides(), which computes per-band stride boundaries and writes data_bands+1 entries into the caller-supplied output array. The function was called with ld->freq_res (a 9-entry, per-parameter-set array) as that output buffer instead of a dedicated scratch buffer sized for the number of frequency bands (up to 28+1). Because data_bands is derived from start_band/end_band/band_stride and can exceed MPS_MAX_PARAM_SETS, this results in an out-of-bounds write into the AACMPSLosslessData structure, and the corrupted/overflowed values are then read back and used as array indices into ld->last_data, causing further out-of-bounds accesses. An intermediate fix (c2364e92) attempted to mitigate this by clamping the written values to 2 bits, but that only reduced (did not eliminate) the aliasing/overflow problem and was itself reverted; the real fix (770bc1c23a) introduces a properly sized local temporary array (freq_stride_map) so get_freq_strides() no longer writes into ld->freq_res at all. Root cause: The output buffer passed to get_freq_strides() (ld->freq_res, sized for MPS_MAX_PARAM_SETS=9 per-set entries) is too small for the number of entries the function actually writes (up to data_bands+1, where data_bands can reach 28 for the finest stride/widest band range). Additionally, using ld->freq_res as both an input (ld->freq_res[set_idx] selects band_stride) and output (overwritten in-place with band-index data) creates unintended aliasing that corrupts state used later in the same function.

findings.message: In ff_aac_ec_data_dec(), get_freq_strides() is called with ld->freq_res used directly as the output ('freq_strides') scratch buffer: `get_freq_strides(ld->freq_res, stride_table[ld->freq_res[set_idx]], start_band, end_band)`. ld->freq_res is declared as `int16_t freq_res[MPS_MAX_PARAM_SETS]` (MPS_MAX_PARAM_SETS == 9), i.e. it is meant to hold one frequency-resolution value per parameter set. However get_freq_strides() writes indices 0..data_bands inclusive into this buffer, where data_bands = (end_band - start_band - 1) / band_stride + 1. Since band_stride can be as small as 1 (stride_table[0] == 1) and end_band can be as large as MPS_MAX_PARAM_BANDS (28), data_bands can be up to 28, so get_freq_strides() can write up to 29 int16_t entries into a 9-element array, producing a large out-of-bounds write that corrupts adjacent fields of the AACMPSLosslessData structure (coarse_quant_no, etc.) and its own control data (ld->freq_res[set_idx]) that is still being read in the same function. The subsequent reads `ld->last_data[ld->freq_res[j]]` and `ld->freq_res[j + 0]`/`ld->freq_res[j + 1]` used as array indices into ld->last_data (size MPS_MAX_PARAM_BANDS) then use corrupted/attacker-influenced values, leading to further out-of-bounds reads/writes on ld->last_data. This is triggerable via a crafted USAC/MPEG-Surround (Mpsp212) AAC bitstream.
findings.suggestion: Do not reuse ld->freq_res (a MPS_MAX_PARAM_SETS-sized, per-parameter-set array) as the scratch buffer that get_freq_strides() fills with per-band stride boundaries. Use a local temporary array sized for the maximum number of frequency bands (e.g. int16_t freq_stride_map[MPS_MAX_PARAM_BANDS + 1]) as the destination for get_freq_strides(), and use that temporary array for all subsequent indexing (ld->last_data[freq_stride_map[j]], freq_stride_map[j+0]..freq_stride_map[j+1]) instead of ld->freq_res. This avoids aliasing/overwriting the control array and avoids out-of-bounds writes since data_bands can exceed MPS_MAX_PARAM_SETS.
findings.title: Out-of-bounds write on ld->freq_res via get_freq_strides() aliasing in ff_aac_ec_data_dec()

Additionally, using ld->freq_res as both an input (ld->freq_res[set_idx] selects band_stride) and output (overwritten in-place with band-index data) creates unintended aliasing that corrupts state used later in the same function.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 2e32276872d3 on top of intro baad75cafa6b via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (BufferOverflow): The USAC MPS212 (MPEG Surround) entropy-coded pair decoder ec_pair_dec() in libavcodec/aac/aacdec_usac_mps212.c passes a local pointer array p_data[2] into huff_decode(), which for certain bitstream configurations (2D time-differential coding with diff_freq set) advances the pointers by one element as a side effect (data[0] += 1; data[1] += 1;). Since the pointer array is passed by reference, this advancement is visible to the caller. The caller then reuses these now-advanced pointers, still bounded by the full nb_bands count, as both source and destination for attach_lsb(), which walks nb_bands elements starting at the (possibly advanced) pointer. This can read and write one int16_t element past the end of the fixed-size 28-element stack arrays that back the pointers, corrupting adjacent stack memory. Root cause: huff_decode() mutates the caller's array-of-pointers argument (advancing data[0]/data[1] by one element in certain code paths) as an implementation detail to signal 'first element already consumed', but ec_pair_dec() was written assuming p_data[] always points at the base of the fixed-size data_pair[] arrays. Combined with an unconditional fixed iteration count (nb_bands) in attach_lsb(), the mismatch between the (possibly shifted) pointer and the full-length loop bound produces an out-of-bounds access.

agent_reasoning: The intro commit added MPS212 bitstream parsing but did not validate the attacker-controlled bsOttBandsPhase and bsResidualBands fields against the legal number of bands (numBands) derived from bsFreqRes. These fields are later used as loop/array bounds in parse_mps212(), enabling an out-of-bounds read for crafted files. I applied the same fix as fix_sha: reject bsFreqRes==0, compute numBands via the Table 39 lookup, validate both fields against numBands (returning AVERROR_INVALIDDATA on violation), and use the Table 109 default for otts_bands_phase when not explicitly present. The resulting diff matches the fix commit's diff exactly and applies cleanly against intro_parent.

findings.message: decode_usac_element_pair() reads the raw 5-bit bitstream fields bsOttBandsPhase (via get_bits(gb, 5)) into e->mps.otts_bands_phase, and, when residual coding is enabled, bsResidualBands into e->mps.residual_bands, without validating them against the maximum number of frequency bands (numBands) allowed for the current freq_res setting (per ISO/IEC 23003-1:2007 Table 39, numBands can be as small as 4). Because e->mps.otts_bands_phase is left unbounded (0-31 from 5 bits) it is later used directly as the 'nb_bands' argument passed into ff_aac_ec_data_dec()/parse_mps212() when decoding the OTT IPD (Inter-channel Phase Difference) data, and e->mps.residual_bands is also left unbounded and later combined via FFMAX with otts_bands_phase. Since these values control loop bounds/array indices used to fill fixed-size per-band arrays inside the MPEG Surround (MPS212) decoding path (parse_mps212 / ff_aac_ec_data_dec / ff_aac_map_index_data), a malicious bitstream can supply an out-of-range value larger than the actual number of bands, causing writes/reads beyond the allocated per-band buffers -- an out-of-bounds array access as confirmed by the reporter's PoC (matejsmycka/poc.mp4).
findings.suggestion: Compute the maximum permitted number of bands (numBands) for the given freq_res (per ISO/IEC 23003-1:2007 Table 39) and validate that both bsOttBandsPhase and bsResidualBands do not exceed it, returning AVERROR_INVALIDDATA otherwise, before the values are used to size/index per-band arrays later in parse_mps212(). This is exactly what the fix commit ddcb9dd3b5d21d055774abd61ae609ecb728cb1c implements.
findings.title: Missing range validation of bsOttBandsPhase/bsResidualBands allows out-of-bounds array access in MPS212 (parametric stereo) decoding

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f435ce22e10e on top of intro 6d0c89980c78 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): In libavcodec/h2645_sei.c, the function h2645_sei_to_side_data() handles conversion of parsed HEVC/H.264 SEI messages (including Ambient Viewing Environment) into AVFrameSideData. For the Ambient Viewing Environment SEI, code allocates an AVAmbientViewingEnvironment struct, wraps it in an AVBufferRef, and calls ff_frame_new_side_data_from_buf_ext() to attach it as frame side data, transferring ownership of the buffer. Only after this call does the code populate the struct's ambient_illuminance/ambient_light_x/ambient_light_y fields. Because ownership of the underlying buffer can already be transferred or the buffer already released as part of that call's internal handling (in success or error paths), writing to dst_env afterwards can operate on memory that could already have been freed/exposed elsewhere, producing a use-after-free. This was found via fuzzing with a crafted MP4/HVCC sample (poc_hvcc_modified.mp4). Root cause: The struct fields for the newly-allocated side-data object are initialized AFTER handing the wrapping buffer off to a function (ff_frame_new_side_data_from_buf_ext) that can take ownership of / free that buffer, instead of before. This creates a window in which the memory the code is about to write to is no longer guaranteed to be valid/owned by this code path.

findings.message: In h2645_sei_to_side_data(), when handling the Ambient Viewing Environment SEI, a new AVAmbientViewingEnvironment struct (dst_env) is allocated and wrapped in an AVBufferRef (buf), which is then handed off to ff_frame_new_side_data_from_buf_ext(). This function can fail (returning ret < 0) after having already taken ownership of / freed the buffer (e.g. if av_frame_side_data_add fails or another internal error occurs, the buffer ref is unreferenced/freed as part of cleanup). The code checks 'if (ret < 0) return ret;' correctly to bail out in that case, but only AFTER the buffer has potentially been consumed/freed. However, the fields dst_env->ambient_illuminance, dst_env->ambient_light_x, and dst_env->ambient_light_y are written AFTER the call to ff_frame_new_side_data_from_buf_ext succeeds check, but that write itself happens on the object that could have been freed as part of a partial failure inside ff_frame_new_side_data_from_buf_ext before it returns an error code being checked; more critically, on the success path the ownership of dst_env's underlying buffer has already been transferred to the side-data list, but the fields are still populated afterwards, i.e. dst_env may already be exposed to other consumers (e.g. other threads via frame side data, or freed if the ext function internally frees the buffer on certain failure paths) before initialization completes. This ordering was flagged by fuzzing (poc_hvcc_modified.mp4) as leading to a use-after-free: the buffer can be deallocated before its listed fields are initialized, because the struct data is only initialized after the call that can transfer/release ownership of the buffer, rather than before it.
findings.suggestion: Initialize dst_env->ambient_illuminance, ambient_light_x, and ambient_light_y BEFORE calling ff_frame_new_side_data_from_buf_ext(), so that the AVAmbientViewingEnvironment struct is fully populated before ownership of its backing buffer can be transferred or released by that call. This matches the actual upstream fix which moves the three assignment lines to occur immediately after allocation/before the side-data-adding call that may free/transfer the buffer on error or success paths.
findings.title: Use-after-free: AmbientViewingEnvironment side data written after side-data buffer may be freed on error path

fix_commit_message:
avfilter/vf_vif: Fix out of array access with small dimensions

The hand written boundary mirroring reflected an out of range index only
once, which is insufficient when the image dimension is smaller than the
filter half width (filt_w/2 == 8). A 1x1 input made the index reach 8
and -7, reading out of the src[]/temp[] arrays. Use avpriv_mirror(),
which mirrors repeatedly and stays in range for any dimension.

Fixes: out of array access

findings.message: In vif_filter1d(), when computing the vertical and horizontal 1D filter passes near image edges, out-of-range indices ii/jj are 'mirrored' back into range using a single-step reflection: `ii = ii < 0 ? -ii : (ii >= h ? 2*h - ii - 1 : ii)` (and analogously for jj/w). This single reflection only corrects an index that is out of range by up to h (or w) once. Because the filter half-width is filt_w/2 == 8, an index can be out of range by more than the image dimension when h or w is smaller than filt_w/2 (e.g. a 1x1 input). In that case a single reflection does not bring the index back into [0, h-1] (or [0, w-1]); the resulting ii/jj can still be negative or >= h/w (e.g. reaching 8 or -7 for h=w=1), causing src[ii*src_stride+j] and temp[jj] to be read out of bounds, leading to an out-of-bounds heap read / undefined behavior.
findings.suggestion: Replace the hand-rolled single-step reflection with a proper repeated mirroring function such as FFmpeg's avpriv_mirror(), which repeatedly folds the index back into range and is correct regardless of how small the dimension is relative to the filter width. E.g. `ii = avpriv_mirror(ii, h - 1);` and `jj = avpriv_mirror(jj, w - 1);`. Include libavutil/internal.h for avpriv_mirror().

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Insufficient boundary mirroring causes out-of-bounds array access with small image dimensions

ground_truth.root_cause: The mirroring/reflection logic used to clamp filter indices near image boundaries was implemented as a single conditional reflection (`ii < 0 ? -ii : ...`) rather than a proper repeated/folded mirroring, which is only valid when the amount of overshoot does not exceed the array dimension itself. Small image dimensions (smaller than filt_w/2) violate this assumption, allowing indices computed as `i - filt_w/2 + filt_i` to overshoot by more than h or w, producing indices still out of the valid [0, dim-1] range after one reflection.

agent_reasoning: The bug was a stack buffer overflow: `float en[2]` was only 2 elements, but the direction loop `for (g = 0; g < tns->n_filt[w]; g++)` could iterate with g=0,1,2 when n_filt=3 (AAC Main profile, long windows, order==TNS_MAX_ORDER). The access `en[g]` with g=2 reads past the end of the array. Additionally, `en[!g]` (logical NOT) evaluates to en[0] for g>=1, which was semantically wrong for g=1 and caused an out-of-bounds read for g=2. The fix expands `en` to 4 elements, measures energy across 3 frequency segments for the 3-filter case, and corrects the direction comparison to `en[g] < en[g+1]`, ensuring all accesses stay within bounds and the comparison is semantically correct for each filter.
commit_message:
[Merged] aacenc_tns: tune and reduce artifacts

There are a couple of major changes here:

1. Start using TNS coefficient compression.
2. Start using 3 bits per coefficient maximum for short windows.
The bits we save from these 2 changes seem to make a nice impact on the
rest of the file/windows.

3. Remove special case gain checking for short windows.
4. Modify the coefficient loop to support up to 3 windows.
The additional restrictions on TNS were something that was no in the
specifications and furthermore restricting TNS to only low energy short
windows was done to compensate for bugs elsewhere in the code.

Overall, the improvements here reduce crackling artifacts heard in very
noisy tracks.

Signed-off-by: Rostislav Pehlivanov <atomnuker@gmail.com>
fix_commit_message:
aacenc_tns: clamp filter direction energy measurement

The issue is that:

float en[2];
...
tns->n_filt[w] = is8 ? 1 : order != TNS_MAX_ORDER ? 2 : 3;
for (g = 0; g < tns->n_filt[w]; g++) {
    tns->direction[w][g] = slant != 2 ? slant : en[g] < en[!g];

When using the AAC Main profile, n_filt = 3, and slant is by
default 2 (normal long frames), g can go above 1.

en is the evolution of energy in the frequency domain for every
band at the given window. E.g. whether the energy is concentrated
at the top of each band, or the bottom.

For 2-pole filters, its straightforward.
For 3-pole filters, we need more than 2 measurements.

This commit properly implements support for 3-pole filters, by measuring
the band energy across three areas.

Do note that even xHE-AAC caps n_filt to 2, and only AAC Main allows
n_filt == 3.

Fixes https://trac.ffmpeg.org/ticket/11418

aacenc_tns: tune and reduce artifacts

There are a couple of major changes here:

1. Start using TNS coefficient compression.
2. Start using 3 bits per coefficient maximum for short windows.
The bits we save from these 2 changes seem to make a nice impact on the
rest of the file/windows.

3. Remove special case gain checking for short windows.
4. Modify the coefficient loop to support up to 3 windows.
The additional restrictions on TNS were something that was no in the
specifications and furthermore restricting TNS to only low energy short
windows was done to compensate for bugs elsewhere in the code.

Overall, the improvements here reduce crackling artifacts heard in very
noisy tracks.

Signed-off-by: Rostislav Pehlivanov <atomnuker@gmail.com>
pr_description:
The TNS filter direction is determined by comparing energy levels across different frequency regions. Previously, energy was only measured in two segments (start and end), which worked correctly for 1- or 2-filter configurations. However, when using AAC Main profile with long windows, `n_filt` can be 3, requiring energy comparisons across three regions for each filter's direction decision.

This commit renames `n_filt` to a pre-computed constant (shared across all windows, since it only depends on window type and order), expands the energy array from 2 to 4 elements, and adds proper 3-segment energy measurement when `n_filt != 2`. For the 2-filter case, the band energy is split into start and end halves as before, with `en[2] = en[0]` to support the symmetric direction comparison. For the 1- or 3-filter case, the band energy is measured in three thirds (start, middle, end), with `en[3] = en[0]` for the wraparound comparison.

The filter direction comparison is updated from `en[g] < en[!g]` to `en[g] < en[g + 1]`, which correctly expresses "is the energy in this band's region lower than the next region" for all filter indices including g=2 in the 3-filter case.
pr_title: aacenc_tns: properly support 3-filter TNS direction energy measurement

findings.message: The array `en` is declared as `float en[2]` (2 elements, indices 0 and 1), but the loop `for (g = 0; g < tns->n_filt[w]; g++)` can iterate with g=0, 1, 2 when `n_filt[w]` is set to 3 (which happens when `!is8 && order == TNS_MAX_ORDER`, i.e., AAC Main profile with long windows). Inside the loop, the expression `en[g] < en[!g]` accesses `en[2]` when g=2, which is a stack-buffer-overflow read past the end of the 2-element array. The `!g` expression also only ever evaluates to 0 or 1, so the comparison is semantically wrong for g=2 as well. An attacker can trigger this by encoding audio with the AAC Main profile (`-profile:a aac_main` or `-aac_pred true`).
findings.suggestion: Expand the `en` array to accommodate 3-filter cases (e.g., `float en[4]`) and compute energy measurements across three regions instead of two. Also change `en[g] < en[!g]` to `en[g] < en[g + 1]` so the direction comparison is meaningful for all filter indices.
findings.title: Stack buffer overflow via out-of-bounds access on en[2] array when n_filt=3

Vulnerability (LogicError): When demuxing-specific fields (parse_queue, raw_packet_buffer, raw_packet_buffer_size) were moved from FFFormatContext to FormatContextInternal, the call to ff_flush_packet_queue() in avformat_free_context() was guarded with 'if (s->iformat)' to prevent accessing demuxer-only fields on muxer contexts. However, ff_flush_packet_queue() also frees si->packet_buffer, which resides on FFFormatContext and is used by muxers (in mux.c via ff_interleave_add_packet). By guarding the entire ff_flush_packet_queue() call behind s->iformat, the muxer's packet_buffer is never freed when the format context is destroyed. If a muxing process fails while packets remain in the interleaving queue, those packets will leak. Root cause: The commit cb80ec0b moved parse_queue, raw_packet_buffer, and raw_packet_buffer_size to FormatContextInternal (demuxer-only). To prevent invalid memory access on muxer contexts, the entire ff_flush_packet_queue() call was guarded behind 'if (s->iformat)'. However, ff_flush_packet_queue() also clears si->packet_buffer which lives on FFFormatContext (accessible for both muxers and demuxers). The overly broad guard prevents packet_buffer from being freed for muxers.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix e262411f329d on top of intro e424abc3a093 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): The check `if (!eval->exprs)` on line 116 only validates against a NULL pointer, but does not catch the case where `eval->exprs` is a non-NULL empty string (""). When an empty expression string is provided (e.g., via `aeval=:1`), `eval->exprs` points to an empty string. `av_strdup("")` on line 107 returns a valid non-NULL pointer, so the ENOMEM check on line 113 passes. The NULL check on line 116 also passes because the pointer is non-NULL. Then `av_strtok("", "|", &buf)` on line 149 returns NULL immediately since there are no tokens, so the while loop never executes and `last_expr` remains uninitialized/NULL with `nb_channels` staying at 0. When `expected_nb_channels > 0`, the code on line 154-156 calls `ADD_EXPRESSION(last_expr)` with a NULL `last_expr`, which passes NULL to `av_expr_parse()` as the expression string. Inside `av_expr_parse`, `strlen()` is called on this NULL pointer, causing a SEGV (null pointer dereference). Root cause: The input validation check `if (!eval->exprs)` only tests for a NULL pointer but not for an empty string. In C, an empty string `""` is a valid non-NULL pointer, so the check passes. The code then fails to parse any expressions from the empty string, leaving `last_expr` as NULL, which is later passed to `av_expr_parse` causing a null pointer dereference.

+This filter accepts the following options:

+@section aeval
+
+Modify an audio signal according to the specified expressions.
+
+This filter accepts one or more expressions (one for each channel),
+which are evaluated and used to modify a corresponding audio signal.
+
+This filter accepts the following options:
+
+@table @option
+@item exprs
+Set the '|'-separated expressions list for each separate channel. If
+the number of input channels is greater than the number of
+expressions, the last specified expression is used for the remaining
+output channels.
+
+@item channel_layout, c
+Set output channel layout. If not specified, the channel layout is
+specified by the number of expressions. If set to @samp{same}, it will
+use by default the same input channel layout.
+@end table
+
+Each expression in @var{exprs} can contain the following constants and functions:
+
+@table @option
+@item ch
+channel number of the current expression
+
+@item n
+number of the evaluated sample, starting from 0
+
+@item s
+sample rate
+
+@item t
+time of the evaluated sample expressed in seconds
+
+@item nb_in_channels
+@item nb_out_channels
+input and output number of channels
+
+@item val(CH)
+the value of input channel with number @var{CH}
+@end table
+
+Note: this filter is slow. For faster processing you should use a
+dedicated filter.
+
+@subsection Examples
+
+@itemize
+@item
+Half volume:
+@example
+aeval=val(ch)/2:c=same
+@end example
+
+@item
+Invert phase of the second channel:
+@example
+eval=val(0)|-val(1)
+@end example
+@end itemize

findings.message: The check `if (!eval->exprs)` on line 116 only validates against a NULL pointer, but does not catch the case where `eval->exprs` is a non-NULL empty string (""). When an empty expression string is provided (e.g., via `aeval=:1`), `eval->exprs` points to an empty string. `av_strdup("")` on line 107 returns a valid non-NULL pointer, so the ENOMEM check on line 113 passes. The NULL check on line 116 also passes because the pointer is non-NULL. Then `av_strtok("", "|", &buf)` on line 149 returns NULL immediately since there are no tokens, so the while loop never executes and `last_expr` remains uninitialized/NULL with `nb_channels` staying at 0. When `expected_nb_channels > 0`, the code on line 154-156 calls `ADD_EXPRESSION(last_expr)` with a NULL `last_expr`, which passes NULL to `av_expr_parse()` as the expression string. Inside `av_expr_parse`, `strlen()` is called on this NULL pointer, causing a SEGV (null pointer dereference).
findings.suggestion: Change the check from `if (!eval->exprs)` to `if (!eval->exprs || !*eval->exprs)` to also reject empty strings. This ensures that an empty expression string is caught early and reported as an error, rather than allowing execution to continue to `av_expr_parse` with a NULL expression pointer.

ground_truth.root_cause: The input validation check `if (!eval->exprs)` only tests for a NULL pointer but not for an empty string. In C, an empty string `""` is a valid non-NULL pointer, so the check passes. The code then fails to parse any expressions from the empty string, leaving `last_expr` as NULL, which is later passed to `av_expr_parse` causing a null pointer dereference.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f2c46512ec48 on top of intro c002e9bc863c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): The prepareForSwap function only copies dynamic element buffers when the buffer is inside the nursery (ChunkPtrIsInsideNursery), but fails to consider the case where a tenured object with a buffer marked as nursery-owned is swapped with a nursery object. When swapping a nursery object with a tenured object, the tenured object can end up with a pointer to a buffer that is marked as nursery-owned. During the next nursery collection, this buffer will be freed because the GC believes it belongs to the nursery, causing a use-after-free when the tenured object later accesses the freed buffer. Root cause: The introduction of the buffer allocator for JSObject elements changed how dynamic element buffers are managed during object swaps. The new code only copies buffers when they are physically inside the nursery memory region, but fails to consider cases where a buffer is allocated via AllocBuffer with nursery ownership semantics. When swapping objects between nursery and tenured heaps, the buffer ownership metadata can become inconsistent with the object's heap location, causing the GC to incorrectly free the buffer. The secondary issue is that shifted elements (array elements that have been logically removed from the front) are not accounted for when copying the buffer.

fix_commit_message:
Bug 1941876 - Fix handling of dynamic elements when swapping objects r=jandem

There are two problems here. Firstly, swapping a nursery and a tenured object
can leave dynamic element buffers with the wrong ownership kind. For example
we could have a tenured object with a nursery-owned buffer. This could cause
UAF if the buffer we collected in the next nursery collection.

Secondly, the code to copy dynamic elements doesn't account for shifted
elements.

I added the testcase but also updated the testObjectSwap JSAPI test to catch
this problem. The change to BufferAllocator::checkChunkGCStateNotInUse is to
speed up this test.

findings.message: When copying dynamic element buffers during object swap, the code uses memmove with 'elements' (which points to the shifted position) rather than the unshifted header. Additionally, when assigning the new elements pointer, it does not account for the number of shifted elements. This causes the copied buffer to have an incorrect header pointer, leading to memory corruption when the shifted elements are accessed.

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable code path where dynamic element buffers are only copied when physically inside the nursery (ChunkPtrIsInsideNursery check on line 1038), but fails to check buffer allocator ownership metadata. This misses cases where a tenured object has a buffer marked as nursery-owned, causing the buffer to be incorrectly freed during GC.

Orchestrates the object swap operation by calling prepareForSwap for both objects (lines 1304, 1307, 1312, 1315) and then fixupAfterSwap. Understanding this flow is essential to see that when swapping a nursery object with a tenured object, the tenured object can end up with a buffer pointer that has nursery ownership semantics even though the buffer is not in nursery memory.

Restores object state after swap but only handles slots correctly (lines 1093-1094). Lines 1097-1100 handle dynamic elements but rely on prepareForSwap having correctly saved the buffer. If prepareForSwap didn't copy a nursery-allocated buffer, fixupAfterSwap won't correct the issue, allowing the dangling pointer to persist.

Shows how element buffers are handled during nursery collection. This function allocates new tenured buffers (lines 931-941) and copies elements. A reviewer must understand that the GC will free nursery-allocated buffers after this, which is why the buffer ownership metadata must be consistent with the actual allocation site.

The new code only copies buffers when they are physically inside the nursery memory region, but fails to consider cases where a buffer is allocated via AllocBuffer with nursery ownership semantics. When swapping objects between nursery and tenured heaps, the buffer ownership metadata can become inconsistent with the object's heap location, causing the GC to incorrectly free the buffer. The secondary issue is that shifted elements (array elements that have been logically removed from the front) are not accounted for when copying the buffer.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix c0937884a036 on top of intro a0f1dba96115 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (RaceCondition): The `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch` function unconditionally uses `NS_DispatchToMainThread` to dispatch messages. However, when ServiceWorkerContainer is exposed on worker threads (via WorkerNavigator), this causes messages to be dispatched to the main thread instead of the worker thread. This results in a race condition where the worker's JS runtime may be accessed from the main thread while it's being used on the worker thread, leading to memory safety violations and potential exploitation. Root cause: When exposing ServiceWorkerContainer to worker threads in Bug 1131324, the code change removed `MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread())` from `DispatchMessage()` to allow it to work on worker threads, but failed to update the corresponding `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch()` function. This function still used `NS_DispatchToMainThread`, causing messages to always be dispatched to the main thread regardless of which thread the ServiceWorkerContainer belongs to.

findings.message: The `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch` function unconditionally uses `NS_DispatchToMainThread` to dispatch messages. However, when ServiceWorkerContainer is exposed on worker threads (via WorkerNavigator), this causes messages to be dispatched to the main thread instead of the worker thread. This results in a race condition where the worker's JS runtime may be accessed from the main thread while it's being used on the worker thread, leading to memory safety violations and potential exploitation.

related_locations.description: DispatchMessage function receives messages from wrong thread, removed MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread()) in this commit which should have been a warning sign

findings.suggestion: When exposing ServiceWorkerContainer to worker threads, the dispatch mechanism must dispatch to the current thread (the thread that owns the ServiceWorkerContainer), not unconditionally to the main thread. Use `NS_DispatchToCurrentThread` instead of `NS_DispatchToMainThread`.
findings.title: Thread-unsafe dispatch in ServiceWorkerContainer

fix_commit.author: Olli Pettay
fix_commit.message: Bug 1942169 - Dispatch messages to the current thread r=asuth

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable code that unconditionally dispatches to the main thread using NS_DispatchToMainThread, regardless of whether the ServiceWorkerContainer belongs to a window (main thread) or worker (worker thread). This causes messages to be dispatched to the wrong thread when the container is on a worker, leading to race conditions where the worker's JS runtime may be accessed from the main thread while in use on the worker thread.

This function was modified in Bug 1131324 to support worker threads (MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread()) was removed), but the corresponding caller EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch was not updated. A reviewer must see that DispatchMessage can execute on worker threads but is being dispatched to the main thread unconditionally, creating a thread-safety violation. The function accesses JS context and global objects that must be accessed on the correct thread.

This function receives messages from service workers and calls EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch. A reviewer must understand that this function can be called on either the main thread (for window contexts) or worker threads (for worker contexts), and the dispatching must respect the current thread context. The function makes no thread checks before calling the vulnerable dispatch function.

This function exposes ServiceWorkerContainer on worker threads via WorkerNavigator.serviceWorker, making it accessible in worker contexts. This is the code path introduced in Bug 1131324 that enabled the vulnerability. A reviewer must understand that ServiceWorkerContainer can now exist on worker threads, not just main thread, which makes the thread-agnostic dispatch critical.

This function delivers messages to ServiceWorkerContainer by calling container->ReceiveMessage(). A reviewer must understand that this call can occur on any thread (main or worker) depending on where the ServiceWorkerContainer lives. The function operates on the thread owning the ClientSource/global object, which can be a worker thread, triggering the race condition when the message is incorrectly dispatched to the main thread.

ground_truth.root_cause: When exposing ServiceWorkerContainer to worker threads in Bug 1131324, the code change removed `MOZ_ASSERT(NS_IsMainThread())` from `DispatchMessage()` to allow it to work on worker threads, but failed to update the corresponding `EnqueueReceivedMessageDispatch()` function. This function still used `NS_DispatchToMainThread`, causing messages to always be dispatched to the main thread regardless of which thread the ServiceWorkerContainer belongs to.

pr_description: Differential Revision: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D213725
pr_title: Bug 1131324 - Expose ServiceWorkerContainer on WorkerNavigator. r=dom-worker-reviewers,webidl,smaug

agent_reasoning: The bug-introducing commit added PipeWire video-capture support with the cleanup order reversed in ~PipeWireNode(): pw_proxy_destroy(proxy_) was called first, freeing the proxy and its listener_list, before spa_hook_remove(&node_listener_) ran. Since the hook internally references the proxy's listener_list, the subsequent spa_hook_remove() would access freed memory — a use-after-free. The fix swaps the two lines so the hook is removed while the proxy (and its listener_list) is still alive, then the proxy is safely destroyed.

pr_description:
When destroying a PipeWire camera node, the spa hook must be removed before the proxy object is destroyed. The hook is associated with the proxy's listener_list; destroying the proxy first frees that list while the hook still holds a reference to it. Calling spa_hook_remove() afterwards would then access freed memory.

This change corrects the destruction order in PipeWireNode::~PipeWireNode() so that spa_hook_remove() is called before pw_proxy_destroy(), ensuring the hook is cleanly unregistered from the still-valid proxy before the proxy is torn down.
pr_title: PipeWire camera: Fix cleanup order to avoid use-after-free

findings.message: The destructor calls pw_proxy_destroy() before spa_hook_remove(), which destroys the proxy object before removing the hook that is associated with it. The hook contains a listener_list reference (proxy->listener_list) that is freed when pw_proxy_destroy() is called. The subsequent spa_hook_remove() then attempts to access this freed memory to remove the hook from the list, causing a use-after-free vulnerability.
findings.suggestion: Swap the order of cleanup operations: remove the hook first before destroying the proxy object, since the hook is associated with the proxy and its listener_list.
findings.title: Use-After-Free due to incorrect cleanup order in PipeWireNode destructor

fix_commit.author: Jan Grulich
fix_commit.message: Bug 1942551 - WebRTC backport: PipeWire camera: Fix cleanup order r=pehrsons,webrtc-reviewers

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable cleanup sequence where pw_proxy_destroy() is called before spa_hook_remove(). The proxy destruction frees the listener_list that the hook still references, causing use-after-free when spa_hook_remove() tries to access it.

Constructor establishes the data dependency between proxy_ and node_listener_. Line 99-100 creates the proxy via pw_registry_bind, and line 108-109 registers the hook listener on that proxy using pw_node_add_listener. This shows the hook is tied to the proxy's lifetime and requires the proxy to remain valid during hook removal.

Triggers destruction of PipeWireNode objects via std::erase_if on nodes_ vector. When a unique_ptr<PipeWireNode, PipeWireNodeDeleter> is erased, it invokes the custom deleter containing the vulnerable cleanup sequence. This is a key path that exercises the bug during device removal.

ground_truth.root_cause: Incorrect destruction order in resource cleanup. The hook is associated with the proxy object and internally references the proxy's listener_list. By destroying the proxy first, the listener_list is freed, but the hook still holds a dangling reference to it. When spa_hook_remove() tries to remove the hook from the list, it accesses freed memory.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 8354ae880cf5 on top of intro 9385dab26b90 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (TypeConfusion): The change to emitGuardIsNumber removed automatic conversion of Int32/Float32 inputs to Double. This broke an implicit assumption in visitSign that when input and output types differ, the input is always Double and output is Int32. When MSign now receives Int32 input with Double output, the else branch incorrectly asserts the opposite and uses LSignDI (Double input, Int32 output) instead of a proper LSignID (Int32 input, Double output). This causes: 1) Writing to an unrelated general purpose register instead of the allocated float output register, 2) The allocated float register retains its previous value, enabling type confusion where uninitialized/stale float data can be read as legitimate values. Root cause: The change in emitGuardIsNumber (bug 1941826) removed automatic conversion of Int32/Float32 inputs to Double for number guards. This was intended to enable better Float32 optimizations. However, downstream code in visitSign had hardcoded assumptions that when MSign input and output types differ, the input is always Double and output is Int32. The change created a new valid case (Int32 input, Double output) that was not handled, causing assertion failures and type confusion when the wrong LIR instruction was selected.
commit_message:
[Merged] Bug 1941826: Don't guard for number types in emitGuardIsNumber. r=jandem

This aligns Warp transpilation with CacheIR, because in CacheIR `NumberOperandId`
can mean either `Double` or `Int32`. (There isn't yet an explicit
`DoubleOperandId` to denote a value is guaranteed to be a Double.)

Float32 optimisations can be more easily applied when `MToDouble` isn't emitted
and we also no longer need the `MToDouble::canProduceFloat32` override added in
D215775.

Differential Revision: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D234348

findings.message: The change to emitGuardIsNumber removed automatic conversion of Int32/Float32 inputs to Double. This broke an implicit assumption in visitSign that when input and output types differ, the input is always Double and output is Int32. When MSign now receives Int32 input with Double output, the else branch incorrectly asserts the opposite and uses LSignDI (Double input, Int32 output) instead of a proper LSignID (Int32 input, Double output). This causes: 1) Writing to an unrelated general purpose register instead of the allocated float output register, 2) The allocated float register retains its previous value, enabling type confusion where uninitialized/stale float data can be read as legitimate values.
findings.suggestion: When removing the automatic type conversion in emitGuardIsNumber, all downstream consumers that rely on specific type combinations need to be audited and updated. The visitSign function in Lowering.cpp needs to handle the new case where input is Int32 and output is Double by adding a new LIR instruction (LSignID) and corresponding code generation.
findings.title: Missing type conversion case in visitSign causes JIT type confusion

findings.message: The visitSign function only handles two cases: (1) same input/output types, and (2) Double input with Int32 output. After the change in emitGuardIsNumber, a third case became possible: Int32 input with Double output. The assertions at lines 2100-2101 assume the impossible third case cannot happen, but it now can. When this case is hit, the code incorrectly creates an LSignDI instruction (for Double->Int32) when it should create an LSignID instruction (for Int32->Double). This register type mismatch leads to writing to wrong registers and type confusion.
findings.suggestion: Add explicit handling for the Int32 input / Double output case by creating a new LSignID LIR instruction and corresponding CodeGenerator visitor. The fix should enumerate all four possible type combinations explicitly rather than relying on implicit assumptions.
findings.title: Incomplete type handling in LIRGenerator::visitSign

must_cover.reason: Contains the vulnerable change that removed automatic Int32/Float32 to Double conversion. When IsNumberType(def->type()) returns true for Int32, the function now returns early without converting to Double, breaking the postcondition that downstream code expects.

Creates MSign instruction with NumberOperandId input and Int32 output type. This function relies on emitGuardIsNumber to ensure proper type handling, and passes the incorrectly-typed operand to the MSign constructor, propagating the type confusion to the lowering phase.

Contains the broken assumption at lines 2188-2192. When input type differs from output type and output is Int32, the code assumes input MUST be Double and creates LSignDI instruction. This assumption is violated when emitGuardIsNumber allows Int32 to pass through, causing wrong LIR instruction selection (LSignDI expects Double input but receives Int32), leading to wrong register writes and type confusion.

The change created a new valid case (Int32 input, Double output) that was not handled, causing assertion failures and type confusion when the wrong LIR instruction was selected.

This aligns Warp transpilation with CacheIR, because in CacheIR `NumberOperandId`
can mean either `Double` or `Int32`. (There isn't yet an explicit
`DoubleOperandId` to denote a value is guaranteed to be a Double.)

Float32 optimisations can be more easily applied when `MToDouble` isn't emitted
and we also no longer need the `MToDouble::canProduceFloat32` override added in
D215775.

commit_message:
[Merged] Bug 1867249, part 1: Implemented new cache to determine selected nodes. r=sefeng,dom-core

Determining if a node is selected is a super-hot code path,
which at times introduces jank both in Reflow and Painting.
This is due to each node comparing its position to the range's start and end point,
which even happens several times (`nsINode::IsSelected()` and `Selection::LookupSelection()`).
In worst cases, this can lead to reflow which takes several minutes.

This patch introduces a cache which contains all fully selected nodes,
and lives throughout one `PresShell::DoReflow()` call.
Collecting all selected nodes of a selection is very fast.
The selected nodes are then stored in a hash set.
During reflow the check if a node is selected first checks the cache
if the node is fully selected, and otherwise goes through the existing
code to check if the node is partially selected.

findings.message: The `ContentIteratorBase` class declares raw pointer members (`mCurNode`, `mFirst`, `mLast`, `mClosestCommonInclusiveAncestor`) without default initialization. When the `Init()` method fails early (e.g., due to invalid range boundaries), these pointers retain their indeterminate values. Since `IsDone()` checks `!mCurNode` and `GetCurrentNode()` returns `mCurNode`, using an iterator after a failed `Init()` call leads to accessing garbage memory.
findings.suggestion: Default-initialize all pointer members to nullptr. Additionally, add [[nodiscard]] attribute to Init() methods to enforce checking return values at compile time.

Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): When Error.captureStackTrace is called with a startAt function that hasn't been seen yet on the stack, the stackChain vector remains empty. However, the code for reparenting async stacks unconditionally accesses stackChain[stackChain.length() - 1], which causes an out-of-bounds access when stackChain is empty. The condition for entering the reparenting block checks multiple criteria (activation change, async stack presence, etc.) but fails to verify that stackChain actually contains frames to reparent. The vulnerability arises because the macro's auto-generated UNLINK handler simply nulls out the RefPtr without first calling RemoveMutationObserver(this). Bug 1937634 - Make txMozillaXSLTProcessor::mStylesheetDocument strong. r=peterv

Differential Revision: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D232262
pr_description:
## Summary

`txMozillaXSLTProcessor::mStylesheetDocument` was previously a raw (weak) pointer to a `Document`. This PR converts it to a `RefPtr<mozilla::dom::Document>` to ensure the processor holds a proper owning reference for the lifetime of its association with the stylesheet document.

Previously the raw pointer carried an implicit assumption that some other owner would keep the document alive for the duration of the XSLT processor's use. Using a `RefPtr` makes that ownership explicit and avoids the risk of the document being freed while the processor still holds a reference to it.

The member is intentionally not added to the cycle-collection participant list: the XSLT processor registers itself as a mutation observer on the document via `AddMutationObserver(this)` in `ImportStylesheet()` and deregisters in the corresponding cleanup paths. Participating in cycle collection for this member would require a custom unlink handler to safely deregister the observer before the reference is cleared, which is not implemented here. The `RefPtr` alone is sufficient to guarantee lifetime safety without that complexity.

## Test plan

- [ ] Run existing XSLT-related tests (`dom/xslt/`)
- [ ] Verify no regressions in cycle-collector-related tests

findings.message: The change to make mStylesheetDocument a strong reference (RefPtr) added it to the NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE macro, which handles both traverse and unlink operations automatically. However, when the cycle collector unlinks mStylesheetDocument (sets it to null), it does not call RemoveMutationObserver(this) first. The txMozillaXSLTProcessor registers itself as a mutation observer on mStylesheetDocument via AddMutationObserver(this) in ImportStylesheet(). When the document is unlinked during cycle collection, the document still holds a dangling pointer to the txMozillaXSLTProcessor as a mutation observer. When the document is later destroyed and tries to notify observers, it accesses freed memory, causing a use-after-free crash in nsINode::LastRelease().
findings.suggestion: When using NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE with mStylesheetDocument, a separate UNLINK handler must be implemented that calls mStylesheetDocument->RemoveMutationObserver(this) before the reference is cleared. The correct approach is to use NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE_CLASS with separate UNLINK_BEGIN/END and TRAVERSE_BEGIN/END macros, where UNLINK calls Reset() or explicitly removes the mutation observer before unlinking the document reference.
findings.suggestion_code:
NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_WRAPPERCACHE_CLASS(txMozillaXSLTProcessor)

NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK_BEGIN(txMozillaXSLTProcessor)
  NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK(mOwner, mSource)
  MOZ_RELEASE_ASSERT(tmp->mState == State::None);
  tmp->Reset(IgnoreErrors());  // This calls RemoveMutationObserver
  NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK_PRESERVED_WRAPPER
NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_UNLINK_END

NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_TRAVERSE_BEGIN(txMozillaXSLTProcessor)
  NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_TRAVERSE(
      mOwner, mStylesheetDocument, mEmbeddedStylesheetRoot, mSource, mVariables)
NS_IMPL_CYCLE_COLLECTION_TRAVERSE_END

Vulnerability (DataRace): The EnsureLocale() function modifies mLocale member variable from the main thread without proper synchronization, while GetLocale() reads mLocale concurrently from worker threads. findings.suggestion: Add a guard to prevent re-initialization of mLocale after it's been set. Introduce a boolean flag mLocaleInitialized and check it at the beginning of EnsureLocale() to return early if already initialized. Mark the flag with MOZ_GUARDED_BY for thread safety annotation.
findings.title: Data race on mLocale string member without synchronization

findings.message: EnsureLocale() is called from multiple locations without coordination: IDBFactory::AllowedForWindowInternal (main thread), WorkerPrivate::GetLoadInfo (main thread), and RemoteWorkerChild::ExecWorkerOnMainThread (main thread). While all these callers run on the main thread, DOM worker threads concurrently access GetLocale() which reads mLocale. The lack of synchronization between the writing main thread and reading worker threads creates a TOCTOU-style race where mLocale can be modified between the worker thread's check and use.
findings.suggestion: Ensure EnsureLocale() is idempotent by only initializing mLocale once. Once initialized, subsequent calls should be no-ops. This prevents the string buffer from being reallocated while worker threads may be reading it.
findings.title: Unsafe concurrent access to mLocale from multiple call sites
