RED-129256, Fix TOUCH command from script in no-touch mode (#13512)

When a client in no-touch mode issues a TOUCH command on a key, the
key’s access time should be updated, but in scripts, and module's
RM_Call, it isn’t updated.
Command proc should be matched to the executing client, not the current
client.

Co-authored-by: Udi Ron <udi@speedb.io>
fix_commit_message:
Fix crash in lookupKey() when `executing_client` is NULL (#14415)

This PR is based on:
https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey/pull/2347

This was introduced in https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13512

The server crashes with a null pointer dereference when lookupKey() is
called from handleClientsBlockedOnKey(). The crash occurs because
server.executing_client is NULL, but the code attempts to access
server.executing_client->cmd->proc without checking.

**Crash scenario:**
Client 1 enables CLIENT NO-TOUCH
Client 2 blocks on BRPOP mylist 0
Client 1 executes RPUSH mylist elem
When unblocking Client 2, lookupKey() dereferences NULL
server.executing_client → crash

**Solution**
Added proper null checks before dereferencing server.executing_client:
Check if LOOKUP_NOTOUCH flag is already set before attempting to modify
it
Verify both server.current_client and server.executing_client are not
NULL before accessing their members
Maintain the TOUCH command exception for scripts

**Testing**
Added regression test in tests/unit/type/list.tcl that reproduces and
verifies the fix for this crash scenario.

This fix is based on valkey-io/valkey#2347

Co-authored-by: Uri Yagelnik <uriy@amazon.com>
Co-authored-by: Ran Shidlansik <ranshid@amazon.com>

findings.message: In lookupKey(), the CLIENT NO-TOUCH check was changed to use server.executing_client->cmd->proc instead of server.current_client->cmd->proc, in order to correctly detect the TOUCH command when it is invoked via scripts/RM_Call. However, the code only null-checks server.current_client before entering the branch; it never checks whether server.executing_client itself is NULL before dereferencing it. server.executing_client is NULL in several legitimate contexts, most notably when handleClientsBlockedOnKey() runs after a key-modifying command (e.g. RPUSH) unblocks a client blocked on BRPOP: the lookupKey() call performed while serving the unblocked client's read happens outside of any executing client context. If the client that owns/triggered this lookup path has CLIENT_NO_TOUCH set (server.current_client non-NULL and flagged), the code proceeds to dereference server.executing_client->cmd->proc while server.executing_client is NULL, producing a NULL pointer dereference and crashing the server.
findings.suggestion:
Guard the dereference of server.executing_client with an explicit NULL check before accessing its cmd field, and skip re-evaluating/altering the LOOKUP_NOTOUCH flag if it is already set. Only dereference server.executing_client when it is non-NULL, e.g.:

if (((flags & LOOKUP_NOTOUCH) == 0) &&
    (server.current_client && server.current_client->flags & CLIENT_NO_TOUCH) &&
    (server.executing_client && server.executing_client->cmd->proc != touchCommand))
    flags |= LOOKUP_NOTOUCH;
findings.suggestion_code:
if (((flags & LOOKUP_NOTOUCH) == 0) &&
    (server.current_client && server.current_client->flags & CLIENT_NO_TOUCH) &&
    (server.executing_client && server.executing_client->cmd->proc != touchCommand))
    flags |= LOOKUP_NOTOUCH;

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 08d714d0e5d5 on top of intro 701f06657d20 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): Redis's clientsCron periodically frees a client's command-argument vector (c->argv) if the client appears idle, to reduce per-connection memory overhead. The idle check introduced in PR #13521 only verified `!c->argv || c->argc`, which fails to detect a client that is idle in the middle of sending a multibulk command (header received, args not yet complete), a state identifiable via a non-zero c->multibulklen with c->argc still 0. In that state the cron job frees argv and resets argv_len to 0 concurrently with the client's own parsing state machine. When the client subsequently sends more data and the parser (processMultibulkBuffer) resumes, the growth calculation for argv uses the now-zeroed argv_len, which can cause a zero-size realloc and leave c->argv as NULL while argc/multibulklen still indicate pending arguments, leading to a NULL pointer dereference / crash when the parser writes the next argument into argv[c->argc]. Root cause: Missing/incorrect idle-check condition: the function used to decide whether it's safe to free a client's argv only considered c->argc, not c->multibulklen, so it incorrectly treated a client that is mid-command-parse (multibulk header received but args pending) as idle/safe-to-free. This is compounded by replaceClientCommandVector() not keeping c->argv_len in sync with c->argc, which the companion fix also addresses.
commit_message:
Reuse c->argv after command execution to reduce memory allocation overhead (#13521)

inspred by https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/12730

Before this PR, we allocate new memory to store the user command
arguments, however, if the size of the current `c->argv` is larger than
the current command, we can reuse the previously allocated argv to avoid
allocating new memory for the current command.
And we will free `c->argv` in client cron when the client is idle for 2
seconds.

findings.message:
clientsCronFreeArgvIfIdle() frees c->argv and resets c->argv_len to 0 whenever `c->argc == 0` and the client has been idle for more than 2 seconds. However, `c->argc == 0` does not mean the client is not in the middle of receiving a command: if the client has sent a partial multibulk request (e.g. only the `*3
$3
SET
` header), `c->multibulklen` is non-zero while `c->argc` is still 0, because no argv elements have been parsed yet. The idle check only guards on `!c->argv || c->argc`, so it does not exclude this in-the-middle-of-parsing state, and the cron job frees argv (setting it to NULL) and sets argv_len to 0 out from under the client. When the client later sends the rest of the command and processMultibulkBuffer() resumes parsing, it computes the new argv size as `min(c->argv_len*2, c->argc+c->multibulklen)` which evaluates to `min(0, multibulklen)` = 0 (since argv_len is 0), so it calls zrealloc(NULL, 0), which can return NULL. c->argv is then left NULL while argc/multibulklen indicate more arguments are expected, and subsequent writes to c->argv[c->argc] dereference a NULL pointer, crashing the server.
findings.suggestion: Guard clientsCronFreeArgvIfIdle so it never frees argv while the client is still in the middle of parsing a command, by also checking c->multibulklen (and ensuring argv_len tracking stays consistent elsewhere, e.g. in replaceClientCommandVector). Additionally, add a defensive assertion in processMultibulkBuffer that argv_len is non-zero before growing argv, to fail loudly instead of silently producing a NULL argv.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 6ea4e2c949c7 on top of intro 7665bdc91aa6 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DataRace): Redis's dict.h `struct dict` packs the `pauserehash` (15-bit) and `useStoredKeyApi` (1-bit) bit-fields into the same machine word. Mutating a bit-field requires a read-modify-write of the whole storage unit it shares with adjacent bit-fields, which is not atomic. PR #13696 ('Offload lookupCommand into IO threads when threaded IO is enabled') made I/O threads call lookupCommand()->dictFind() on the global server.commands dict concurrently with the main thread's rehash-pause bookkeeping (dictNext()/dictPauseRehashing/dictResumeRehashing, which mutate pauserehash). This produced a genuine, TSAN/ASAN-detectable data race between the main thread's RMW of pauserehash and the I/O thread's read of useStoredKeyApi on the same storage word, even though the two bit-fields are logically independent. Root cause: Two logically-independent bit-fields (pauserehash and useStoredKeyApi) inside struct dict share the same underlying storage unit, so a write to one requires a non-atomic read-modify-write that can race with a concurrent read/write of the other. This latent structural hazard became an actual exploitable/observable data race once PR #13696 introduced concurrent, unsynchronized access to the command dict (server.commands) from I/O threads via lookupCommand()->dictFind(), racing with the main thread's rehash-pause bookkeeping on the same dict.
commit_message:
Offload `lookupCommand` into IO threads when threaded IO is enabled (#13696)

From flame graph, we could see `lookupCommand` in main thread costs much
CPU, so we can let IO threads to perform `lookupCommand`.

To avoid race condition among multiple IO threads, made the following
changes:
- Pause all IO threads when register or unregister commands
- Force a full rehashing of the command table dict when resizing

fix_commit_message:
Fix race condition for lookupCommand (#14466)

Fixes data race where main thread modifies pauserehash in dictNext while
IO thread reads `useStoredKeyApi()` in `lookupCommand()->dictFind()`
path.
ASAN detected overlapping memory access at same byte offset
causing race condition. When bit fields are adjacent in a struct,
modifying one bit field requires a read-modify-write operation on the
entire memory unit, which can cause race conditions with concurrent
access to other bit fields in the same unit.
This was introduced by https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13696,
although it was changed by https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/14440,
but this issue still exist.

The fix moves `useStoredKeyApi` to share a memory word with
`pauseAutoResize` instead. Since `pauseAutoResize` is never modified for
`server.commands`, this eliminates the race condition while maintaining
memory efficiency through bit field packing.

```
make SANITIZER=thread
./runtest --tsan --config io-threads 4 --accurate --verbose --dump-logs --single unit/obuf-limits --loop --stop
```

findings.message: PR #13696 changed processInputBuffer() so that, when an I/O thread is handling a client (c->running_tid != IOTHREAD_MAIN_THREAD_ID), it calls lookupCommand(c->argv, c->argc) directly from the I/O thread and caches the result in c->iolookedcmd, instead of deferring the whole lookup to the main thread. lookupCommand() ends up calling dictFind() on server.commands, which reads the dict's `useStoredKeyApi : 1` bit-field. That bit-field is packed into the same storage word as the `pauserehash : 15` bit-field in `struct dict` (src/dict.h). The main thread concurrently mutates `pauserehash` (e.g. via dictPauseRehashing/dictResumeRehashing invoked while iterating with dictNext()), which requires a non-atomic read-modify-write of the entire shared storage unit. Because C bit-fields sharing a machine word are not individually atomic, a main-thread RMW on `pauserehash` racing with an IO-thread read of `useStoredKeyApi` on the very same word constitutes a data race (confirmed by ThreadSanitizer/ASAN). Before this commit, lookupCommand()/dictFind() on server.commands was only ever executed on the main thread, so no concurrent access to this shared storage word existed; this commit is what introduces genuine multi-threaded access to the racy bit-fields.
findings.suggestion: Do not share a storage unit between a bit-field that is mutated concurrently from the main thread (pauserehash, via dictNext()/dictPauseRehashing) and a bit-field that is read from other threads (useStoredKeyApi), for dicts such as server.commands that can be looked up from I/O threads. Either give pauserehash a full-width, non-bitfield type (as ultimately done in the ac tual fix) so mutating it cannot perform an RMW on neighboring bits, or avoid calling lookupCommand()/dictFind() on server.commands from I/O threads altogether without additional synchronization.
findings.title: Data race on adjacent bit-fields of struct dict when lookupCommand is offloaded to IO threads

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Data race on adjacent bit-fields of struct dict when lookupCommand is offloaded to IO threads

ground_truth.root_cause: Two logically-independent bit-fields (pauserehash and useStoredKeyApi) inside struct dict share the same underlying storage unit, so a write to one requires a non-atomic read-modify-write that can race with a concurrent read/write of the other. This latent structural hazard became an actual exploitable/observable data race once PR #13696 introduced concurrent, unsynchronized access to the command dict (server.commands) from I/O threads via lookupCommand()->dictFind(), racing with the main thread's rehash-pause bookkeeping on the same dict.

agent_reasoning: Without this change, dbRandomKey()'s while(1) loop only bails out via the maxtries counter when `server.masterhost` is set (i.e., on a replica). Once CLIENT PAUSE WRITE/ALL was introduced, expireIfNeeded() gained a second path where it returns "expired" without deleting the key whenever the server is paused — including on a primary. If a primary's keyspace consists entirely of volatile, already-expired keys and the server is paused, dbRandomKey() repeatedly draws the same expired key, expireIfNeeded() refuses to remove it, and the maxtries condition (gated only on masterhost) never fires, causing an infinite loop that hangs the single-threaded event loop (DoS). Adding `|| areClientsPaused()` to the maxtries condition restores the invariant that the safety valve fires whenever expireIfNeeded() can leave an expired key in place without eventually returning 0.

findings.message: dbRandomKey() retries dictGetFairRandomKey() in a while(1) loop whenever the randomly-picked key is volatile and logically expired, relying on expireIfNeeded() to either actually delete the key (allowing the loop to terminate on a non-expired pick) or on a maxtries safety valve to force termination when the DB cannot make progress. The safety valve `if (allvolatile && server.masterhost && --maxtries == 0) return keyobj;` was written in 2018 to cover only the replica case, where expireIfNeeded() always returns 1 (treats the key as expired) without deleting it, because replicas never delete expired keys themselves. This same commit (47579bdf5, 'Add support for client pause WRITE (#8170)') introduced a second scenario in which expireIfNeeded() also returns 1 without deleting the key: when the server is paused via CLIENT PAUSE (checkClientPauseTimeoutAndReturnIfPaused() in expireIfNeeded, src/db.c ~line 1523-1527). On a primary/master instance (server.masterhost == NULL) whose keyspace consists entirely of volatile keys that are all already logically expired, and which is currently under a client pause, dbRandomKey() will repeatedly: pick a key -> find it has an expire set -> skip the masterhost-gated safety check (since server.masterhost is NULL) -> call expireIfNeeded() which returns 1 without deleting the key because the server is paused -> continue the loop and try again. Because the dictionary never shrinks and the random key is always the same logically-expired volatile key (or one of a small set), the function never returns and the event loop hangs, causing a denial of service. The maxtries safeguard added here needed to also break out of the loop when pause-driven expire suppression (not just replica-driven expire suppression) is in effect, but it was never updated to do so when client-pause write support was introduced.
findings.suggestion: Make the dbRandomKey() loop-termination guard aware of every condition under which expireIfNeeded() can refuse to delete an expired key, not only server.masterhost. Specifically, OR in the client-pause/expire-suppressed condition (later expressed as isPausedActions(PAUSE_ACTION_EXPIRE)) so the maxtries safety valve also fires when the server is a primary that is currently pause-suppressing expirations.
findings.title: dbRandomKey() loop-break guard ignores client-pause expire suppression, causing infinite loop

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 2a189709e098 on top of intro 05aed4cab976 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): incrDecrCommand() (backing INCR/DECR/INCRBY/DECRBY) replies to the client by reading data out of the 'new' robj representing the key's new string value, via addReplyLongLongFromStr(c,new). This call happens after notifyKeyspaceEvent(), which can synchronously run a loaded module's keyspace-notification callback. If that callback calls RM_StringDMA (direct memory access) on the same key, it can trigger reallocation/release of the underlying sds buffer backing 'new', so the later addReplyLongLongFromStr reads freed/stale memory -- a classic use-after-free. Root cause: PR #13505 optimized INCR/DECR (and related commands) to avoid re-serializing the integer to a string for the reply, by replying directly from the heap-allocated robj ('new') that was just stored into the keyspace, rather than from a stack-local integer copy. However the reply-generation call was left positioned after signalModifiedKey()/notifyKeyspaceEvent(), which can re-enter into module keyspace-notification subscriber callbacks. Those callbacks run with full API access (including RM_StringDMA) to the key that now holds 'new', so they can free/reallocate the buffer 'new' points to before the deferred reply call reads it. Previously, replies used a stack copy of the integer value (or values were small/shared integer objects that aren't actually freed by dict replacement), so no live reference into freed heap memory was retained across the notification call.

findings.message: incrDecrCommand() was changed (in PR #13505) to reply to the client with addReplyLongLongFromStr(c,new) -- reading the string value directly from the 'new' robj that now represents the key's value -- instead of replying with the integer value that had been copied onto the stack (addReplyLongLong(c, value)). This reply call was placed AFTER signalModifiedKey() and notifyKeyspaceEvent() are invoked. notifyKeyspaceEvent() can synchronously invoke registered keyspace-notification module hooks, and such a hook may call RM_StringDMA (or otherwise mutate/replace the string) on the very key that was just incremented/decremented. Since 'new' may no longer be a shared integer object (the optimization added a fast-path reusing the object only under narrow conditions; otherwise it's a freshly allocated, refcount==1 string object owned by the dict), a module hook that frees or reallocates the underlying sds buffer leaves 'new' as a dangling pointer. The subsequent addReplyLongLongFromStr(c,new) then reads freed/stale memory -- a use-after-free. This previously went unnoticed because for small values Redis used shared integer objects, so dropping/replacing a reference didn't actually free the object; the refactor's use of a real heap-allocated string object for the reply source, combined with calling the reply function after the notification hook can run, exposed the UAF.
findings.suggestion: Build/queue the client reply using the value BEFORE invoking signalModifiedKey()/notifyKeyspaceEvent(), so no module hook can mutate or free the underlying object between computing the reply source and actually sending the reply. The upstream fix moves addReplyLongLongFromStr(c,new) to immediately after the object is stored in the keyspace (before signalModifiedKey/notifyKeyspaceEvent/server.dirty++).

Vulnerability (LogicError): A network client sends a command with invalid arity while Redis uses multiple IO threads. The IO thread looks up key positions for prefetch before the main thread checks command arity. Root cause: processInputBuffer calls getSlotFromCommand on client argv before commandCheckArity. commit_message:
Improve multithreaded performance with memory prefetching (#14017)

This PR is based on: https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey/pull/861

> ### Memory Access Amortization
> (Designed and implemented by [dan
touitou](https://github.com/touitou-dan))
> 
> Memory Access Amortization (MAA) is a technique designed to optimize
the performance of dynamic data structures by reducing the impact of
memory access latency. It is applicable when multiple operations need to
be executed concurrently. The principle behind it is that for certain
dynamic data structures, executing operations in a batch is more
efficient than executing each one separately.
> 
> Rather than executing operations sequentially, this approach
interleaves the execution of all operations. This is done in such a way
that whenever a memory access is required during an operation, the
program prefetches the necessary memory and transitions to another
operation. This ensures that when one operation is blocked awaiting
memory access, other memory accesses are executed in parallel, thereby
reducing the average access latency.
> 
> We applied this method in the development of dictPrefetch, which takes
as parameters a vector of keys and dictionaries. It ensures that all
memory addresses required to execute dictionary operations for these
keys are loaded into the L1-L3 caches when executing commands.
Essentially, dictPrefetch is an interleaved execution of dictFind for
all the keys.

### Implementation of Redis
When the main thread processes clients with ready-to-execute commands
(i.e., clients for which the IO thread has parsed the commands), a batch
of up to 16 commands is created. Initially, the command's argv, which
were allocated by the IO thread, is prefetched to the main thread's L1
cache. Subsequently, all the dict entries and values required for the
commands are prefetched from the dictionary before the command
execution.

#### Memory prefetching for main hash table
As shown in the picture, after https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13806
, we unify key value and the dict uses no_value optimization, so the
memory prefetching has 4 steps:

1. prefetch the bucket of the hash table
2. prefetch the entry associated with the given key's hash
3. prefetch the kv object of the entry
4. prefetch the value data of the kv object

we also need to handle the case that the dict entry is the pointer of kv
object, just skip step 3.

MAA can improves single-threaded memory access efficiency by
interleaving the execution of multiple independent operations, allowing
memory-level parallelism and better CPU utilization. Its key point is
batch-wise interleaved execution. Split a batch of independent
operations (such as multiple key lookups) into multiple state machines,
and interleave their progress within a single thread to hide the memory
access latency of individual requests.

The difference between serial execution and interleaved execution:
**naive serial execution**
```
key1: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
key2: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
```
**interleaved execution**
```
key1: step1   → step2   → done
key2:   step1 → step2   → done
key3:     step1 → step2 → done
         ↑ While waiting for key1’s memory, progress key2/key3
```

#### New configuration
This PR involves a new configuration `prefetch-batch-max-size`, but we
think it is a low level optimization, so we hide this config:
When multiple commands are parsed by the I/O threads and ready for
execution, we take advantage of knowing the next set of commands and
prefetch their required dictionary entries in a batch. This reduces
memory access costs. The optimal batch size depends on the specific
workflow of the user. The default batch size is 16, which can be
modified using the 'prefetch-batch-max-size' config.
When the config is set to 0, prefetching is disabled.

---------

Co-authored-by: Ozan Tezcan <ozantezcan@gmail.com>

fix_commit_message:
Fix command arity check in IO threads (#14134)

We need to check the command arity in IO threads, if it is not correct,
we should reset it, as we may do memory prefetching according to the
`iolookedcmd`. Accessing `argv` using the key positions returned by
`getKeysFromCommand` is unsafe and must be avoided for invalid commands.

This bug starts to have an impact after #14017

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

intro_commit_message:
Improve multithreaded performance with memory prefetching (#14017)

This PR is based on: https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey/pull/861

> ### Memory Access Amortization
> (Designed and implemented by [dan
touitou](https://github.com/touitou-dan))
> 
> Memory Access Amortization (MAA) is a technique designed to optimize
the performance of dynamic data structures by reducing the impact of
memory access latency. It is applicable when multiple operations need to
be executed concurrently. The principle behind it is that for certain
dynamic data structures, executing operations in a batch is more
efficient than executing each one separately.
> 
> Rather than executing operations sequentially, this approach
interleaves the execution of all operations. This is done in such a way
that whenever a memory access is required during an operation, the
program prefetches the necessary memory and transitions to another
operation. This ensures that when one operation is blocked awaiting
memory access, other memory accesses are executed in parallel, thereby
reducing the average access latency.
> 
> We applied this method in the development of dictPrefetch, which takes
as parameters a vector of keys and dictionaries. It ensures that all
memory addresses required to execute dictionary operations for these
keys are loaded into the L1-L3 caches when executing commands.
Essentially, dictPrefetch is an interleaved execution of dictFind for
all the keys.

### Implementation of Redis
When the main thread processes clients with ready-to-execute commands
(i.e., clients for which the IO thread has parsed the commands), a batch
of up to 16 commands is created. Initially, the command's argv, which
were allocated by the IO thread, is prefetched to the main thread's L1
cache. Subsequently, all the dict entries and values required for the
commands are prefetched from the dictionary before the command
execution.

#### Memory prefetching for main hash table
As shown in the picture, after https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13806
, we unify key value and the dict uses no_value optimization, so the
memory prefetching has 4 steps:

1. prefetch the bucket of the hash table
2. prefetch the entry associated with the given key's hash
3. prefetch the kv object of the entry
4. prefetch the value data of the kv object

we also need to handle the case that the dict entry is the pointer of kv
object, just skip step 3.

MAA can improves single-threaded memory access efficiency by
interleaving the execution of multiple independent operations, allowing
memory-level parallelism and better CPU utilization. Its key point is
batch-wise interleaved execution. Split a batch of independent
operations (such as multiple key lookups) into multiple state machines,
and interleave their progress within a single thread to hide the memory
access latency of individual requests.

The difference between serial execution and interleaved execution:
**naive serial execution**
```
key1: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
key2: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
```
**interleaved execution**
```
key1: step1   → step2   → done
key2:   step1 → step2   → done
key3:     step1 → step2 → done
         ↑ While waiting for key1’s memory, progress key2/key3
```

#### New configuration
This PR involves a new configuration `prefetch-batch-max-size`, but we
think it is a low level optimization, so we hide this config:
When multiple commands are parsed by the I/O threads and ready for
execution, we take advantage of knowing the next set of commands and
prefetch their required dictionary entries in a batch. This reduces
memory access costs. The optimal batch size depends on the specific
workflow of the user. The default batch size is 16, which can be
modified using the 'prefetch-batch-max-size' config.
When the config is set to 0, prefetching is disabled.

---------

Co-authored-by: Uri Yagelnik <uriy@amazon.com>
Co-authored-by: Ozan Tezcan <ozantezcan@gmail.com>

commands are prefetched from the dictionary before the command
execution.

#### Memory prefetching for main hash table
As shown in the picture, after https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13806
, we unify key value and the dict uses no_value optimization, so the
memory prefetching has 4 steps:

1. prefetch the bucket of the hash table
2. prefetch the entry associated with the given key's hash
3. prefetch the kv object of the entry
4. prefetch the value data of the kv object

we also need to handle the case that the dict entry is the pointer of kv
object, just skip step 3.

MAA can improves single-threaded memory access efficiency by
interleaving the execution of multiple independent operations, allowing
memory-level parallelism and better CPU utilization. Its key point is
batch-wise interleaved execution. Split a batch of independent
operations (such as multiple key lookups) into multiple state machines,
and interleave their progress within a single thread to hide the memory
access latency of individual requests.

The difference between serial execution and interleaved execution:
**naive serial execution**
```
key1: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
key2: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
```
**interleaved execution**
```
key1: step1   → step2   → done
key2:   step1 → step2   → done
key3:     step1 → step2 → done
         ↑ While waiting for key1’s memory, progress key2/key3
```

#### New configuration
This PR involves a new configuration `prefetch-batch-max-size`, but we
think it is a low level optimization, so we hide this config:
When multiple commands are parsed by the I/O threads and ready for
execution, we take advantage of knowing the next set of commands and
prefetch their required dictionary entries in a batch. This reduces
memory access costs. The optimal batch size depends on the specific
workflow of the user. The default batch size is 16, which can be
modified using the 'prefetch-batch-max-size' config.
When the config is set to 0, prefetching is disabled.

commit_message:
Improve multithreaded performance with memory prefetching (#14017)

This PR is based on: https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey/pull/861

> ### Memory Access Amortization
> (Designed and implemented by [dan
touitou](https://github.com/touitou-dan))
> 
> Memory Access Amortization (MAA) is a technique designed to optimize
the performance of dynamic data structures by reducing the impact of
memory access latency. It is applicable when multiple operations need to
be executed concurrently. The principle behind it is that for certain
dynamic data structures, executing operations in a batch is more
efficient than executing each one separately.
> 
> Rather than executing operations sequentially, this approach
interleaves the execution of all operations. This is done in such a way
that whenever a memory access is required during an operation, the
program prefetches the necessary memory and transitions to another
operation. This ensures that when one operation is blocked awaiting
memory access, other memory accesses are executed in parallel, thereby
reducing the average access latency.
> 
> We applied this method in the development of dictPrefetch, which takes
as parameters a vector of keys and dictionaries. It ensures that all
memory addresses required to execute dictionary operations for these
keys are loaded into the L1-L3 caches when executing commands.
Essentially, dictPrefetch is an interleaved execution of dictFind for
all the keys.

### Implementation of Redis
When the main thread processes clients with ready-to-execute commands
(i.e., clients for which the IO thread has parsed the commands), a batch
of up to 16 commands is created. Initially, the command's argv, which
were allocated by the IO thread, is prefetched to the main thread's L1
cache. Subsequently, all the dict entries and values required for the
commands are prefetched from the dictionary before the command
execution.

#### Memory prefetching for main hash table
As shown in the picture, after https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13806

memory prefetching has 4 steps:

1. prefetch the bucket of the hash table
2. prefetch the entry associated with the given key's hash
3. prefetch the kv object of the entry
4. prefetch the value data of the kv object

we also need to handle the case that the dict entry is the pointer of kv
object, just skip step 3.

MAA can improves single-threaded memory access efficiency by
interleaving the execution of multiple independent operations, allowing
memory-level parallelism and better CPU utilization. Its key point is
batch-wise interleaved execution. Split a batch of independent
operations (such as multiple key lookups) into multiple state machines,
and interleave their progress within a single thread to hide the memory
access latency of individual requests.

The difference between serial execution and interleaved execution:
**naive serial execution**
```
key1: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
key2: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
```
**interleaved execution**
```
key1: step1   → step2   → done
key2:   step1 → step2   → done
key3:     step1 → step2 → done
         ↑ While waiting for key1’s memory, progress key2/key3
```

#### New configuration
This PR involves a new configuration `prefetch-batch-max-size`, but we
think it is a low level optimization, so we hide this config:
When multiple commands are parsed by the I/O threads and ready for
execution, we take advantage of knowing the next set of commands and

+start_server {config "minimal.conf" tags {"external:skip"} overrides {enable-debug-command {yes} io-threads 2}} {
+    set server_pid [s process_id]
+    # Since each thread may perform memory prefetch independently, this test is
+    # only run when the number of IO threads is 2 to ensure deterministic results.
+    if {[r config get io-threads] eq "io-threads 2"} {
+        test {prefetch works as expected when killing a client from the middle of prefetch commands batch} {
+            # Create 16 (prefetch batch size) +1 clients
+            for {set i 0} {$i < 16} {incr i} {
+                set rd$i [redis_deferring_client]
+            }
+
+            # set a key that will be later be prefetch
+            r set a 0
+
+            # Get the client ID of rd4
+            $rd4 client id
+            set rd4_id [$rd4 read]
+
+            # Create a batch of commands by suspending the server for a while
+            # before responding to the first command
+            pause_process $server_pid
+
+            # The first client will kill the fourth client
+            $rd0 client kill id $rd4_id
+
+            # Send set commands for all clients except the first
+            for {set i 1} {$i < 16} {incr i} {
+                [set rd$i] set a $i
+                [set rd$i] flush
+            }
+
+            # Resume the server
+            resume_process $server_pid
+
+            # Read the results
+            assert_equal {1} [$rd0 read]
+            catch {$rd4 read} err
+            assert_match {I/O error reading reply} $err
+
+            # verify the prefetch stats are as expected
+            set info [r info stats]
+            set prefetch_entries [getInfoProperty $info io_threaded_total_prefetch_entries]
+            assert_range $prefetch_entries 2 15; # With slower machines, the number of prefetch entries can be lower
+            set prefetch_batches [getInfoProperty $info io_threaded_total_prefetch_batches]
+            assert_range $prefetch_batches 1 7; # With slower machines, the number of batches can be higher
+
+            # Verify the final state
+            $rd15 get a
+            assert_equal {OK} [$rd15 read]
+            assert_equal {15} [$rd15 read]
+        }
+
+        test {prefetch works as expected when changing the batch size while executing the commands batch} {
+            # Create 16 (default prefetch batch size) clients
+            for {set i 0} {$i < 16} {incr i} {
+                set rd$i [redis_deferring_client]
+            }
+
+            # Create a batch of commands by suspending the server for a while
+            # before responding to the first command
+            pause_process $server_pid
+
+            # Send set commands for all clients the 5th client will change the prefetch batch size
+            for {set i 0} {$i < 16} {incr i} {
+                if {$i == 4} {
+                    [set rd$i] config set prefetch-batch-max-size 1
+                }
+                [set rd$i] set a $i
+                [set rd$i] flush
+            }
+            # Resume the server
+            resume_process $server_pid
+            # Read the results
+            for {set i 0} {$i < 16} {incr i} {
+                assert_equal {OK} [[set rd$i] read]
+                [set rd$i] close
+            }
+
+            # assert the configured prefetch batch size was changed
+            assert {[r config get prefetch-batch-max-size] eq "prefetch-batch-max-size 1"}
+        }
+ 
+        proc do_prefetch_batch {server_pid batch_size} {
+            # Create clients
+            for {set i 0} {$i < $batch_size} {incr i} {
+                set rd$i [redis_deferring_client]
+            }
+
+            # Suspend the server to batch the commands
+            pause_process $server_pid
+
+            # Send commands from all clients
+            for {set i 0} {$i < $batch_size} {incr i} {
+                [set rd$i] set a $i
+                [set rd$i] flush
+            }
+
+            # Resume the server to process the batch
+            resume_process $server_pid
+
+            # Verify responses
+            for {set i 0} {$i < $batch_size} {incr i} {
+                assert_equal {OK} [[set rd$i] read]
+                [set rd$i] close
+            }
+        }
+
+        test {no prefetch when the batch size is set to 0} {
+            # set the batch size to 0
+            r config set prefetch-batch-max-size 0
+            # save the current value of prefetch entries
+            set info [r info stats]
+            set prefetch_entries [getInfoProperty $info io_threaded_total_prefetch_entries]
+
+            do_prefetch_batch $server_pid 16
+
+            # assert the prefetch entries did not change
+            set info [r info stats]
+            set new_prefetch_entries [getInfoProperty $info io_threaded_total_prefetch_entries]
+            assert_equal $prefetch_entries $new_prefetch_entries
+        }
+
+        test {Prefetch can resume working when the configuration option is set to a non-zero value} {
+            # save the current value of prefetch entries
+            set info [r info stats]
+            set prefetch_entries [getInfoProperty $info io_threaded_total_prefetch_entries]
+            # set the batch size to 0
+            r config set prefetch-batch-max-size 16
+
+            do_prefetch_batch $server_pid 16
+
+            # assert the prefetch entries did not change
+            set info [r info stats]
+            set new_prefetch_entries [getInfoProperty $info io_threaded_total_prefetch_entries]
+            # With slower machines, the number of prefetch entries can be lower
+            assert_range $new_prefetch_entries [expr {$prefetch_entries + 2}] [expr {$prefetch_entries + 16}]
+        }
+    }
+}

pr_description:
This PR is based on: https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey/pull/861

> ### Memory Access Amortization
> (Designed and implemented by [dan
touitou](https://github.com/touitou-dan))
> 
> Memory Access Amortization (MAA) is a technique designed to optimize
the performance of dynamic data structures by reducing the impact of
memory access latency. It is applicable when multiple operations need to
be executed concurrently. The principle behind it is that for certain
dynamic data structures, executing operations in a batch is more
efficient than executing each one separately.
> 
> Rather than executing operations sequentially, this approach
interleaves the execution of all operations. This is done in such a way
that whenever a memory access is required during an operation, the
program prefetches the necessary memory and transitions to another
operation. This ensures that when one operation is blocked awaiting
memory access, other memory accesses are executed in parallel, thereby
reducing the average access latency.
> 
> We applied this method in the development of dictPrefetch, which takes
as parameters a vector of keys and dictionaries. It ensures that all
memory addresses required to execute dictionary operations for these
keys are loaded into the L1-L3 caches when executing commands.
Essentially, dictPrefetch is an interleaved execution of dictFind for
all the keys.

### Implementation of Redis
When the main thread processes clients with ready-to-execute commands
(i.e., clients for which the IO thread has parsed the commands), a batch
of up to 16 commands is created. Initially, the command's argv, which
were allocated by the IO thread, is prefetched to the main thread's L1
cache. Subsequently, all the dict entries and values required for the
commands are prefetched from the dictionary before the command
execution.

#### Memory prefetching for main hash table
As shown in the picture, after https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13806
, we unify key value and the dict uses no_value optimization, so the
memory prefetching has 4 steps:

1. prefetch the bucket of the hash table
2. prefetch the entry associated with the given key's hash
3. prefetch the kv object of the entry
4. prefetch the value data of the kv object

we also need to handle the case that the dict entry is the pointer of kv
object, just skip step 3.

MAA can improves single-threaded memory access efficiency by
interleaving the execution of multiple independent operations, allowing
memory-level parallelism and better CPU utilization. Its key point is
batch-wise interleaved execution. Split a batch of independent
operations (such as multiple key lookups) into multiple state machines,
and interleave their progress within a single thread to hide the memory
access latency of individual requests.

The difference between serial execution and interleaved execution:
**naive serial execution**
```
key1: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
key2: step1 → wait → step2 → wait → done
```
**interleaved execution**
```
key1: step1   → step2   → done
key2:   step1 → step2   → done
key3:     step1 → step2 → done
         ↑ While waiting for key1’s memory, progress key2/key3
```

#### New configuration
This PR involves a new configuration `prefetch-batch-max-size`, but we
think it is a low level optimization, so we hide this config:
When multiple commands are parsed by the I/O threads and ready for
execution, we take advantage of knowing the next set of commands and
prefetch their required dictionary entries in a batch. This reduces
memory access costs. The optimal batch size depends on the specific
workflow of the user. The default batch size is 16, which can be
modified using the 'prefetch-batch-max-size' config.
When the config is set to 0, prefetching is disabled.

---------

Co-authored-by: Uri Yagelnik <uriy@amazon.com>
Co-authored-by: Ozan Tezcan <ozantezcan@gmail.com>

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 03816c15f759 on top of intro dcf02298110f via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): During RDB loading of hash objects that carry hash-field-expiration (HFE) metadata (RDB_TYPE_HASH_METADATA and RDB_TYPE_HASH_LISTPACK_EX), rdbLoadObject() reads an extra 'min expiration time' value before the rest of the hash payload. If this read fails (e.g., because the replication connection to the master was broken/short mid-stream during diskless full sync), the code calls rdbReportCorruptRDB() unconditionally. That macro forces rdbReportError()'s corruption_error flag to 1, routing execution into the 'corrupt file' branch which logs and then unconditionally calls exit(1), killing the replica process. The condition is actually a transient network/short-read condition, not file corruption, and should instead route through rdbReportReadError() (corruption_error=0), which logs and gracefully resumes/aborts the load without terminating the process. Root cause: The HFE min-expire-time RDB loading code added in commit dcf02298110 (#13391) reused rdbReportCorruptRDB() for a read-error check that can legitimately fire on a benign short read over a replication socket, instead of using rdbReportReadError() which is the designated helper for exactly this short-read/connection-drop scenario elsewhere in rdb.c. This mixes up the 'corrupted on-disk file' failure class with the 'broken network stream' failure class, both of which flow through the shared rdbReportError()/corruption_error parameter.
commit_message:
HFE - RDB serialize also hash min expiration (For ROF flow) (#13391)

* Following this feature, Redis (ROF) may implement flow that allows hashes to be
  dumped directly from RDB to FLUSH without parsing. In this scenario, it is still
  essential to determine when to update hashes due to expired fields. By writing
  and reading the next minimum hash-field expiration before serializing objects
  to and from RDB, we can effectively track and expire hash fields without the need
  to parse the hash during loading.

    Before:
    #define RDB_TYPE_HASH_METADATA 22
    #define RDB_TYPE_HASH_LISTPACK_EX 23
    
    After:
    /* Hash with HFEs. Doesn't attach min TTL at start */
    #define RDB_TYPE_HASH_METADATA_PRE_GA 22      
    /* Hash LP with HFEs. Doesn't attach min TTL at start */
    #define RDB_TYPE_HASH_LISTPACK_EX_PRE_GA 23   
    /* Hash with HFEs. Attach min TTL at start */
    #define RDB_TYPE_HASH_METADATA 24             
    /* Hash LP with HFEs. Attach min TTL at start */
    #define RDB_TYPE_HASH_LISTPACK_EX 25          


* Manually test loading RDB file before the change and verify hash and its HFEs 
  is as expected.
* Added `subexpires` counter to `redis-check-rdb`

fix_commit_message:
Fix short read of hfe key that causes exit() on replica (#14143)

If replica detects broken connection while reading min expiration time
of hfe key, it calls exit().
Fixed it to handle the error gracefully without calling exit. 

To reproduce the issue, the short-read test was modified to generate
many small hfe keys, increasing the likelihood of a connection drop
while reading min expiration time:

```tcl
for {set k 0} {$k < 50000} {incr k} {
  for {set i 0} {$i < 1} {incr i} {
    r hsetex "$k hfe_small" EX [expr {int(rand()*10)}] FIELDS 1 [string repeat A [expr {int(rand()*10)}]] 0[string repeat A [expr {int(rand()*10)}]]
  }
}
```

We can't have the test use only hfe keys, so a few were added alongside
other data. I couldn't reproduce the issue this way but with the test's
randomization, it should hit this scenario in one of the runs.

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

findings.message: When loading RDB_TYPE_HASH_METADATA (and similarly RDB_TYPE_HASH_LISTPACK_EX) objects, rdbLoadObject() reads a serialized 'min expiration time' field via rdbLoadMillisecondTime() and then checks rioGetReadError(rdb) to detect a failed read. On failure it calls rdbReportCorruptRDB(), which invokes rdbReportError() with corruption_error=1. During diskless replication full sync, a transient/broken network connection to the master produces exactly this kind of short read (not actual data corruption), but because corruption_error is hard-coded to 1 via the CorruptRDB macro, rdbReportError() takes the 'In diskless loading, in case of corrupt file, log and exit' branch and falls through to exit(1), killing the replica process. The correct handling (as used elsewhere for genuine short reads over a socket) is to call rdbReportReadError(), which sets corruption_error=0 so rdbReportError() logs 'assuming connection error, resuming operation' and returns without exiting. This is purely a classification/logic bug: a recoverable network short-read condition is misclassified as a file-corruption condition, leading to replica self-termination (DoS) that is remotely triggerable by any master (or MITM on the replication link) that drops the connection at the right moment while streaming an HFE-enabled hash key.
findings.suggestion: Use rdbReportReadError() instead of rdbReportCorruptRDB() when a short/broken read of the min-expire time is detected via rioGetReadError(), for both the RDB_TYPE_HASH_METADATA and RDB_TYPE_HASH_LISTPACK_EX load paths, so that a dropped replication connection is treated as a recoverable connection error (log + resume) rather than unconditionally terminating the process via exit(1).

agent_reasoning: luaExtractErrorInformation() only assigned err_info->msg inside the `if (lua_isstring(lua, -1))` branch after fetching the table's "err" field. For error tables lacking an "err" field, or where it's present but not a string (e.g. `error{}` or `error({err=123})`), msg was never assigned and remained NULL (callers zero-initialize the errorInfo struct). Downstream consumers (luaCallFunction, luaReplyToRedisReply, luaEngineLoadFunctions) unconditionally use err_info.msg as a %s argument to sdscatfmt()/as an sds reply, so a NULL msg causes a NULL pointer dereference and crashes the server. The fix adds an else branch assigning a safe default "ERR unknown error" string whenever the err field isn't a string, guaranteeing msg is always a valid sds string.
commit_message:
Sort out the mess around Lua error messages and error stats (#10329)

This PR fix 2 issues on Lua scripting:
* Server error reply statistics (some errors were counted twice).
* Error code and error strings returning from scripts (error code was missing / misplaced).

## Statistics
a Lua script user is considered part of the user application, a sophisticated transaction,
so we want to count an error even if handled silently by the script, but when it is
propagated outwards from the script we don't wanna count it twice. on the other hand,
if the script decides to throw an error on its own (using `redis.error_reply`), we wanna
count that too.
Besides, we do count the `calls` in command statistics for the commands the script calls,
we we should certainly also count `failed_calls`.
So when a simple `eval "return redis.call('set','x','y')" 0` fails, it should count the failed call
to both SET and EVAL, but the `errorstats` and `total_error_replies` should be counted only once.

string, Redis will raise a Lua table in the following format:

```

    err='<error message (including error code)>',
    source='<User source file name>',
    line='<line where the error happned>',
    ignore_error_stats_update=true/false,
}
```

The `luaRaiseError` was renamed to `luaError` and is now simply called `lua_error` to raise
the table on the top of the Lua stack as the error object.
The reason is that since its functionality is changed, in case some Redis branch / fork uses it,
it's better to have a compilation error than a bug.

The `source` and `line` fields are enriched by the error handler (if possible) and the
`ignore_error_stats_update` is optional and if its not present then the default value is `false`.
If `ignore_error_stats_update` is true, the error will not be counted on the error stats.

When parsing Redis call reply, each error is translated to a Lua table on the format describe
above and the `ignore_error_stats_update` field is set to `true` so we will not count errors
twice (we counted this error when we invoke the command).

Lua `pcall` function. Before, the error was a string and now its a table. To keep backward
comparability the PR override the `pcall` implementation and extract the error message from

```
127.0.0.1:6379> lpush l 1
(integer) 2
127.0.0.1:6379> eval "return redis.call('get', 'l')" 0
(error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value. script: e471b73f1ef44774987ab00bdf51f21fd9f7974a, on @user_script:1.

127.0.0.1:6379> info Errorstats
# Errorstats
errorstat_WRONGTYPE:count=1

127.0.0.1:6379> info commandstats
# Commandstats
cmdstat_eval:calls=1,usec=341,usec_per_call=341.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=1
cmdstat_info:calls=1,usec=35,usec_per_call=35.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_lpush:calls=1,usec=14,usec_per_call=14.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=0
cmdstat_get:calls=1,usec=10,usec_per_call=10.00,rejected_calls=0,failed_calls=1
```

We can now construct the error message (sent as a reply to the user) from the error table,
so this solves issues where the error message was malformed and the error code appeared
in the middle of the error message:

```diff
127.0.0.1:6379> eval "return redis.call('set','x','y')" 0
-(error) ERR Error running script (call to 71e6319f97b0fe8bdfa1c5df3ce4489946dda479): @user_script:1: OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
+(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory' @user_script:1. Error running script (call to 71e6319f97b0fe8bdfa1c5df3ce4489946dda479)
```

```diff
127.0.0.1:6379> eval "redis.call('get', 'l')" 0
-(error) ERR Error running script (call to f_8a705cfb9fb09515bfe57ca2bd84a5caee2cbbd1): @user_script:1: WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value
+(error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value script: 8a705cfb9fb09515bfe57ca2bd84a5caee2cbbd1, on @user_script:1.
```

Notica that `redis.pcall` was not change:
```
127.0.0.1:6379> eval "return redis.pcall('get', 'l')" 0
(error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value
```

Notice that Some commands (like GEOADD) changes the cmd variable on the client stats so we
can not count on it to update the command stats. In order to be able to update those stats correctly
we needed to promote `realcmd` variable to be located on the client struct.

Tests was added and modified to verify the changes.

Related PR's: #10279, #10218, #10278, #10309

findings.message: luaExtractErrorInformation() is invoked whenever a Lua script (EVAL/EVALSHA/FCALL) raises an error whose Lua error object is a table (as opposed to a plain string). The function reads the table's 'err' field and, only if it is a Lua string, sets err_info->msg. If the 'err' field is absent or is not a string (e.g. the script returns an empty table such as `error{}`, or `err` is a number/boolean/table), no else branch exists and err_info->msg is left at its zero-initialized value of NULL (the caller always does `errorInfo err_info = {0};`). The NULL msg is subsequently passed as a %s argument to sdscatfmt()/addReplyErrorFormatEx() in luaCallFunction() and luaReplyToRedisReply(), and also concatenated in function_lua.c when loading Lua functions. sds/format routines that dereference the pointer with strlen()-like operations will crash on the NULL pointer, allowing any client capable of running EVAL to trigger a server-wide crash (denial of service) with a script as simple as `EVAL 'error{}' 0`.
findings.suggestion: Add an else branch after the 'err' field lua_isstring() check that assigns a safe default message (e.g. sdsnew("ERR unknown error")) so err_info->msg is never left NULL, matching how all downstream consumers rely on it being a valid sds string.
findings.title: luaExtractErrorInformation() may leave err_info->msg NULL for malformed error tables

fix_commit.message: Ensure empty error tables in scripts don't crash (#14163)

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: luaExtractErrorInformation() may leave err_info->msg NULL for malformed error tables

ground_truth.root_cause: Missing else/default-value handling for the 'err' table field in luaExtractErrorInformation(): the code only assigns err_info->msg inside the `if (lua_isstring(lua, -1))` branch, with no fallback for the case where the error table lacks an 'err' field or the field's type is not a string, so the caller's zero-initialized NULL msg pointer propagates downstream unchecked.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix d649637ebd1b on top of intro 5d0d64b062c1 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): activeDefragHExpiresOB(), introduced to support incremental active-defrag of hash-field-expire (HFE) buckets, reallocates a hash kvobj via activeDefragAlloc(). That helper both allocates the replacement and frees the original pointer in one call. The function, however, continues to use `keystr`, a pointer taken from the original (now-freed) object, to perform a dictionary lookup (kvstoreDictFindLink) immediately afterward, resulting in a use-after-free read of the freed allocation's key data during active defragmentation of hash keys that have field TTLs. Root cause: activeDefragAlloc() couples allocation-of-replacement with freeing-of-original into a single call. activeDefragHExpiresOB() retained a reference (keystr) into the original object's memory for use after that call, not realizing the original memory had already been released by the time it performed the dict lookup/update. The ordering of free vs. use was inverted: the free needed to happen only after all derived pointers from the old object were no longer needed.
commit_message:
Add support to defrag ebuckets incrementally (#13842)

In PR #13229, we introduced the ebucket for HFE.
Before this PR, when updating eitems stored in ebuckets, the lack of
incremental fragmentation support for non-kvstore data structures (until
PR #13814) meant that we had to reverse lookup the position of the eitem
in the ebucket and then perform the update.
This approach was inefficient as it often required frequent traversals
of the segment list to locate and update the item.

To address this issue, in this PR, This PR implements incremental
fragmentation for hash dict ebuckets and server.hexpires.
By incrementally defrag the ebuckets, we also perform defragmentation
for the associated items, eliminates the need for frequent traversals of
the segment list for defragging the eitem.

---------

Co-authored-by: Copilot <175728472+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
fix_commit_message:
Fix defrag issues for stream defrag and HFE (#14323)

This PR fixes three defrag issues.

1. Fix the issue that forget to update cgroup_ref_node when the consume
group was reallocated.
This crash was introduced by https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/14130
In this PR, when performing defragmentation on `s->cgroups` using
`defragRadixTree()`, we no longer rely on the automatic data
defragmentation of `defragRadixTree()`. Instead, we manually defragment
the consumer group and then update its reference in `s->cgroups`.

2. Fix a use-after-free issue caused by updating dictionary keys after
HFE key is reallocated.
This issue was introduced by https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/13842

3. Fix the issue that forgot to be updated NextSegHdr->firstSeg when the
first segment was reallocated.
This issue was introduced by https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/13842

---------

findings.message:
In activeDefragHExpiresOB(), `keystr` is captured as `kvobjGetKey(kvobj)` at the top of the function, i.e. it is a pointer into the memory owned by the original (pre-defrag) `kvobj` allocation. Later, the code calls `kvobj = activeDefragAlloc(kvobj)`. activeDefragAlloc() (see src/defrag.c, activeDefragAlloc) allocates a new copy of the object AND immediately frees the old pointer via zfree_no_tcache() when a move actually happens (i.e. when je_get_defrag_hint() indicates the allocation should be moved). After this call returns, the original `kvobj` memory (and therefore the `keystr` pointer that lives inside it) has already been released back to the allocator.

The very next statement, `link = kvstoreDictFindLink(db->keys, slot, keystr, NULL);`, dereferences/dereferences-through `keystr` (the dict uses the sds string key for hashing/compare) to locate the dictEntry for the key in db->keys. Because `keystr` points into freed memory, this is a use-after-free read: the freed chunk may have been reused by a concurrent/interleaved allocation inside the same defrag cycle (e.g. the zmalloc_no_tcache() call that created the new object, or any other allocation performed between the free and the lookup), causing kvstoreDictFindLink to hash/compare garbage data. This can lead to a failed lookup (serverAssert(link != NULL) crash), silent corruption of the wrong dict entry, or a straightforward heap-use-after-free that can be leveraged for information disclosure or further memory corruption depending on allocator behavior.

The bug is reachable whenever active defrag is enabled/triggered (e.g. `CONFIG SET activedefrag yes` with sufficient fragmentation, or `DEBUG MALLOC-STATS`/`DEBUG JMAP` style forced defrag cycles) and a hash key with field TTLs (HFE / hash-field-expire buckets, i.e. keys that appear in db->hexpires) becomes a defrag move candidate (je_get_defrag_hint returns non-zero for that kvobj's allocation). The HFE defrag stage (defragStageHExpires -> ebScanDefrag -> activeDefragHExpiresOB) then exercises exactly this path.
findings.suggestion: Do not free the old kvobj allocation until after keystr (and any other data derived from the old object) has been fully used to update the DB dict references. Split the allocate-and-free helper into an allocate-without-free step (activeDefragAllocWithoutFree) performed first, use keystr to locate/update the dict links against the still-valid old pointer, then explicitly free the old pointer only afterward (activeDefragFree). This is exactly what the upstream fix (commit d649637ebd1b7b7792a4224a42e1ef8824743378) does.
findings.title: Use-after-free: hash key (keystr) dereferenced via dict lookup after owning kvobj is freed during active defrag

agent_reasoning: Computing capacity before normalizing the inputs could make slot initialization exceed the supplied buffer, while oversized slot sizes could truncate when stored as u16 and corrupt allocator bookkeeping. The adapted implementation bounds and normalizes both inputs before calculating capacity using 64-bit arithmetic, and keeps slot distribution consistent with the allocated buffer. This historical mini-slot implementation has no sz*nBig multiplication, so the later two-size allocator's multiplication changes are not applicable. Only src/main.c and src/sqlite.h.in were edited; no test files or repository history were changed.

More efficient implementation of a lookaside allocator that supports mini (in this case, harcoded to 128B) slots.

pr_description:
Support 128-byte mini slots alongside full-size lookaside slots. Normalize slot sizes and counts before computing buffer capacity, cap slot sizes at 65528 bytes and requested capacity at 0x7fff0000 bytes, and use 64-bit allocation arithmetic. Account for the actual allocated buffer size when distributing slots.

Document lookaside configuration limits, buffer requirements, defaults, and allocation-failure behavior.

findings.message: In setupLookaside(), the total allocation size `szAlloc = sz*(sqlite3_int64)cnt` is computed at the very start of the function, before `sz` is sanitized via ROUNDDOWN8() and before `cnt` is clamped. More critically, there is no upper-bound check on `sz` before it is stored as `db->lookaside.sz = (u16)sz`. If a caller passes sz >= 65536 (e.g., sz=65536), ROUNDDOWN8(65536)=65536 which passes the `sz <= sizeof(LookasideSlot*)` guard; `szAlloc` is then computed correctly and a large buffer is allocated, but `db->lookaside.sz = (u16)65536` wraps to 0. Subsequent lookaside allocations use the stored slot size of 0 rather than the true 65536, leading to incorrect pointer arithmetic and out-of-bounds memory accesses. Additionally, the integer expression `sz*nBig` in `nSm = (szAlloc - sz*nBig)/LOOKASIDE_SMALL` is a 32-bit signed multiplication that overflows for large values of sz. The fix adds `if( sz>65528 ) sz = 65528;` and `if( sz>0 && cnt>(0x7fff0000/sz) ) cnt = 0x7fff0000/sz;` before computing szAlloc, ensuring both parameters are bounded before use.
findings.suggestion: Add upper-bound checks on sz and cnt before computing szAlloc: clamp sz to 65528 (max value that fits in u16 after ROUNDDOWN8) and clamp cnt so that sz*cnt does not exceed a safe maximum (e.g., 0x7fff0000). Move the szAlloc computation to after the sanitization steps. Also cast sz and nBig to 64-bit before multiplying in the nSm calculation.

ground_truth.root_cause: The introducing commit (115d663c05) refactored setupLookaside() to compute szAlloc at the top of the function before sanitizing sz and cnt. The original design lacked an upper-bound check on sz before truncating it to u16 in db->lookaside.sz, and the two-size lookaside arithmetic (nSm = (szAlloc - sz*nBig)/LOOKASIDE_SMALL) used 32-bit signed multiplication that could overflow. +/* The core implementation of the CONCAT(...) and CONCAT_WS(SEP,...)
+** functions.
+**
+** Return a string value that is the concatenation of all non-null
+** entries in argv[].  Use zSep as the separator.
+*/
+static void concatFuncCore(
+  sqlite3_context *context,
+  int argc,
+  sqlite3_value **argv,
+  int nSep,
+  const char *zSep
+){
+  i64 j, k, n = 0;
+  int i;
+  char *z;
+  for(i=0; i<argc; i++){
+    n += sqlite3_value_bytes(argv[i]);
+  }
+  n += (argc-1)*(i64)nSep;
+  z = sqlite3_malloc64(n+1);
+  if( z==0 ){
+    sqlite3_result_error_nomem(context);
+    return;
+  }
+  j = 0;
+  for(i=0; i<argc; i++){
+    k = sqlite3_value_bytes(argv[i]);
+    if( k>0 ){
+      const char *v = (const char*)sqlite3_value_text(argv[i]);
+      if( ALWAYS(v!=0) ){
+        if( j>0 && nSep>0 ){
+          memcpy(&z[j], zSep, nSep);
+          j += nSep;
+        }
+        memcpy(&z[j], v, k);
+        j += k;
+      }
+    }
+  }
+  z[j] = 0;
+  assert( j<=n );
+  sqlite3_result_text64(context, z, n, sqlite3_free, SQLITE_UTF8);
+}

+  concatFuncCore(context, argc, argv, 0, "");

+/*

findings.message: In concatFuncCore(), the total buffer size is computed as `n += (argc-1)*nSep`. Both `argc` (int) and `nSep` (int) are 32-bit signed integers. When `nSep` is large (e.g., a separator string larger than ~2 MB) and `argc` is moderately large, the product `(argc-1)*nSep` overflows a 32-bit signed integer before being assigned to the `i64` accumulator `n`. This results in `n` being smaller than the actual bytes needed. The subsequent `sqlite3_malloc64(n+1)` therefore allocates a buffer that is too small, and the later `memcpy` calls in the write loop write past the end of the heap allocation — a heap buffer overflow exploitable for memory corruption.
findings.suggestion: Cast `nSep` (or `argc-1`) to `i64` before the multiplication to ensure the arithmetic is performed in 64-bit space, preventing overflow before the result is added to `n`.
findings.suggestion_code: n += (argc-1)*(i64)nSep;
findings.title: Integer overflow in separator-size calculation in concatFuncCore()

fix_commit.author: drh
fix_commit.message: Add a typecast to avoid 32-bit integer overflow in the concat_ws() function with an enormous separator values and many arguments.

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Integer overflow in separator-size calculation in concatFuncCore()
Related location for: Integer overflow in separator-size calculation in concatFuncCore()

ground_truth.root_cause: The multiplication `(argc-1)*nSep` is evaluated entirely in 32-bit signed integer arithmetic (both operands are `int`). The result is only widened to `i64` when assigned to `n`, but by that point the overflow has already occurred. The fix is to cast one operand to `i64` before the multiplication so the arithmetic is performed in 64-bit.

findings.message: In the zipfileInflate() function, sqlite3_result_blob() is called with nOut (the expected uncompressed size taken from the ZIP file header) as the blob length. However, when inflate() decompresses the data, the actual number of bytes written to aRes may be less than nOut if the ZIP file is malformed or crafted. The buffer aRes is allocated with nOut bytes but only str.total_out bytes are actually written. Passing nOut to sqlite3_result_blob() causes it to read and expose up to (nOut - str.total_out) bytes beyond the initialized region of the heap buffer, constituting an out-of-bounds read that can leak uninitialized heap memory or cause a crash.
findings.suggestion: Replace nOut with (int)str.total_out in the sqlite3_result_blob() call so only the bytes actually produced by inflate() are returned. This matches what the fix commit (5a05c59d4d) does.
findings.suggestion_code: sqlite3_result_blob(pCtx, aRes, (int)str.total_out, zipfileFree);
findings.title: Out-of-bounds read in zipfileInflate() due to using header-declared size instead of actual decompressed size

fix_commit.author: drh
fix_commit.message: Do not return too many bytes from the zipfile extension given a malformed ZIP file.

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Out-of-bounds read in zipfileInflate() due to using header-declared size instead of actual decompressed size
Related location for: Out-of-bounds read in zipfileInflate() due to using header-declared size instead of actual decompressed size

ground_truth.root_cause: The code assumes the ZIP header's stated uncompressed size exactly matches what inflate() actually writes. For well-formed ZIP files this holds, but a malicious or corrupted ZIP can set the uncompressed size to a larger value than what the compressed payload actually decompresses to, causing inflate() to write fewer bytes than nOut while Z_STREAM_END is still returned (e.g. because avail_in ran out). Trusting nOut instead of str.total_out then exposes uninitialized heap bytes.

pr_title: Update the zipfile module so that it matches the documentation.
release_caveats: Actual Git committer date predates 2021: conflicts with current paper. Recommend explicitly removing/excepting introduction-age cutoff, keeping fixing-date window.

agent_reasoning: The shared tombstone allocation originally stored the page count and computed byte size in int variables. A large database-controlled count could truncate the allocation size, producing an undersized allocation. Widening nTomb and nByte to i64 preserves the full allocation size while retaining this snapshot's existing size formula and allocator error handling. Only the two source declarations were edited; no tests or Fossil metadata were changed. Workspace validation passed against intro_parent.

intro_commit_message:
When tokendata=1 queries require multiple segment-cursors, allow those cursors to share a single array of in-memory tombstone pages.

FossilOrigin-Name: e0175d07e4094db5ea4b0378a5ff480dafb6ba9da86a113fa767c4c89c3c866f
pr_description: Allow segment cursors used by tokendata=1 queries to share a reference-counted array of in-memory tombstone pages. Calculate tombstone allocation sizes using 64-bit values so large page counts reach the allocator without truncation.
pr_title: Share FTS5 tombstone arrays across token-data segment cursors
release_caveats: Eligibility uses recorded canonical mainline fix alias; preserve construction fix and canonical fix separately. Independently checked ancestry/date and mapping evidence.

findings.message: In fts5SegIterAllocTombstone(), both nTomb and nByte are declared as int. When nPgTombstone is large (attacker-controlled via corrupt FTS5 index), the expression SZ_FTS5TOMBSTONEARRAY(nTomb+1), which expands to offsetof(Fts5TombstoneArray,apTombstone)+(nTomb+1)*sizeof(Fts5Data*), overflows the 32-bit int. The multiplication (nTomb+1)*sizeof(Fts5Data*) wraps around to a small or even negative value, causing sqlite3Fts5MallocZero to allocate a far smaller buffer than required. Subsequent writes to the tombstone array entries then access memory outside the allocated bounds, constituting an out-of-bounds memory access exploitable from a corrupt database file.
findings.suggestion: Widen nTomb and nByte to i64 (64-bit) before performing the size arithmetic, and cast nPgTombstone explicitly to i64 when assigning. This prevents the multiplication from overflowing. The fix commit does exactly this: 'const i64 nTomb = (i64)pIter->pSeg->nPgTombstone' and 'i64 nByte = SZ_FTS5TOMBSTONEARRAY(nTomb+1)'.
findings.title: Integer overflow in FTS5 tombstone array size calculation causes under-allocation

fix_commit.author: drh
fix_commit.message: Optimize allocation of large tombstone arrays in fts5.

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Integer overflow in FTS5 tombstone array size calculation causes under-allocation
Related location for: Integer overflow in FTS5 tombstone array size calculation causes under-allocation

ground_truth.root_cause: The variables nTomb and nByte in fts5SegIterAllocTombstone() are both typed as int (32-bit signed). The field nPgTombstone is also int and its value comes from the serialized database format, making it attacker-controllable. When nTomb is large (e.g., ~256M on a 64-bit system where sizeof(Fts5Data*)==8), the product nTomb*sizeof(Fts5Data*) exceeds INT_MAX, wrapping around to a small or negative value. The resulting nByte value is passed to the allocator, which allocates a much smaller block than the code expects.

pr_title: When tokendata=1 queries require multiple segment-cursors, allow those cursors to share a single array of in-memory tombstone pages.
release_caveats: Eligibility uses recorded canonical mainline fix alias; preserve construction fix and canonical fix separately. Independently checked ancestry/date and mapping evidence.

agent_reasoning: The bounds check used the 30-byte local-file header size even though the data pointer advances past the 46-byte central-directory header. This understated the required buffer length by 16 bytes and could allow out-of-bounds reads. The source now uses ZIPFILE_CDS_FIXED_SZ in the guard, matching the data pointer offset and rejecting truncated payloads before subsequent reads. Only the one-line source correction was applied; test files and Fossil metadata were not edited. Workspace validation passed against intro_parent.

findings.message: In zipfileGetEntry(), when reading Central Directory Structure (CDS) entries from a blob (in-memory ZIP), the bounds check uses ZIPFILE_LFH_FIXED_SZ (30) instead of ZIPFILE_CDS_FIXED_SZ (46). The pointer aRead is set to &aBlob[iOff + ZIPFILE_CDS_FIXED_SZ] (i.e., offset +46), but the bounds check only verifies iOff + ZIPFILE_LFH_FIXED_SZ + nFile + nExtra > nBlob (i.e., offset +30). This 16-byte discrepancy means that when nBlob - iOff - nFile - nExtra falls between 30 and 45 inclusive, the bounds check passes but the subsequent read starting at offset iOff+46 (and extending through nFile+nExtra bytes) is out of bounds, causing a heap buffer overread.
findings.suggestion: Replace ZIPFILE_LFH_FIXED_SZ with ZIPFILE_CDS_FIXED_SZ in the bounds check so that the verified range matches the actual accessor offset. The check must account for the CDS fixed-size header (46 bytes) at which aRead starts, not the LFH fixed-size header (30 bytes).
findings.title: Wrong size constant in bounds check allows out-of-bounds read in zipfile extension

fix_commit.message: Fix a typo in [0819fe670f9ceec7] that lead to incomplete protection against buffer overflow in the zipfile extension. [forum:/forumpost/2025-12-30T23:57:19z|Forum post 2025-12-30T23:57:19z]

Related location for: Wrong size constant in bounds check allows out-of-bounds read in zipfile extension

ground_truth.root_cause: A copy-paste or naming mistake in the newly added bounds check: the developer wrote ZIPFILE_LFH_FIXED_SZ (the Local File Header constant, value 30) when the intent was ZIPFILE_CDS_FIXED_SZ (the Central Directory Structure constant, value 46). Since aRead is placed at iOff + ZIPFILE_CDS_FIXED_SZ (offset 46), the safety guard must use that same constant to correctly bound the subsequent read of nFile+nExtra bytes.

pr_description: FossilOrigin-Name: 0819fe670f9ceec79f84eb09c234dc29f6581332f86a53d6a0547697404efff1
pr_title: Fix another potential buffer overread in the zipfile extension.

agent_reasoning: The original allocation computed nOut+1 as a signed int, which can overflow when a malicious delta declares an output size of INT_MAX. The source edit casts nOut to i64 before addition and passes the result to sqlite3_malloc64, preventing this signed overflow. Only the allocation line was changed; no tests or Fossil metadata were modified. Workspace validation passed against intro_parent.

findings.message: In rbuFossilDeltaFunc(), the variable `nOut` is declared as `int` (32-bit signed integer). When a maliciously crafted fossil delta encodes an output size of INT_MAX (2147483647), the expression `nOut+1` wraps around to a negative value due to signed integer overflow. This negative (or unexpectedly small) value is then passed to `sqlite3_malloc()`, causing the allocator to return a much smaller buffer than expected. Subsequent writes by `rbuDeltaApply()` using the full `nOut` bytes then overflow this under-allocated buffer, potentially enabling heap corruption.
findings.suggestion: Cast nOut to a 64-bit integer before adding 1, and use sqlite3_malloc64() to handle allocations larger than INT_MAX safely.
findings.suggestion_code: aOut = sqlite3_malloc64((i64)nOut+1);
findings.title: Signed integer overflow in sqlite3_malloc size argument

fix_commit.author: drh
fix_commit.message: Fix a possible signed integer overflow in the RBU extension given a maliciously crafted delta. [bugs:/info/2026-06-10T06:41:54Z|Bug 2026-06-10T06:41:54Z].

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Signed integer overflow in sqlite3_malloc size argument

ground_truth.root_cause: The output size `nOut` is stored as a 32-bit signed `int`. The expression `nOut+1` used as the malloc size argument is also computed in 32-bit signed arithmetic. When `nOut` equals INT_MAX (0x7fffffff), adding 1 produces undefined behaviour (signed overflow) that in practice results in a negative or zero value being passed to sqlite3_malloc(), causing a much smaller allocation than required.

pr_description: FossilOrigin-Name: e26ef165fe2f7524684af0d269d38475ea8b9489
pr_title: Add support for "fossil deltas" to RBU and "sqldiff --rbu".
release_caveats: Actual Git committer date predates 2021: conflicts with current paper. Recommend explicitly removing/excepting introduction-age cutoff, keeping fixing-date window.

agent_reasoning: The sign-handling logic could multiply INT64_MIN by -1 when processing a corrupt end_block record, causing signed integer overflow. The parser now forces the multiplier to 1 at that boundary, using a local constant expression because this snapshot lacks a shared FTS constant. Unsigned accumulation and explicit signed conversions match the supplied fix's parsing context and avoid overflow before the guard. Only ext/fts3/fts3_write.c was edited; test files and Fossil metadata were left unchanged.
