agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 5666bca708c0 on top of intro 36f07e9a0448 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): RegExpMatchGlobalAtom_OneCharPattern in V8's regexp runtime uses SIMD (via Highway) to scan a subject string for occurrences of a single-character atom pattern, processing the bulk of the string in vector-width blocks and then falling back to a scalar loop for any trailing characters that don't fill a full SIMD lane. The scalar tail loop was written as `for (SChar c = *block; block < end; c = *(++block))`, which unconditionally reads `*block` in the for-loop initializer before the `block < end` bound check is performed. When the SIMD loops consume the subject string exactly to its end (leaving zero remaining scalar characters), `block` already equals `end`, and this initializer read accesses one character past the end of the allocated string buffer -- an out-of-bounds read. Root cause: The scalar cleanup loop's for-statement puts a pointer dereference in the initializer clause, which is unconditionally evaluated once before the loop's controlling condition is checked. This violates the invariant that `block` must be checked against `end` before every dereference, allowing a read exactly at (one past) the end of the subject string's backing buffer when there are no trailing characters left to scan.

findings.message: In the scalar 'remaining characters' tail loop of RegExpMatchGlobalAtom_OneCharPattern, the loop is written as a C-style for loop where the initializer unconditionally dereferences `*block` before the loop condition `block < end` is evaluated: `for (SChar c = *block; block < end; c = *(++block))`. Because the initializer executes exactly once regardless of the loop condition, when the preceding SIMD block-processing loops have already advanced `block` to equal `end` (i.e., there are zero remaining scalar characters to process), this initializer still performs `*block`, reading one character past the end of the allocated subject string buffer. Although the loaded value is discarded (the loop body never executes since `block < end` is false), the read itself is undefined behavior and can be flagged by ASan/MSan or crash on the last page of a mapped buffer, constituting an out-of-bounds read vulnerability.
findings.suggestion: Do not dereference `*block` in the loop initializer before verifying `block < end`. Restructure the loop so the character is only loaded after the bounds check, e.g. move the load inside the loop body: `for (; block < end; ++block) { SChar c = *block; ... }`. This guarantees the pointer is never dereferenced once it has reached `end`.
findings.title: Out-of-bounds read of one character past subject buffer end in scalar tail loop

agent_reasoning: Without the added check, GetCycleRoot(isolate) is invoked unconditionally on every async parent module during ancestor gathering. GetCycleRoot() casts the module's cycle_root field directly to a SourceTextModule handle. For a parent module that fails synchronously while depending on an async child, cycle_root is never assigned and remains the uninitialized hole value. Calling ->status() on that casted hole treats the Hole oddball as if it were a SourceTextModule object, reading a 'status' field at an offset into memory that isn't actually a module object header — a type confusion that can leak or corrupt memory. The fix guards the call with `!IsTheHole(m->cycle_root(), isolate)` so GetCycleRoot() is only dereferenced when cycle_root has actually been initialized, eliminating the type confusion while preserving the original intent of the spec-derived check.

findings.message: In SourceTextModule::GatherAvailableAncestors, the loop over async parent modules evaluates `m->GetCycleRoot(isolate)->status() != kErrored` as the FIRST operand of the `&&`, meaning it is evaluated unconditionally for every async parent `m`, before checking whether `m` is already present in `exec_list`. GetCycleRoot() reads the module's `cycle_root` Tagged field and casts/dereferences it as a SourceTextModule (via Cast<SourceTextModule>). However, `cycle_root` is only guaranteed to be initialized (set to something other than the_hole) once a module has gone through specific points of the evaluation state machine. There is a scenario — an async parent module that depends on an async child but which itself fails synchronously before its cycle_root is ever assigned — where `cycle_root` remains the_hole when this function later runs (triggered when the async child eventually completes and walks up to gather available ancestors). Calling GetCycleRoot(isolate) in that state casts the Hole object to a SourceTextModule handle and then dereferences `->status()` on it, which is a type confusion / hole leak: the hole value is treated as a valid HeapObject of type SourceTextModule, and arbitrary offset reads are performed against it. Before this commit, the exec_list membership check was evaluated first, which happened to short-circuit away many calls to GetCycleRoot() on modules whose cycle_root had not been set; reordering the && operands here made the GetCycleRoot() call happen unconditionally on every iteration, which is a prerequisite for hitting the unguarded hole case that the later fix addresses.
findings.suggestion: Before calling GetCycleRoot(isolate) on m, explicitly check that m->cycle_root() is not the_hole (i.e. that CycleRoot has actually been initialized for this module). Only call GetCycleRoot()->status() once that is confirmed; otherwise treat the module as not having an errored cycle root for the purposes of this check (matching the later upstream fix, which adds `!IsTheHole(m->cycle_root(), isolate) &&` as the first conjunct and a DCHECK that cycle_root is only the_hole when m->status() == kErrored).

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix e194d3a40d8e on top of intro b9068d13bb1c via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (DataRace): V8's WebAssembly implementation stores per-module function signatures (and related C++ fast-API call signatures added during instantiation) in a `WasmModuleSignatureStorage` object held as a `mutable` field on the otherwise-const `WasmModule` struct. This storage can be appended to concurrently during module instantiation on one thread while another thread (e.g. performing `performance.measureMemory()` / memory-consumption tracing) reads its size via `WasmModule::EstimateStoredSize()` / `EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()`. The code that mutates `signature_storage` is correctly protected by `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_`, but the code that reads it for memory estimation purposes was not holding that same mutex, creating a data race on the underlying vector-of-vectors storage. Root cause: When `signature_zone` (a Zone) was replaced by the custom `WasmModuleSignatureStorage` class in commit b9068d13bb1, the new class's `TotalReservedSize()` accessor was invoked from `WasmModule::EstimateStoredSize()`/`EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` exactly as the old Zone accessor had been — i.e., without any synchronization — even though the class's own doc comment states that `signature_storage` is mutated during instantiation on a `const WasmModule`. The call chain `NativeModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` → `module_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` executes before `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_` is acquired in that function, so a concurrent instantiation thread appending to `signature_storage` races with the reading thread.
commit_message:
[wasm] Introduce WasmModuleSignatureStorage

This replaces a Zone we used for storing signatures, array types, and
struct types. Zones are meant for temporary storage and are not very
memory efficient.

The new WasmModuleSignatureStorage provides pointer stability and a
similar interface than a zone, but has less memory overhead.

findings.message: WasmModule::EstimateStoredSize() reads `signature_storage.TotalReservedSize()` (and the aggregate `WasmModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` which calls EstimateStoredSize()) without acquiring any lock. However, `signature_storage` (introduced in this commit, replacing the former `signature_zone`) is `mutable` and is concurrently mutated during instantiation (e.g. when fast API call signatures are added) while protected by `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_` elsewhere in the codebase. `NativeModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` in wasm-code-manager.cc calls `module_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` at the very top of the function, before acquiring `allocation_mutex_` (the mutex is only taken later, around the `owned_code_`/`new_owned_code_`/`debug_info_` bookkeeping). Because the memory-consumption estimation can run concurrently (e.g. from `d8`'s performance.measureMemory or background profiling) with module instantiation on another thread that appends to `signature_storage`, this is a data race (TOCTOU/missing synchronization) on the underlying `std::vector<std::vector<uint8_t>> storage_` backing store, which can corrupt the vector's internal size/capacity bookkeeping or allow a torn read, leading to incorrect memory accounting and, under race conditions on reallocation, potential use of stale/invalid pointers or crashes. The original Zone-based implementation (`signature_zone.allocation_size_for_tracing()`) had the same unprotected access pattern, but the comment on the class explicitly acknowledges concurrent mutation during instantiation is expected, making the omission of locking in the size-estimation path a clear oversight.
findings.suggestion: Protect all accesses to `signature_storage` (both reads from EstimateStoredSize/EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption and writes during instantiation) with `NativeModule::allocation_mutex_`. In NativeModule::EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption(), acquire the allocation_mutex_ before calling `module_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` (which transitively reads signature_storage), and only release it after that call completes but before calling into `debug_info_->EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption()` to avoid a lock-order inversion with WasmScript::SetBreakPointForFunction. Also move `signature_storage.TotalReservedSize()` out of EstimateStoredSize() into EstimateCurrentMemoryConsumption() so it is always evaluated under the lock.

findings.message: Shell::ResetOnProfileEndListener(Isolate*) is responsible for tearing down the per-isolate profiler-end callback state before an Isolate is disposed. The function was modified to add an early 'if (options.enable_inspector) return;' guard BEFORE the call to profiler_end_callback_.erase(isolate). When the inspector is enabled, the function returns immediately without erasing the isolate's entry from the profiler_end_callback_ map (which stores v8::Global<Function>/v8::Global<Context> handles keyed by Isolate*). Callers of ResetOnProfileEndListener (e.g. SourceGroup::ExecuteInThread, Worker::ExecuteInThread, Shell::Main, Shell::QuitOnce) call this function immediately before disposing the Isolate, expecting all isolate-associated state to be cleaned up. Because the erase is skipped whenever the inspector is enabled, the stale map entry (and the dangling Isolate* key, plus Global handles bound to a soon-to-be-destroyed Isolate) survives isolate disposal. Any later interaction that touches profiler_end_callback_ with the freed Isolate pointer (e.g. HasOnProfileEndListener/TriggerOnProfileEndListener being invoked again, e.g. if the isolate address is reused or the map is iterated/looked up) results in a use-after-free, since the stored Global<Function>/Global<Context> objects reference memory owned by the disposed isolate.
findings.suggestion: Perform the profiler_end_callback_.erase(isolate) call unconditionally, before checking options.enable_inspector, so the per-isolate map entry is always cleaned up regardless of whether the inspector console (D8Console) is installed. Only the D8Console-specific cleanup (console_delegate cast and DisposeProfiler()) should be skipped when the inspector is enabled.

agent_reasoning: The intro commit added an optimization in BuildCheckSmi that skips the runtime Smi check when TryGetInt32Constant proves the value lies in Smi range, without considering whether the input's value representation is tagged. For non-tagged representations this is safe because the fallback switch performs an equivalent value-range check. For tagged inputs, the fallback check (CheckSmi) verifies pointer tag bits rather than numeric value, and TryGetInt32Constant can return a value derived from a HeapNumber constant recorded via numeric-equality reasoning (CheckFloat64SameValue), not tag-verified equality. This mismatch allows the compiler to elide a necessary tag check, causing type confusion between Smi and HeapNumber, and a corresponding missing GC write barrier downstream. The fix restricts the elision to non-tagged value representations only, matching the upstream fix commit exactly, with no test files modified.
commit_message:
[maglev] Improve constant handling for BuildCheckSmi and the Array ctor

This patch improves the handling of constants in two places in the
Maglev graph builder:

1. In `BuildCheckSmi`: We can now often avoid emitting a runtime smi
check if the input is a constant that is known to be a smi at compile
time.
2. In `TryReduceConstructArrayConstructor`: When determining the
elements kind for a newly constructed array, we can now extract type
information from constant arguments even if they don't have a precise
NodeType set. This allows for more accurate elements kind selection.

These changes should lead to slightly better code generation in cases
involving constants.

fix_commit_message:
[maglev] Restrict BuildCheckSmi constant elision to non-tagged inputs

The elision added in CL 6988172 (commit 6469250a124a) skipped the
runtime check whenever TryGetInt32Constant(object) returned a value in
Smi range. For non-tagged input representations this is sound, because
the switch below emits a value-range check (CheckInt32IsSmi /
CheckUint32IsSmi / CheckFloat64IsSmi / CheckHoleyFloat64IsSmi /
CheckIntPtrIsSmi), which is exactly what Smi::IsValid proves.

For kTagged inputs the emitted check is CheckSmi, a tag-bit check.
Value-equivalence does not imply Smi tagging: a tagged node can be equal
in value to a Smi-range constant while actually holding a HeapNumber at
runtime. This happens when BuildCheckNumericalValue's HeapNumber branch
records a Constant(HeapNumber N) in the node's checked_value alternative
after a CheckFloat64SameValue; since CheckFloat64SameValue only proves
numeric equality, both Smi(N) and HeapNumber(N) pass it.
TryGetInt32Constant recurses through the alternative and returns N, so
the elision drops the tag check and a HeapNumber pointer can flow into
downstream consumers (e.g. the kSmi-field store path via
StoreTaggedFieldNoWriteBarrier), causing a type confusion and a missing
write barrier.

Gate the elision on value_representation() != kTagged. For tagged Smi
inputs the earlier StaticTypeIs(kSmi) / EnsureType(kSmi) early returns
already handle elision via type-system facts, which carry the tag
guarantee the value-equivalence alternative does not.

findings.message:
MaglevGraphBuilder::BuildCheckSmi() added an optimization that skips emitting the runtime Smi check whenever TryGetInt32Constant(object) returns a value that lies within the Smi range (Smi::IsValid). This is only sound when the emitted check would have been a value-range check (e.g. for kInt32/kUint32/kFloat64/kHoleyFloat64/kIntPtr inputs, where the subsequently-emitted CheckInt32IsSmi/CheckUint32IsSmi/CheckFloat64IsSmi/CheckHoleyFloat64IsSmi/CheckIntPtrIsSmi checks are exactly what Smi::IsValid proves).

However, for kTagged inputs the runtime check that would otherwise be emitted is CheckSmi, which is a tag-bit check, not a value-range check. TryGetInt32Constant() can recurse through a node's 'checked_value' alternative, which BuildCheckNumericalValue's HeapNumber branch can populate with a Constant(HeapNumber N) after only a CheckFloat64SameValue (a numeric-equality check that both a Smi(N) and a HeapNumber(N) satisfy). Consequently, for a kTagged node whose alternative records a HeapNumber constant with a value in Smi range, BuildCheckSmi incorrectly elides the CheckSmi tag check and returns the object as though it were proven to be a Smi.

This allows a HeapNumber pointer to flow into code paths that assume a Smi (e.g. field stores using StoreTaggedFieldNoWriteBarrier because the field is believed to hold only Smis), producing a type confusion and a missing write barrier - a serious, exploitable memory-safety bug reachable from JavaScript via Maglev-compiled code.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the constant-value-based elision to non-tagged input representations, since only those cases have the following switch emit an equivalent value-range check. For kTagged inputs, rely only on the earlier type-system checks (StaticTypeIs(kSmi) / EnsureType(kSmi)) which correctly carry the tag guarantee; do not elide the CheckSmi tag check based on value-equivalence alone.
findings.title: BuildCheckSmi constant elision unsound for tagged inputs, allowing HeapNumber to bypass Smi check

For non-tagged representations the two are equivalent because the fallback switch performs an explicit value-range check; but for kTagged inputs the fallback check (CheckSmi) verifies the pointer's tag bits, a distinct property not implied by numeric equivalence, especially since the 'checked_value' alternative can be populated with a HeapNumber constant purely from a same-value float comparison.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 4e101ceb0b0b on top of intro 8d161a06cdbf via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): When --trace-deopt-verbose is enabled, Runtime_WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish in src/runtime/runtime-wasm.cc logs the wasm function being deoptimized by calling NativeModule::GetCode(). It passes a 'declared function index' (relative to the module's non-imported functions) into GetCode(), which expects a 'module function index' (including imported functions) and internally re-derives the declared index by subtracting num_imported_functions. This double conversion produces an incorrect (potentially negative) index used to access the NativeModule's code_table_ array, leading to an out-of-bounds read / DCHECK failure and an incorrect diagnostic function index/name being logged. Root cause: Two different kinds of wasm function indices exist in V8's codebase: the 'declared function index' (excludes imported functions) and the 'module function index' (includes imported functions). NativeModule::GetCode() expects the latter and performs its own conversion via declared_function_index(). The introducing commit passed the already-declared index directly to GetCode() without converting it back to a module-scoped index, causing the conversion to be applied twice.
commit_message:
[wasm][deoptimizer] Resolve feedback vector in WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish only

Previously the deoptimizer would try to lookup the feedback vector in
the vector of feedback vectors in the wasm trusted instance.
This was implemented at a time when I still assumed that there will
always be a valid feedback vector, however due to multi-instance
scenarios, this turned out to be incorrect. Later on this was fixed in
the WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish to allocate and fill in those feedback
vectors for which we didn't find one yet.

Moving the lookup of the feedback vector to the builtin exclusively
simplifies the code and also removes an access to the heap from within
the deoptimizer (which we'd ideally reduce down to zero if possible).

intro_commit_message:
[wasm][deoptimizer] Resolve feedback vector in WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish only

Previously the deoptimizer would try to lookup the feedback vector in
the vector of feedback vectors in the wasm trusted instance.
This was implemented at a time when I still assumed that there will
always be a valid feedback vector, however due to multi-instance
scenarios, this turned out to be incorrect. Later on this was fixed in
the WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish to allocate and fill in those feedback
vectors for which we didn't find one yet.

Moving the lookup of the feedback vector to the builtin exclusively
simplifies the code and also removes an access to the heap from within
the deoptimizer (which we'd ideally reduce down to zero if possible).

findings.message: In Runtime_WasmLiftoffDeoptFinish, when v8_flags.trace_deopt_verbose is enabled and a feedback vector needs to be allocated, the code calls trusted_instance_data->native_module()->GetCode(declared_func_index). However, declared_func_index is already the index relative to the first *declared* (non-imported) wasm function (it was decoded directly from the Smi stored in the liftoff frame's feedback-vector slot). NativeModule::GetCode(uint32_t index) expects a *module-scoped* function index (including imports) and internally converts it via declared_function_index(module(), index), which subtracts module->num_imported_functions again. Passing an already-declared index therefore causes a second, erroneous subtraction of num_imported_functions, producing a negative or otherwise wrong index used to access code_table_[...]. In debug builds this trips the DCHECK_LE/DCHECK_GT assertions inside declared_function_index(); in release builds (where DCHECKs are compiled out) it results in an out-of-bounds read into the NativeModule's code_table_ vector, which can crash the process or leak adjacent heap memory contents through code->DebugName() in the trace output. The same wrong index is also printed in the PrintF diagnostic message, misreporting the actual function.
findings.suggestion: Convert declared_func_index into a module-scoped function index before calling GetCode(), matching the convention used elsewhere (e.g. int module_func_index = trusted_instance_data->native_module()->num_imported_functions() + declared_func_index;), and use that value both for GetCode() and for the printed index.
findings.title: Wrong function-index kind passed to NativeModule::GetCode() in wasm deopt tracing

fix_commit.author: Matthias Liedtke
fix_commit.message: [runtime][wasm] Fix --trace-deopt-verbose using the wrong kind of index

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Wrong function-index kind passed to NativeModule::GetCode() in wasm deopt tracing

ground_truth.root_cause: Two different kinds of wasm function indices exist in V8's codebase: the 'declared function index' (excludes imported functions) and the 'module function index' (includes imported functions). NativeModule::GetCode() expects the latter and performs its own conversion via declared_function_index(). The introducing commit passed the already-declared index directly to GetCode() without converting it back to a module-scoped index, causing the conversion to be applied twice.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 604e1bec5911 on top of intro 8a41470735aa via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): In V8's Maglev compiler, MaglevGraphBuilder::TryInferApiHolderValue() attempts to statically infer the 'holder' object for an API function call based on known receiver map information. As part of this, it calls MapInference::InsertMapChecks(), which can internally decide that graph building must abort (nulling out the builder's current basic block, e.g. current_block_) if it cannot safely insert the required map-check nodes. However, TryInferApiHolderValue() only had a single return type (compiler::HolderLookupResult) and mapped both the abort case and the legitimate 'holder could not be inferred' case to the same 'not_found' sentinel value. Its caller, TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction(), used this sentinel to decide to fall through and build a generic CallBuiltin node, unaware that graph building had actually aborted. This caused further IR nodes (including exception handler attachment via AttachExceptionHandlerInfo) to be emitted against an invalid/null current_block_, leading to a null-pointer dereference and crash. Root cause: Conflating two semantically distinct outcomes ('holder not found' vs 'graph building aborted') into a single sentinel return value, so the caller cannot detect that the compiler has entered a dead/aborted state and must stop emitting nodes.
commit_message:
[maglev] Introduce MapInference

This CL introduces `MapInference`, similar to TurboFan, to manage map
knowledge in Maglev.  Instead of clearing possible maps on side effects,
we now mark them as stale. This allows us to either ignore them or
re-verify them using `CheckMaps`.

All previous users of NodeInfo::possible_maps were updated to use the
MapInference interface; in addition to fetching the set of possible
maps, they are now required to call InsertMapChecks once the decision
has been made to use possible_maps.

InsertMapChecks only emits map checks when needed, ie when at least one
stale unstable map exists. Unreliable maps are "stale" when a side
effect may have occurred after we've last recorded them.

The --maglev-use-unreliable-maps flag, on by default, currently controls
whether Maglev uses stale unreliable maps by default, ie when no
explicit variant is passed to MapInference methods. Note that there is
no guarantee that *not* enabling this flag is identical to previous
behavior, since map tracking changed underneath (it should be similar
though). This flag is likely to be removed soon.

This CL also introduces KNA tracing: --trace-maglev-kna.

fix_commit_message:
[maglev] Don't swallow aborts in TryInferApiHolderValue

InsertMapChecks can abort (and null current_block_), but we'd
return the default "not found" sentinel, causing the caller in
TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction to fall through and emit a
CallBuiltin into a dead block. AttachExceptionHandlerInfo then
dereferences current_block_ and crashes.

Return std::optional instead; nullopt means the caller must
propagate DoneWithAbort.

findings.message: TryInferApiHolderValue() returns a plain compiler::HolderLookupResult. When inference.InsertMapChecks(zone()) detects that graph building has aborted (e.g. because a required map check could not be safely inserted and the current basic block was terminated/nulled), the function collapses this distinct 'abort' condition into the same 'not_found' sentinel value that it also returns for the ordinary, non-abort 'holder could not be inferred' case. The caller, MaglevGraphBuilder::TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction, cannot distinguish these two cases: it simply assigns the return value to api_holder and continues normal control flow via the switch on api_holder.lookup, falling through to emit further graph nodes (a CallBuiltin) into what is actually a dead/aborted block. AttachExceptionHandlerInfo (and other downstream code that assumes current_block_ is valid) then dereferences the now-null/invalid current_block_, causing a crash. This was introduced when MapInference was added and InsertMapChecks (which can internally abort graph building) was called with its abort result discarded/mapped to the ordinary not-found path.
findings.suggestion: Change TryInferApiHolderValue's return type to std::optional<compiler::HolderLookupResult> (or otherwise separately signal the abort condition) so that when InsertMapChecks aborts, the function returns std::nullopt instead of the same sentinel used for ordinary 'not found'. The caller (TryBuildCallKnownApiFunction) must check for this and immediately propagate ReduceResult::DoneWithAbort() instead of falling through to build further nodes in the now-dead block.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 63226679f9f5 on top of intro 551ade488094 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (NullPointerDereference): While refactoring MaglevGraphBuilder::CanInlineCall into a shared MaglevReducer<BaseT>::CanInlineCall template (used by both the maglev builder and turbolev), the recursion-detection check was changed to consult MaglevReducer::current_provenance().unit — data that is sourced from the MaglevGraphLabeller, a component that is only actively maintained when GDB JIT interface support / tracing (--gdbjit, ENABLE_GDB_JIT_INTERFACE) is enabled. In release/non-tracing builds this provenance's `unit` pointer can be null. Calling `->shared_function_info()` on it during non-eager function inlining dereferences a null pointer and crashes the process (SIGSEGV). Additionally, because the graph labeller bookkeeping was being unconditionally performed for this data (regardless of whether gdbjit/tracing was enabled), it caused a related performance regression, which the fix commit also addresses by gating maglev_gdbjit metadata collection behind the actual gdbjit/tracing flags. Root cause: The direct-recursion self-inlining check was changed from reading the builder's own always-valid MaglevCompilationUnit pointer to instead reading MaglevGraphLabeller-derived provenance data, which is only guaranteed to be populated when GDB JIT interface support or graph tracing is active. This coupled a functional correctness check to an optional, debug-only subsystem, producing a null-pointer dereference when that subsystem was disabled (the common release-build case).

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability was in the `fd_renumber` implementation in `crates/wasi/src/preview2/preview1/mod.rs`. The `remove()` helper added the source FD to a `free` Vec, but `fd_renumber` re-inserted the descriptor at `to` without: (a) handling the `from == to` identity case (which left the FD in both `used` and `free`), or (b) removing `to` from `free` when it was a previously-closed FD (creating a duplicate `free` entry). Either scenario caused `push()` — called later during operations like `path_open` — to pop a "free" FD that was still live in `used`, triggering the `assert!(self.insert(fd, desc).is_none())` panic. The fix changes `free` to a `BTreeSet` (preventing duplicates structurally), removes the flawed `remove()` helper, rewrites `fd_close` to explicitly manage both `used` and `free`, and rewrites `fd_renumber` to be a no-op for `from == to` and to explicitly evict `to` from `free` before inserting into `used`. The `Deref`/`DerefMut` impls on `Descriptors` are also removed so all accesses go through `.used` explicitly, making the accounting auditable.

pr_description:
## Summary

The `fd_renumber` syscall implementation had a subtle accounting bug that could corrupt the internal file descriptor tracking state and cause a host panic.

The `Descriptors` structure tracks open file descriptors in a `used` BTreeMap and a `free` list of available FD numbers to reuse. Previously, the `remove()` helper removed an FD from `used` and pushed it onto the `free` Vec. The `fd_renumber` implementation called `remove(from)` and then unconditionally inserted the descriptor at `to`.

This caused two corruption scenarios:

1. **Identity renumber (`from == to`)**: The FD was removed from `used` and added to `free`, then immediately re-inserted into `used`. The FD now exists in both `used` and `free` simultaneously.

2. **Renumber to a previously-closed FD**: If `to` was already on the `free` list (from a prior `fd_close`), inserting into `used` did not remove it from `free`. Again, the FD existed in both structures.

In either case, the next call to `push()` (e.g. from `path_open`) would pop the poisoned FD from `free`, then call `assert!(self.used.insert(fd, desc).is_none())`. Since the FD was already present in `used`, the insert returned `Some(...)`, triggering an unconditional panic — a guest-triggered host denial of service.

## Changes

- Changed `free` from `Vec<u32>` to `BTreeSet<u32>`, eliminating the possibility of duplicate entries
- Removed the `Deref`/`DerefMut` impls on `Descriptors` (which obscured direct `used` map access) and updated all call sites to explicitly use `.used.get()`, `.used.insert()`, etc.
- Replaced the `remove()` helper with inlined removal logic in `fd_close`, making the accounting explicit
- Rewrote `fd_renumber` to: (a) return `EBADF` if `from` is not open, (b) skip all mutation when `from == to`, and (c) explicitly remove `to` from `free` before inserting into `used` when renumbering to a previously-freed FD
- Updated `push()` to use `pop_last()` on the BTreeSet

## Test plan

- [ ] Existing preview1 fd_renumber tests pass
- [ ] `fd_renumber(n, n)` no longer corrupts FD state
- [ ] After `fd_renumber(fd, u32::MAX)`, subsequent `path_open` returns a valid FD without panicking
- [ ] `fd_close` correctly populates the free set so FD numbers are reused safely
pr_title: fix(wasip1): prevent duplicate FD entries from fd_renumber

findings.message: The `fd_renumber` implementation calls `descriptors.remove(from)`, which internally removes the fd from `used` AND pushes it onto the `free` Vec. It then unconditionally calls `descriptors.insert(to.into(), desc)`. Two cases corrupt state: (1) when `from == to`, the fd is added to `free` and immediately re-inserted into `used`, leaving it present in both structures; (2) when `to` is a previously-closed fd already on `free`, it is inserted into `used` without being removed from `free`, again creating a duplicate. A later call to `push()` (e.g., from `path_open`) pops the poisoned fd from `free` and executes `assert!(self.insert(fd, desc).is_none())`. Because the fd is already present in `used`, the insert returns `Some(...)` and the assertion fires, causing an unconditional host panic (denial of service).

related_locations.description: remove() pushes freed fd onto self.free — the source of the corrupted free-list entry
push() pops from free and asserts the insert returns None — panics when fd is already in used

findings.suggestion: Guard fd_renumber with two fixes: (1) make fd_renumber(n, n) a no-op (do not call remove when from == to); (2) when from != to, explicitly remove `to` from the free set before inserting it into used. The fix also changes `free` from a Vec to a BTreeSet so that membership checks and targeted removals are O(log n) instead of O(n).

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability is a data race in safe Rust: `Memory::_new` (called by both `Memory::new` and `Memory::new_async`) accepted any `MemoryType` without checking `ty.is_shared()`. Because `wasmtime::Memory` exposes safe byte-slice accessors (`data`, `data_mut`, `read`, `write`) that are not atomic, wrapping a WebAssembly shared linear memory in a `Memory` object allowed a second thread to concurrently mutate those bytes through the `SharedMemory` API, violating Rust's aliasing rules without any `unsafe` block in user code. The fix adds `if ty.is_shared() { bail!(...) }` at the top of `Memory::_new`, ensuring shared memory types are rejected and callers are directed to `SharedMemory::new` instead. This is the only change needed in this version of the codebase because the export/dispatch logic already correctly routes shared-memory exports to `SharedMemory` (via the `m.memory.memory.shared` flag check in `Extern::from_wasmtime_export`), and there is no coredump feature in this older codebase that also needs patching.
commit_message:
[Merged] Add shared memories (#4187)

* Add shared memories

This change adds the ability to use shared memories in Wasmtime when the
[threads proposal] is enabled. Shared memories are annotated as `shared`
in the WebAssembly syntax, e.g., `(memory 1 1 shared)`, and are
protected from concurrent access during `memory.size` and `memory.grow`.

[threads proposal]: https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads/blob/master/proposals/threads/Overview.md

In order to implement this in Wasmtime, there are two main cases to
cover:
    - a program may simply create a shared memory and possibly export it;
    this means that Wasmtime itself must be able to create shared
    memories
    - a user may create a shared memory externally and pass it in as an
    import during instantiation; this is the case when the program
    contains code like `(import "env" "memory" (memory 1 1
    shared))`--this case is handled by a new Wasmtime API
    type--`SharedMemory`

Because of the first case, this change allows any of the current
memory-creation mechanisms to work as-is. Wasmtime can still create
either static or dynamic memories in either on-demand or pooling modes,
and any of these memories can be considered shared. When shared, the
`Memory` runtime container will lock appropriately during `memory.size`
and `memory.grow` operations; since all memories use this container, it
is an ideal place for implementing the locking once and once only.

The second case is covered by the new `SharedMemory` structure. It uses
the same `Mmap` allocation under the hood as non-shared memories, but
allows the user to perform the allocation externally to Wasmtime and
share the memory across threads (via an `Arc`). The pointer address to
the actual memory is carefully wired through and owned by the
`SharedMemory` structure itself. This means that there are differing
views of where to access the pointer (i.e., `VMMemoryDefinition`): for
owned memories (the default), the `VMMemoryDefinition` is stored
directly by the `VMContext`; in the `SharedMemory` case, however, this
`VMContext` must point to this separate structure.

To ensure that the `VMContext` can always point to the correct
`VMMemoryDefinition`, this change alters the `VMContext` structure.
Since a `SharedMemory` owns its own `VMMemoryDefinition`, the
`defined_memories` table in the `VMContext` becomes a sequence of
pointers--in the shared memory case, they point to the
`VMMemoryDefinition` owned by the `SharedMemory` and in the owned memory
case (i.e., not shared) they point to `VMMemoryDefinition`s stored in a
new table, `owned_memories`.

This change adds an additional indirection (through the `*mut
VMMemoryDefinition` pointer) that could add overhead. Using an imported
memory as a proxy, we measured a 1-3% overhead of this approach on the
`pulldown-cmark` benchmark. To avoid this, Cranelift-generated code will
special-case the owned memory access (i.e., load a pointer directly to
the `owned_memories` entry) for `memory.size` so that only
shared memories (and imported memories, as before) incur the indirection
cost.

fix_commit_message:
Prevent using shared memories with `Memory` (#12022)

* Prevent using shared memories with `Memory`

This commit fixes a few issues where it was possible to represent a wasm
shared linear memory with the `wasmtime::Memory` type. This is not sound
because `wasmtime::Memory` provides safe Rust access to the bytes where
that is not possible with wasm shared memories. Shared memories in Rust
must be represented by `SharedMemory`, not `wasmtime::Memory`.

Specifically this commit prevents two vectors of this happening:

1. `Memory::new` now requires that the memory type specified is
   non-shared. Instead `SharedMemory::new` must be used instead.

2. Core dumps now skip over shared memories when iterating over all
   memories in the store. Supporting shared memories is left to a future
   feature request for now.

* CI fixes

intro_commit_message:
Add shared memories (#4187)

* Add shared memories

This change adds the ability to use shared memories in Wasmtime when the
[threads proposal] is enabled. Shared memories are annotated as `shared`
in the WebAssembly syntax, e.g., `(memory 1 1 shared)`, and are
protected from concurrent access during `memory.size` and `memory.grow`.

[threads proposal]: https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads/blob/master/proposals/threads/Overview.md

In order to implement this in Wasmtime, there are two main cases to
cover:
    - a program may simply create a shared memory and possibly export it;
    this means that Wasmtime itself must be able to create shared
    memories
    - a user may create a shared memory externally and pass it in as an
    import during instantiation; this is the case when the program
    contains code like `(import "env" "memory" (memory 1 1
    shared))`--this case is handled by a new Wasmtime API
    type--`SharedMemory`

Because of the first case, this change allows any of the current
memory-creation mechanisms to work as-is. Wasmtime can still create
either static or dynamic memories in either on-demand or pooling modes,
and any of these memories can be considered shared. When shared, the
`Memory` runtime container will lock appropriately during `memory.size`
and `memory.grow` operations; since all memories use this container, it
is an ideal place for implementing the locking once and once only.

The second case is covered by the new `SharedMemory` structure. It uses
the same `Mmap` allocation under the hood as non-shared memories, but
allows the user to perform the allocation externally to Wasmtime and
share the memory across threads (via an `Arc`). The pointer address to
the actual memory is carefully wired through and owned by the
`SharedMemory` structure itself. This means that there are differing
views of where to access the pointer (i.e., `VMMemoryDefinition`): for
owned memories (the default), the `VMMemoryDefinition` is stored
directly by the `VMContext`; in the `SharedMemory` case, however, this
`VMContext` must point to this separate structure.

To ensure that the `VMContext` can always point to the correct
`VMMemoryDefinition`, this change alters the `VMContext` structure.
Since a `SharedMemory` owns its own `VMMemoryDefinition`, the
`defined_memories` table in the `VMContext` becomes a sequence of
pointers--in the shared memory case, they point to the
`VMMemoryDefinition` owned by the `SharedMemory` and in the owned memory
case (i.e., not shared) they point to `VMMemoryDefinition`s stored in a
new table, `owned_memories`.

This change adds an additional indirection (through the `*mut
VMMemoryDefinition` pointer) that could add overhead. Using an imported
memory as a proxy, we measured a 1-3% overhead of this approach on the
`pulldown-cmark` benchmark. To avoid this, Cranelift-generated code will
special-case the owned memory access (i.e., load a pointer directly to
the `owned_memories` entry) for `memory.size` so that only
shared memories (and imported memories, as before) incur the indirection
cost.

findings.message: The `Memory::_new` helper (called by both `Memory::new` and `Memory::new_async`) accepts any `MemoryType`, including shared memories, without checking `ty.is_shared()`. Because `wasmtime::Memory` exposes safe Rust methods that return `&[u8]` slices (e.g., `Memory::data`), allowing it to wrap a WebAssembly shared linear memory is unsound: another thread may concurrently write to the same bytes through the `SharedMemory` API, creating a data race in safe Rust code. The fix adds `if ty.is_shared() { bail!(...) }` at the entry of `_new`. Additionally, the core-dump path (`WasmCoreDump::new`) collected all store memories as `Vec<Memory>` without filtering out shared ones, exposing shared memory bytes via the unsynchronised `Memory::data` API during crash capture.
findings.suggestion: Add a guard at the top of `Memory::_new` (or equivalently in `Memory::new`) that rejects shared `MemoryType` values: `if ty.is_shared() { bail!("shared memories must be created through `SharedMemory`") }`. In `WasmCoreDump::new`, filter out shared memories before collecting them into `store_memories`: `store_memories.retain(|m| !m.wasmtime_ty(store).shared);`

agent_reasoning: The bug was that the ISLE `fcopysign` lowering rules for x64 passed operands `a` and `b` directly to vector bitwise AND instructions (ANDPS/ANDPD) without first forcing them into XMM registers. Cranelift's load-sinking pass would then fold a scalar `f32.load` or `f64.load` directly into the vector instruction's memory operand, but those instructions only have a 128-bit memory form — not 32-bit or 64-bit — so the emitted code performed an unintended 128-bit (16-byte) memory read instead of a 4-byte or 8-byte read. Near the end of a valid memory region this could read into unmapped memory (crashing the host) or out-of-sandbox data. The fix adds explicit `(a Xmm a)` and `(b Xmm b)` bindings at the top of each rule, ensuring operands are materialized into registers before being used in vector AND instructions, which prevents load-sinking from widening the load to 128 bits.

       (bitcast_gpr_to_xmm $I32 src))
 
 (rule (lower (has_type $I64 (bitcast src @ (value_type $F64))))
       (bitcast_xmm_to_gpr $F64 src))

       (bitcast_gpr_to_xmm $I64 src))

+            (a Xmm a) ;; force into reg so we don't sink a 128-bit load.
+            (b Xmm b))
+        (x64_orps
+          (x64_andnps sign_bit a)
+          (x64_andps sign_bit b))))

+      (let ((sign_bit Xmm (imm $F64 0x8000000000000000))
+            (a Xmm a) ;; force into reg so we don't sink a 128-bit load.
+            (b Xmm b))
+        (x64_orpd
+          (x64_andnpd sign_bit a)
+          (x64_andpd sign_bit b))))

+
+(rule (lower (has_type (use_sse41) (trunc a @ (value_type $F32))))

fix_commit_message:
Cranelift: x64: fix incorrect load-sinking in `copysign` operator. (#12435)

* Cranelift: x64: do not incorrectly widen loads sunk into `fcopysign`.

The implementation of the `fcopysign` operator uses vector bitwise AND
instructions on the floating-point/vector registers containing the
inputs to the operator. This is a reasonable implementation as the
instruction set does not have scalar (single-lane) bitwise
operators. However, when load-sinking automatically kicks in for an
operand to an `andps`, it can turn a 64-bit load (`f64.load`) into a
128-bit load incorrectly.

This load-widening can cause out-of-bounds accesses where they were
not expected. When dynamic bounds checks are enabled, we compile
assuming the correct load-operator width is codegen'd; a too-wide load
could read beyond the checked bound, either into unmapped
memory (crashing the process) or, worse, valid data outside the
sandbox. In the case of `fcopysign` the result of that read is not
directly available, because it will go into the high (unused)
lane, but the out-of-bounds read itself is a problem.

Thanks to louismerlin for reporting!

* Re-bless Cranelift filetests.

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

intro_commit_message:
x64: Lower fcopysign, ceil, floor, nearest, and trunc in ISLE (#4730)

https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/pull/4730
pr_description:
## Summary

The ISLE lowering rules for `fcopysign` on x64 use vector bitwise AND instructions (`ANDPS`/`ANDPD`, `ANDNPS`/`ANDNPD`) to manipulate the sign bit of floating-point values. These vector instructions operate on 128-bit XMM registers.

Previously, the operands `a` and `b` were passed directly to the vector AND instructions without first being materialized into XMM registers. Cranelift's load-sinking optimization can transparently fold a memory load into an instruction's memory operand. When the operand came from a scalar `f32.load` or `f64.load`, load-sinking would fold the load directly into the `ANDPS`/`ANDPD` instruction's memory operand slot. Because those vector instructions have no scalar (32-bit or 64-bit) memory form — only 128-bit — this caused the emitted code to perform a 128-bit (16-byte) memory read instead of the intended 32-bit or 64-bit load.

This widened load can read up to 12 or 8 extra bytes beyond the intended boundary, which can:
- Cause an out-of-bounds read into guard pages (DoS via segfault / process abort), or
- Read data outside the wasm linear memory sandbox when guard pages are disabled.

## Fix

Force operands `a` and `b` into XMM registers explicitly at the start of each `fcopysign` ISLE rule by binding them with `(a Xmm a)` and `(b Xmm b)`. This prevents load-sinking from widening a scalar load to 128 bits, since the operand will already reside in a register by the time the AND instructions are emitted.

## Test plan

- [ ] Existing filetest `cranelift/filetests/filetests/isa/x64/simd-bitwise-avx.clif` updated to reflect that `fcopysign` with a loaded operand now emits an explicit scalar `vmovss`/`vmovsd` rather than folding the load into `vandps`/`vandpd`.
- [ ] Run `cargo test -p cranelift-codegen` to verify no regressions.
- [ ] Confirm that the generated assembly for `fcopysign` with a memory operand uses a scalar load instruction followed by a register-form AND instruction.
pr_title: Cranelift: x64: force `fcopysign` operands into registers to prevent incorrect load-sinking

(rule (lower (has_type $F64 (fcopysign a @ (value_type $F64) b)))
      (let ((sign_bit Xmm (imm $F64 0x8000000000000000)))
        (x64_orpd
          (x64_andnpd sign_bit a)
          (x64_andpd sign_bit b))))

findings.message: The ISLE lowering rules for `fcopysign` (both F32 and F64 variants) pass operands `a` and `b` directly to vector bitwise AND instructions (`x64_andps`/`x64_andnps` for F32, `x64_andpd`/`x64_andnpd` for F64) without first forcing them into XMM registers. Cranelift's load-sinking pass can then transparently fold a memory load (e.g., from `f64.load`) directly into these vector AND instructions as a memory operand. Because these vector instructions (`ANDPS`/`ANDPD`) operate on 128-bit XMM operands, a memory form of the instruction performs a 128-bit (16-byte) load instead of the expected 64-bit (8-byte) load for F64 or 32-bit (4-byte) load for F32. When the wasm linear memory address is near the end of a valid region, this widened load can extend 8 bytes beyond the checked bound — into unmapped guard pages (causing a segfault) or, with guard pages disabled, into out-of-sandbox data. With signals-based-traps disabled and guard pages enabled, the segfault is uncaught and aborts the host process (DoS).
findings.suggestion: Force operands `a` and `b` into XMM registers before using them as operands to vector AND instructions, so load-sinking cannot widen a scalar (32/64-bit) load into a 128-bit vector memory operand. Add explicit register bindings `(a Xmm a)` and `(b Xmm b)` in the `let` block before passing them to `x64_andps`/`x64_andpd` etc.
findings.suggestion_code:
(rule (lower (has_type $F64 (fcopysign a @ (value_type $F64) b)))
      (let ((sign_bit Xmm (imm $F64 0x8000000000000000))
            (a Xmm a) ;; force into reg so we don't sink a 128-bit load.
            (b Xmm b))
        (x64_orpd
          (x64_andnpd sign_bit a)
          (x64_andpd sign_bit b))))

ground_truth.root_cause: The ISLE `fcopysign` lowering rules for x64 do not materialize operands into registers before using them in vector AND operations. Cranelift's generic load-sinking optimization then folds a scalar load directly into the ANDPD/ANDPS instruction's memory operand slot. Because those instructions have no scalar (64-bit or 32-bit) memory form — only 128-bit — the result is an unintended 128-bit memory read, reading 8 extra bytes beyond the intended load boundary.

pr_title: x64: Lower fcopysign, ceil, floor, nearest, and trunc in ISLE (#4730)

agent_reasoning: The bug is in the ISLE rule for `f64x2.splat` fallback (no SSE3): `(rule 0 (lower (has_type $F64X2 (splat src))) (x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00))`. By passing `src` directly, Cranelift's load-sinking can fold an f64.load into the pshufd memory operand. Since pshufd reads 128 bits (16 bytes) but the original load is only 64 bits (8 bytes), this causes an out-of-bounds read of up to 8 extra bytes past the intended address. The fix wraps `src` with `(put_in_xmm src)`, which forces the value into an XMM register first, blocking load-sinking and ensuring pshufd only ever uses a register operand in this path.
commit_message:
[Merged] x64: Avoid using `movddup` without SSSE3 (#6496)

* x64: Avoid using `movddup` without SSSE3

Update the lowerings for 64-bit splats to use `pshufd` instead, as LLVM
does.

* Disable runtest for now

fix_commit_message:
x64: Fix `f64x2.splat` without SSE3 (#13011)

Don't sink a load into `pshufd` which loads 16 bytes, instead force
`put_in_xmm` to ensure only 8 bytes are loaded.

intro_commit_message:
x64: Avoid using `movddup` without SSSE3 (#6496)

* x64: Avoid using `movddup` without SSSE3

Update the lowerings for 64-bit splats to use `pshufd` instead, as LLVM
does.

* Disable runtest for now
pr_description:
When lowering `f64x2.splat` on x86-64 without SSE3, the fallback rule uses `pshufd` to broadcast the lower 64-bit lane to the upper lane. Previously, the source value was passed directly to `x64_pshufd`, which allowed Cranelift's load-sinking mechanism to fold a sinkable `f64.load` directly into the `pshufd` memory operand.

The problem is that `pshufd` is a 128-bit instruction and always reads 16 bytes from memory, but an `f64.load` only intends to read 8 bytes. Sinking the load into `pshufd` therefore causes an over-read of 8 extra bytes beyond the intended load address.

This change wraps the source operand with `put_in_xmm`, which forces the value to be materialized into an XMM register before being passed to `pshufd`. This prevents load-sinking from folding the 8-byte load into the 16-byte `pshufd` memory operand, ensuring the instruction only ever reads from an XMM register operand (not memory) in the non-SSE3 fallback path.

The SSE3 path (`movddup`) is unaffected — it is a 64-bit load-and-broadcast instruction and correctly reads only 8 bytes.
pr_title: x64: Fix `f64x2.splat` load sinking into `pshufd`

location.snippet:
(rule 0 (lower (has_type $F64X2 (splat src)))
        (x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00))

findings.message: In the ISLE lowering for `f64x2.splat` on x86-64 without SSE3, the rule passes `src` directly to `x64_pshufd`. Cranelift's load-sinking mechanism can sink a sinkable memory load into the `pshufd` instruction operand. However, `pshufd` always reads 128 bits (16 bytes) from memory, whereas the original `f64.load` only reads 64 bits (8 bytes). This means the lowering reads up to 8 extra bytes past the intended load address. Depending on Wasmtime configuration: (1) with guard pages disabled, out-of-sandbox data is read into the upper bits of an XMM register (data not visible to WebAssembly but still an unintended read); (2) with guard pages enabled and signals-based-traps enabled, the widened load hits a guard page causing a segfault caught as a WebAssembly trap (incorrect behavior but not a security issue); (3) with guard pages enabled and signals-based-traps disabled, the segfault is uncaught and terminates the host process (DoS).
findings.suggestion: Force the source operand into an XMM register via `put_in_xmm` before passing it to `x64_pshufd`. This prevents Cranelift's load-sinking from widening the load from 8 bytes to 16 bytes. The fix is to change `(x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00)` to `(x64_pshufd (put_in_xmm src) 0b01_00_01_00)`.
findings.suggestion_code:
(rule 0 (lower (has_type $F64X2 (splat src)))
        (x64_pshufd (put_in_xmm src) 0b01_00_01_00))
findings.title: f64x2.splat ISLE rule sinks load into `pshufd` causing 16-byte read instead of 8-byte

ground_truth.root_cause: The ISLE rule `(rule 0 (lower (has_type $F64X2 (splat src))) (x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00))` was introduced in commit 8c530771 as a fallback for `movddup` (SSE3) on processors without SSE3 support. By passing `src` directly (rather than via `put_in_xmm`), the rule allows Cranelift's load-sinking to fold a `f64.load` into the `pshufd` memory operand. The `pshufd` instruction, however, is a 128-bit instruction and always reads 16 bytes from memory—twice as many bytes as intended for an 8-byte float load. The sinkable-load specialization rule (rule 5/6) for this case uses `movddup` gated on `has_sse3`/`use_ssse3`, but on SSE3-less hosts the rule 0 fallback takes effect without any guard preventing load sinking.

Vulnerability (LogicError): After PR #11254 updated the `table_fill_func_ref` and `table_fill_gc_ref` libcall intrinsics to accept a `DefinedTableIndex` (the index into only defined/non-imported tables), the corresponding Winch code path in `visit_table_fill` was not updated. Root cause: PR #11254 changed the calling convention of `table_fill_func_ref` and `table_fill_gc_ref` libcalls from `TableIndex` to `DefinedTableIndex` in both Cranelift codegen and the runtime libcall implementations, but the corresponding Winch code path (`visit_table_fill` in `winch/codegen/src/visitor.rs`) was not updated. The existing helper `prepare_builtin_defined_table_arg` already existed and was used for other table instructions (e.g., `table_grow`), but was overlooked for `table.fill`.

findings.message: After PR #11254 updated the `table_fill_func_ref` and `table_fill_gc_ref` libcall intrinsics to accept a `DefinedTableIndex` (the index into only defined/non-imported tables), the corresponding Winch code path in `visit_table_fill` was not updated. Winch continued to insert the raw `table` u32 value (a module-level `TableIndex`) directly onto the argument stack. When a wasm module contains imported tables, `TableIndex` and `DefinedTableIndex` occupy different index spaces. Passing a module-level index where a defined-table index is expected causes `get_defined_table` to access an out-of-bounds slot, triggering a host panic. Additionally, even without an out-of-bounds access, the mismatch can silently operate on the wrong table.
findings.suggestion: Replace direct insertion of the raw `table` u32 with a call to `prepare_builtin_defined_table_arg(table_index, at, builtin)`, which correctly converts the module-level `TableIndex` to a `DefinedTableIndex` (and resolves the owning vmctx for imported tables), consistent with how `visit_table_grow` and `visit_table_size` handle this.

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability arises from calling `shift_masked_imm ty n` with the memory-access type (`ty`) rather than the type of the `ishl` expression. When these types differ in bit-width (e.g., load type is i32 but the index shift is i64), the masking is wrong. For instance, shift amount 34 with load type i32 gives `34 & 31 = 2`, satisfying the `4 == 1 << 2` guard and causing the code generator to emit an AArch64 `RegScaled` instruction with LSL #2. But the correct CLIF semantics perform a 34-bit shift, which should not be folded into a RegScaled addressing mode at all. With a carefully chosen index value (e.g., 2^30), this produces an out-of-bounds memory access that bypasses sandbox bounds checks — a sandbox escape. The fix captures the `ishl` type as `shift_ty` and passes it to `shift_masked_imm`, ensuring the guard uses the correct bit-width mask.

intro_commit_message:
aarch64: Fix an overflowing shift panic (#10382)

Ensure that a compile-time-shift-amount is masked to avoid a debug
assertion about an overflowing shift.

Closes #10373
pr_description:
When folding an `iadd` + `ishl` pair into a `RegScaled` addressing mode on AArch64, the shift amount must be validated against the type of the `ishl` instruction — not the type of the surrounding memory access (load/store).

Previously, `shift_masked_imm` was called with `ty` (the load/store type), which caused incorrect shift-amount masking when the index shift type differs from the access type. For example, with a `load.i32` and an `ishl.i64` by 34, the old code computed `shift_masked_imm(I32, 34) = 34 & 31 = 2`, making the guard condition `4 == 1 << 2` pass. This erroneously generates a `RegScaled` addressing mode with LSL #2, while the correct CLIF semantics call for a shift of 34 — which should not fold at all.

This PR introduces `shift_ty` as a type binding on the `ishl` pattern in rules 6 and 7, so that `shift_masked_imm shift_ty n` uses the actual type of the shift operand. The guard then correctly computes `shift_masked_imm(I64, 34) = 34`, making the condition `4 == 1 << 34` (false), preventing the invalid fold.

findings.message: In `amode_no_more_iconst` rules 6 and 7 (ISLE lowering for AArch64 address-mode selection), the condition `(if-let true (u64_eq (ty_bytes ty) (u64_shl 1 (shift_masked_imm ty n))))` calls `shift_masked_imm` with `ty` — the type of the memory access (load/store) — rather than the type of the `ishl` value `y`. The `shift_masked_imm` function masks the shift amount `n` to the bit-width of the provided type (e.g., `n & 31` for i32, `n & 63` for i64). When `ty` (the load type, e.g. i32) has fewer bits than the shift operand's type (e.g. i64 for 64-bit WebAssembly memory indices), the mask is incorrect. For example, with load type i32 and shift-value type i64, `n = 34` produces `shift_masked_imm(i32, 34) = 34 & 31 = 2`, making the condition `4 == 1 << 2 = 4` pass. This erroneously generates a `RegScaled` addressing mode with shift 2, whereas the correct CLIF semantics of `ishl.i64 index 34` are a shift of 34. When `index = 2^30`, the CLIF semantics compute `index << 34 = 2^64 ≡ 0 (mod 2^64)`, so the explicit bounds check sees address = base + 0 (passes). But the emitted `LDR [base, index, LSL #2]` instruction computes `base + index * 4 = base + 4 GB`, escaping the sandbox.
findings.suggestion: Capture the type of the `ishl` operand `y` explicitly (as `shift_ty` via `@ (value_type shift_ty)`), then pass `shift_ty` — not `ty` — to `shift_masked_imm`. This ensures the shift amount is masked according to the shift value's bit-width (the correct WebAssembly/Cranelift semantics for ishl) rather than the load's type width. Also change `u64_shl` to `u64_wrapping_shl` to avoid overflow.

        (amode_reg_scaled (amode_add x offset) y))

ground_truth.root_cause: Commit ba1e663bac ('aarch64: Fix an overflowing shift panic') introduced `shift_masked_imm ty n` in rules 6 and 7 to mask the shift amount before comparing it to `log2(ty_bytes)`. However, `ty` here is the type of the memory access (load/store), whereas the shift amount's effective mask must come from the type of the `ishl` value (the index register). When these two types differ in bit-width — as is common in 64-bit WebAssembly where the memory index is i64 but the loaded element size gives a smaller `ty` like i32 — the wrong mask enables false matches: e.g., `shift_masked_imm(i32, 34) = 2` makes the check `4 == 1 << 2` pass, but the correct `shift_masked_imm(i64, 34) = 34` would give `4 == 1 << 34` (false). The generated RegScaled AArch64 instruction then encodes the shift as `log2(ty_bytes) = 2`, diverging from the CLIF-level shift of 34.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix b8d5dc7430eb on top of intro 0c673b703282 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): The `StringPool` struct uses an unsafe lifetime transmutation to store `&'static str` keys in its `map` field that actually point into the memory owned by its own `strings` field. The `TryClone` implementation naively clones both fields independently: `self.map.try_clone()` copies the HashMap, which copies those raw `&'static str` keys (still pointing at the ORIGINAL pool's string allocation), while `self.strings.try_clone()` allocates a fresh, separate copy of the string data. The resulting clone therefore holds a `map` whose keys dangle into the original pool's allocation. Once the original `StringPool` (and thus the original `wasmtime::Linker`) is dropped and its `strings` are deallocated, any lookup through the clone's map accesses freed memory — a classic use-after-free. The fix re-interns every string through the new pool's `insert()` so the cloned map's keys point into the clone's own `strings` allocation. Root cause: The `StringPool` struct deliberately uses `unsafe { mem::transmute::<&str, &'static str>(...) }` to launder borrows of its own `strings` field so they can serve as HashMap keys. This internal invariant — that the 'static keys are actually self-referential borrows — is invisible to the derived/generic `TryClone` machinery. Cloning the map field copies these raw pointers as-is, without relocating them to point into the new clone's storage, breaking the invariant in the copy.

fix(environ): repair unsound StringPool::try_clone() (#12906)

* fix(environ): repair unsound StringPool::try_clone()

The 43.0 release introduced a soundness bug in StringPool::try_clone(): the
cloned map retains &'static str keys pointing into the original pool's
strings storage. Once the original Linker is dropped those keys dangle.

Cloning a Linker, then dropping the original one, leaves a linker whose
registered imports could no longer be found, causing instantiation to
fail with "unknown import".

agent_reasoning: The buggy code used `ty.can_elide_bounds_check(tunables, host_page_size_log2)` to decide whether to call `set_protection` when shrinking an accessible region back to its initial size. This predicate is too conservative: when `memory_guard_size == 0` and `memory_reservation < 4GiB` with `max_memory_size == memory_reservation`, `can_use_virtual_memory` returns true (the compiler assumes virtual-memory semantics) but `can_elide_bounds_check` returns false. Fix pooling allocator predicate to reset VM permissions (#13008)

* Fix pooling allocator predicate to reset VM permissions

This commit fixes a mistake that was introduced in #9583 where the logic
to reset a linear memory slot in the pooling allocator used the wrong
predicate. Specifically VM permissions must be reset if virtual memory
can be relied on at all, and the preexisting predicate of
`can_elide_bounds_check` was an inaccurate representation of this. The
correct predicate to check is `can_use_virtual_memory`.

* Fix failure on 32-bit

pr_description:
When the pooling allocator resets a linear memory slot for reuse, it must revoke memory protections on any pages that were accessible beyond the initial size. The condition guarding `set_protection` previously checked `ty.can_elide_bounds_check(tunables, host_page_size_log2)` as the fallback predicate, but this is too conservative: it returns `false` when there are no guard pages even if the memory reservation is large enough for the compiler to assume virtual-memory semantics for out-of-bounds accesses.

The correct predicate is `ty.can_use_virtual_memory(tunables, host_page_size_log2)`, which returns `true` whenever the compiler relies on virtual-memory semantics regardless of guard-page size. Using this predicate ensures that previously mapped pages are always de-protected before a new Wasm instance is placed into the slot, regardless of the specific combination of `memory_guard_size`, `memory_reservation`, and `max_memory_size` tunables in effect.

This change affects `MemoryImageSlot::assign_init_image` in `crates/wasmtime/src/runtime/vm/cow.rs`.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix db7fb47b8e14 on top of intro bb5e4bbaf9a6 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): Wasmtime's Winch baseline (single-pass) compiler computes an `OperandSize` for each kind of Wasm load via `LoadKind::derive_operand_size()`. This size is used both to emit the machine-code load and, critically, to perform/encode the linear-memory bounds/guard check for the access. The January 2025 `wasm_load` simplification refactor (PR #10012) introduced `operand_size_for_vector()`, which derived a size of 1, 2, or 4 bytes for the SIMD 'vector extend' load variants (`v128.load8x8_{s,u}`, `v128.load16x4_{s,u}`, `v128.load32x2_{s,u}`) based on the *source lane width* rather than the *total bytes actually read*. All of these instructions read a full 8 bytes (64 bits) of linear memory and widen each lane, so the derived size undercounted the real access footprint by a factor of 2x-8x. PR #10127 fixed this by hard-coding `OperandSize::S64` for all `VectorExtendKind` variants. commit_message:
winch: Simplify the handling of `wasm_load`s (#10012)

This commit aims to simplify how `wasm_load`s are currently handled in
the compiler by reducing the number of invariants that need to be
encoded at callsites which make their emission error prone.

Concretely this change:

* Augments `ExtendKind`, to account for unsigned extends; prior to this
  commit it wasn't explicit which loads required unsigned extends.
* Derive `OperandSize` from `ExtendKind`, removing from the caller the
  responsibility of encoding the operand size to use.

findings.message: The Winch baseline compiler's `LoadKind::derive_operand_size()` computes the `OperandSize` that is passed down into `wasm_load`/`load_impl` to perform the Wasm linear-memory bounds check and emit the actual load instruction. For `LoadKind::VectorExtend(vector)` (used for v128 `load8x8`/`load16x4`/`load32x2` sign/zero-extending SIMD loads), this commit routes the size through the newly added `operand_size_for_vector()` helper, which maps V128Extend8x8{S,U} -> OperandSize::S8, V128Extend16x4{S,U} -> OperandSize::S16, and V128Extend32x2{S,U} -> OperandSize::S32. However, all of these Wasm vector-extend-load instructions actually read 8 bytes (64 bits) from linear memory before widening into 8/16/32-bit lanes of a v128 — e.g. `v128.load32x2_s` reads two 32-bit lanes (8 bytes total), not 4. Because the derived (too-small) OperandSize is what callers use both to size the actual memory access and to validate/bound the access against the heap/guard region, the bounds check and the code emitted for the load are checking/loading fewer bytes (1, 2, or 4) than are truly read (8), allowing the load to read up to 4-7 bytes past the validated/intended bound of linear memory for addresses near the end of the accessible region.
findings.suggestion: Derive the operand size for all `VectorExtendKind` variants as 64 bits (`OperandSize::S64`), since every v128 extend-load (load8x8/load16x4/load32x2, signed or unsigned) reads a full 8-byte quantity from linear memory regardless of the resulting narrow lane width. Remove the per-variant 8/16/32-bit mapping in `operand_size_for_vector` (or delete the helper entirely) and have `derive_operand_size` return `OperandSize::S64` directly for `Self::VectorExtend(_)`, matching how the actual load/bounds-check size is computed.
findings.suggestion_code: Self::VectorExtend(_) => OperandSize::S64,
findings.title: Winch derives undersized bounds-check operand size for SIMD vector-extend loads

agent_reasoning: The intro commit added logic to capture the spawned task's error when the oneshot receiver signals a disconnect, using `task.await` and `.expect_err("if the receiver has an error, the task must have failed")`. This conflates two independent signals: the receiver erroring (sender dropped) and the task's own result being an `Err`. A guest component whose `handle` export returns `Ok(())` without ever calling `response-outparam::set` causes the sender to be dropped (so the receiver errors) while the task itself resolves to `Ok(())` — violating the assumption and causing `.expect_err` to panic, crashing the `wasmtime serve` process (a remotely triggerable DoS via a malicious or buggy guest component). The fix replaces the panicking `expect_err` with an explicit three-way match on the task's `Result` (`Ok(Ok(()))`, `Ok(Err(e))`, `Err(e)`), handling the "never called set but didn't error" case gracefully by reporting an error instead of panicking, and returns the error with added context instead of panicking.

findings.message: In `handle_request` in `src/commands/serve.rs`, when the `receiver` oneshot channel errors out (meaning the response-outparam `set` method was never invoked by the guest), the code awaits the spawned task and calls `.expect_err("if the receiver has an error, the task must have failed")` on its result. This assumes that if the guest never called `set`, the task must have returned an `Err`. However, a guest Wasm component can legitimately return `Ok(())` from its `handle` export without ever invoking `response-outparam::set` (e.g. it simply forgets to call it, or returns early without error). In that case `task.await` yields `Ok(Ok(()))`, so `r` is `Ok(())`, and `Result::expect_err` panics because the value is not an `Err`. Since this path is driven directly by externally-supplied/untrusted Wasm guest code processing an HTTP request in the `wasmtime serve` CLI command, any malicious or buggy guest component can deterministically crash the host process serving HTTP traffic, resulting in a remotely triggerable denial of service.
findings.suggestion: Do not assume the task must have returned an error when the receiver fails. Instead, explicitly handle the `Ok(Ok(()))` case (task completed successfully but never invoked `set`) by producing a dedicated error/bail instead of calling `.expect_err()`, which panics on that input. The actual fix (commit ad21d9581d) matches on `task.await` as `Ok(Ok(())) => bail!(...)`, `Ok(Err(e)) => e`, `Err(e) => e.into()`, avoiding the panicking `expect_err` call entirely.
findings.title: Reachable panic via `.expect_err()` when guest handler returns Ok without calling response-outparam::set

The code assumed these always correlate (receiver error implies task error) and used a panicking `expect_err` to extract the task's error, without accounting for the case where the guest task completes with `Ok(())` yet never calls `set`.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 04eee2182605 on top of intro 0a29578f1095 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): When compiling allocation of a wasm GC `array` type whose element type is itself a GC reference (e.g. `(array (mut (ref null $other)))`), the DRC (deferred reference counting) GC compiler mis-computed the 'number of GC references' field stored in the object's common GC header. Instead of storing the element count (length) of the array, it stored the array's total allocation size in bytes (`base_size + len * elem_size`), reusing the `size` ir::Value that was meant only for the allocation-size argument to the raw allocator. Root cause: The commit that introduced transitive dec-ref tracing in the DRC collector (#10401) added a new `num_gc_refs` header field used to bound the slice of outgoing GC edges traced during collection. For arrays of GC-ref elements, the author intended to pass the array length but accidentally reused the `size` local (the array's byte size in memory, computed by `emit_array_size`), since both were available in scope and the mistake (size vs. len) was an easy one given they are used adjacently. There was no type-level distinction between a 'byte size' ir::Value and an 'element count' ir::Value, so the compiler could not catch the mismatch.
commit_message:
Transitively dec-ref objects in the DRC collector (#10401)

* Transitively dec-ref objects in the DRC collector

Previously, the DRC collector only performed shallow reference counting where if
an object's ref count was decremented and reached zero, then we would deallocate
that object, but we would not decrement the reference counts of any other object
that was referenced by it. This commit changes that, so that now we will
decrement the reference counts of other objects referenced by an object that is
being deallocated.

This requires some method of tracing an object's outgoing edges. To avoid
needing to keep around and dispatch upon type-specific information about which
struct fields are GC references, for example, we instead pack all GC references
at the start of the object, just after its header. We additionally keep a count
of how many GC references an object has in its header. This allows us to create
a slice of any object's GC references, and we can uniformly trace any GC
object's outgoing edges. We don't need to reflect on the GC object's actual
type.

A final detail: the DRC collector was previously storing the object size in the
common GC header's reserved bits. It now stores the number of GC refs there
instead, and the object size is stored in its own field in the DRC-specific
header, next to the ref count. This is nice because, since we are making the DRC
header larger anyways, it raises the DRC collector's implementation limit on
object size from `u27::MAX` to `u32::MAX`.

Fixes #9701

* update disas tests

* Remove newly-added debug-assert that isn't true in certain edge cases

Sometimes we need to deallocate uninitialized objects when initializing their
fields fails, and this assertion trips.

* fix some tests by returning an error of the correct kind of trap

rather than a generic anyhow error

* fix tracing GC refs on big-endian architectures

We can't cast to a slice, we need to do conversion from little-endian bytes.

findings.message: In `DrcCompiler::alloc_array` (crates/cranelift/src/gc/enabled/drc.rs), when allocating a `(array (ref ...))` whose elements are themselves GC references, the code computes `num_gc_refs` by reusing the `size` value returned from `emit_array_size`, which is the array's *total byte size* (base header size + len*elem_size), not the *count* of GC-reference elements. This `num_gc_refs` value is packed into the object's GC header (via `emit_gc_raw_alloc` -> `kind_and_reserved = kind | num_gc_refs`) and is later used by the DRC collector's tracing code to compute a slice of the object's outgoing GC-reference edges (count of `VMGcRef`-sized slots immediately following the header). Because `size` is numerically much larger than the true number of elements (and is a byte count rather than an element count), the collector believes the array has far more outgoing GC edges than it actually does. When tracing/dec-refing the array during collection, the GC walks past the end of the actual reference slots and off the end of the object/heap, reading and dec-refing arbitrary heap memory as if it were `VMGcRef` values. This is a heap buffer over-read (and consequent corruption of unrelated heap data via spurious ref-count decrements/frees) triggered simply by creating and then collecting a guest array-of-GC-refs value.
findings.suggestion: Use the array's element length (not its total byte size) when computing `num_gc_refs` for arrays whose elements are GC references. Refactor `emit_array_size` to take the already-computed `len` value instead of the `ArrayInit` (so the length can be reused), compute `len` once via `init.len(...)`, pass it into `emit_array_size`, and set `num_gc_refs = len` (the element count) instead of `num_gc_refs = size` (the byte size) when `array_layout.elems_are_gc_refs` is true.
findings.title: GC array of GC-refs reports byte size instead of element count as num_gc_refs
